prompt: Which of the following regarding benign intracranial hypertension and sagittal sinus thrombosis is INCORRECT? Select ONE answer only.
options: Bilateral haemorrhages in sagittal sinus thrombosis occur as a result of venous infarction
Empty sella syndrome is a feature of benign intracranial hypertension
Papilloedema can be seen in both conditions
Prominence of the temporal horns occurs due to decreased CSF absorption in sagittal sinus thrombosis
Ventricular bleeds are commonly seen in benign intracranial hypertension
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which answer is INCORRECT.

Benign intracranial hypertension - (idiopathic intracranial hypertension)

This condition can easily be overlooked but causes significant morbidity for patients if undiagnosed. Increased intracranial pressure of the CSF on the surrounding brain causes:

Flattening of the posterior aspect of the globe

Tortuosity of the optic nerves

Empty sella syndrome (or partially so)

Small, 'pinched' lateral ventricles (slit-like appearance is a relatively rare, poor sign to rely on).

Sagittal sinus thrombosis

In sagittal sinus thrombosis the development of cerebral oedema secondary to infarction can compress the lateral ventricles, a finding in approximately a third of cases.

In contrast to this, prominent temporal horns, suggestive of developing hydrocephalus can be seen in sagittal sinus thrombosis due to decreased CSF absorption.

Ventricular bleeds might be seen in sagittal sinus thrombosis in the neonatal age group.

Bilateral haemorrhages in the context of sagittal sinus thrombosis are caused by venous infarction.

Papilloedema can be seen with both sagittal sinus thrombosis and idiopathic intracranial hypertension but is not an imaging feature.

prompt: NextWhich of the following is LEAST consistent with a spinal cord infarction? Select ONE answer only.
options: High T2 signal in the adjacent vertebral body
Inverted-V shape of high T2 signal in the posterior columns
High T2 signal extending over three vertebral levels
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which is LEAST consistent with a spinal cord infarction.

Spinal cord infarction

The vascular supply to the spinal cord is derived largely from the vertebral arteries or intercostal arteries with one longitudinal running anterior spinal cord artery and two small longitudinally running posterior spinal cord arteries.

The artery of Adamkiewicz is a particularly large segmental artery supplying the anterior spinal artery from around the level of T9. It is responsible for most of the spinal cord blood supply for the lumbar spinal cord. Damage during aortic surgery or trauma can result in spinal cord infarction.

Usually any vascular insult results in a reasonably rapid onset of symptoms. Spinal cord infarctions are no exception. Often more than one vertebral level is affected.

An MRI will showT2 hyperintensity of at least the central grey matter (if not the whole cross-section of the cord) due to oedema. As with intracranial infarctions there will be restriction of diffusion on the DWI sequences.

Particularly in the thoracic spine, the adjacent vertebral body may also lose its blood supply and undergo infarction.

Subacute combined degeneration

This is a curious condition which can be subtle to detect. A deficiency of vitamin B12 (usually caused by malabsorption) leads to degeneration within the dorsal columns of the cord. The dorsal columns carry nerves responsible for position and vibration sense and as such patients present with loss of these senses as well as sensory ataxia (balance significantly deteriorates when the patient’s eyes are shut thereby excluding visual stabilisation as opposed to sensory stabilisation), and hyperreflexia.

On an MRI scan there will be (if the resolution allows), a longitudinal line of high T2 signal within the cord on sagittal sequences, and often a characteristic 'inverted-V' shape of high T2 signal on axial sequences. In some cases, the 'V' is clearly seen and in others it is harder to appreciate and the finding is more of high T2 signal bilaterally and symmetrically in the region of the posterior columns.

Bilateral white matter involvement

Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease

There are three types of this prion transmitted disease; the one linked to the BSE (bovine spongiform encephalopathy) epidemic of the late 1980s and 1990s, a rare familial variant, and finally a sporadic version which accounts for the vast majority of the cases. prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The main differential for a nasal mass is as follows:

Sinonasal (non-Hodgkin) lymphoma

This most commonly affects older people (60s and older). It is commonly seen in the nasal cavity rather than the sinuses. There will be a homogenous mass with bony destruction which returns low signal on T2 weighted sequences.

By contrast, the lymph nodes of a patient with Hodgkin lymphoma usually return high signal on T2 weighted sequences. These patients are typically younger, in their 20-40s.

Squamous cell carcinoma

This is the most common malignancy of sinonasal track. The maxillary antrum is involved in 80% of cases. It is often seen as an aggressive antral soft tissue mass, which is low in signal on T2.

Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma

This affects 'exclusively' adolescent male patients. There will be dark flow voids on T1 weighted sequences and the mass will be brightly enhancing. Radiation therapy treats this in 80% of cases, and interventional radiological embolisation can be used to treat haemorrhagic complications at presentation if required.

Esthesioneuroblastoma

This tumour has a bimodal distribution, affecting people in their 20s and 60s. There is a dumbbell shaped tumour with waist at the cribriform plate. The mass will brightly enhance.

Antrochoanal polyp

This occurs in young adults with obstructive nasal symptoms. They arise from the maxillary sinuses and causes widening of the maxillary ostium.

The information provided in this vignette is confusing since once calcified, the lesions usually do not demonstrate perilesional oedema (low attenuation). However, the presence of soft tissue calcification around the pelvis region suggests that this is the diagnosis being alluded to.

Neurocysticercosis

Cysticercosis is caused by a tapeworm native to low income countries and carried by pigs. It is the most common parasitic infection involving the central nervous system and the central nervous system is itself commonly affected during the disease process; around 90% of cases show CNS involvement. The larva disseminate via the suparachnoid and intraventricular system and consequentially the meninges are most frequently affected, being involved in around 40% of cases, with particular involvement of the basal cisterns. Parenchymal involvement occurs in around a fifth of cases. The larval cells (termed cysticerci) also migrate to large skeletal muscle and, following destruction, become calcified and visible on plain radiographs as 'rice-grain' calcification. The long axis of the foci of calcification is usually orientated along the muscle fibres in which they are situated.

Parasitic stage

Features

Larval

Small foci of oedema

Vesicular

Small CSF cysts without surrounding oedema but containing a 2-3mm mural nodule (cyst with a dot)

Colloidal vesicular

Ring enhancing cyst with proteinaceous content. The contents never enhance, being derived from the tapeworm, not the host human.

Focal seizures

Nodular granular stage

Cyst shrinks and becomes isointense to brain on T1, hypointense on T2

Calcified stage

Small focal calcifications appearing 1-10years following acute infection

Rice-like muscle calcification

Seizures or asymptomatic

Cavernoma

The classical feature of a cavernoma (aka cavernous haemangioma) on MRI is the ‘popcorn’ appearance caused by a bright lobulated centre surrounded by a rim of hypointensity. Haemosiderin deposition causes the blooming artefact on susceptibility weighted sequences.  It is perhaps slightly counterintuitive that there can be no enhancement on post-contrast CT scans, given the vascular nature of these lesions, however when we consider that flow within the lesion may be very slow then this makes a little more sense. Another important distinguishing feature from other lesions is the fact that, unlike metastases, there is no mass effect or oedema from these lesions, despite the fact that they can often present with seizures. Associated cutaneous manifestations of multiple cavernomas include cafe au lait spots and cherry angiomas, neither of which calcify.

Neurofibromatosis

Type 2 neurofibromatosis (MISME) is characterised by multiple meningiomas, schwannomas and ependymomas. In theory multiple calcified meningiomas each with a rim of surrounding oedema could be present. Neurofibromatosis is also in the differential diagnosis for soft tissue calcification though this relates to curvilinear calcifications related to plexiform neurofibromas (ie type 1 neurofibromatosis).

Osteosarcoma metastases

Osteosarcoma can cause soft tissue calcification, and within the lungs is a classic cause for calcified lung metastases however brain metastases (from all causes) rarely calcify. In the few cases reported in the literature the calcification is more globular than peripheral/rim calcification.

Dermatomyositis

This is a classic cause of soft tissue calcification with striking 'sheets' of calcification occurring in severe cases. Intracranial calcification is not a feature however.

prompt: What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
CADASIL (Cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy). The usual patient is a youngish adult (30-50s) with recurrent TIAs/strokes, seizures, and/or psychiatric symptoms such as depression, psychosis. The classical area affected is the anterior temporal lobes and external capsules.

Moyamoya disease is a unilateral progressive occlusion/arteritis of the distal ICA causing the formation of a large network of tiny collateral vessels seen on angiogram as a ‘puff of smoke’. It is predominantly found in children or young adults.

SLE

The brain parenchyma is not often involved (with the exception of haemorrhage or abscess formation), although neuropsychiatric symptoms do occur.

Wilson disease

Wilson disease is a disorder of copper metabolism. It causes white matter atrophy and T2 hyperintensities predominantly affecting the basal ganglia and thalami. It is not an unreasonable differential diagnosis here but does not usually present as seizures and the extent of the white matter signal changes is slightly atypical for Wilson disease.

Huntington disease

There are relatively few radiological manifestations of Huntington disease. The usual one described is atrophy of the heads of the caudate nuclei with consequential prominence of the adjacent lateral ventricle frontal horns with a ‘box’ like appearance. Various studies have been done to quantify the extent of this atrophy.

explanation:
The limbic system

The limbic system is a complex network of connections between a number of important different regions of the brain. It has roles in emotion, learning, memory, affective disorders and some dementias to name but a few.

Components of the limbic system:

Cortical structures

The olfactory cortex

Parahippocampal gyrus

Hippocampus

Cingulate gyrus

Subcallosal gyrus

Subcortical structures

Amygdala

Septum pellucidum

Hypothalamus

Anterior thalamic nuclei

Mamillary bodies

Two structures bear particular importance in the imaging of dementia; the precuneus and the cingulate gyrus. Both are best appreciated on sagittal views.

Precuneus: The precuneus is located on the medial surface of each hemisphere, in the posterior parietal lobe. It has functions in motor planning, working memory and also connections to the visual pathways.

The cingulate gyrus: The cinculate gyrus is also located on the medial side of each hemisphere and runs anteroposteriorly just above the corpus callosum. The cingulate gyrus has complex functions to do with learning, emotional response and memory.

explanation:
For a detailed explanation of DWI please use a more robust text than what follows. Readers should be warned that this is a very light glossing over of the concepts only.

Diffusion weighted imaging is the summation of both diffusion and T2 effects. The images must be interpreted in the light of findings on the corresponding ADC map which gives diffusion effects only. The more ‘unrestricted’ the water molecules in a given substance are, the more diffusion takes place during the slice acquisition and the faster the dephasing of the magnetism. There are multiple ADC maps with increasing B-values to see how this dephasing responds. Usually you can pick out a DWI image because the CSF is black (aide memoire ‘Dark Water Imaging’). Restriction causes high signal on DWI sequences.

Restriction of diffusion is a binary entity – things either restrict or they do not. The things that restrict diffusion are relatively limited in number and you would be well advised to learn them thoroughly for day to day practice as well as for the exams.

Cytotoxic oedema – failure of the cellular membrane ion pumps leads to an increase in intracellular (restricted) water

Acute infarction - In the early days, as a stroke ages the DWI increases due to the T2 effect and the ADC becomes less bright through shine through. At approximately weeks 1-4 the ADC undergoes pseudonormalisation where restricted diffusion is matched by vasogenic oedema which is not restricted. Chronic infarctions do not restrict diffusion.

Hypercellularity – Limiting the ability of extracellular water to diffuse

Some gliomas

Lymphoma

High viscosity

Abscess

Acute demyelination – a complex mechanism involving glutamate

ADEM

Acute MS

Epidermoid cysts (technically due to waxy content as opposed to protein)

prompt: In which space is the lesion most likely to be?
explanation:
Head and neck anatomy is all about the parapharyngeal space and its relationships. The parapharyngeal space is a small and unobtrusive space itself containing only fat, some branches of the trigeminal nerve and a few vessels but is sat right in the middle of the soft tissues of the neck on each side and as a result gets pushed about when the surrounding spaces are invaded. It is therefore the head and neck radiologist’s best friend.

Huntington disease

There are relatively few radiological manifestations of Huntington disease. The usual one described is atrophy of the heads of the caudate nuclei with consequential prominence of the adjacent lateral ventricle frontal horns with a ‘box’ like appearance. Various studies have been done to quantify the extent of this atrophy.

Parkinson's disease

Generalised cerebral atrophy occurs with Parkinson's disease but is a highly non-specific feature. There are, however, radiological findings in the midbrain which although subtle, are far more specific. Parkinson's disease occurs when there is neuronal loss in the substantia nigra, specifically the pars compacta of the substantia nigra. On a T2 weighted MRI image this appears as blurring of the intermediate signal intensity line which separates the two adjacent low intensity structures (these are the pars reticulata of the substantia nigra and the red nucleus).

A DAT scan (Dopamine Active Transfer) can be performed to confirm the diagnosis. This uses the radiopharmaceutical I-123 Ioflupane to image dopamine transporters in the brain. These are present in the highest concentrations in the putamina and caudate nuclei. In patients with true Parkinson's disease (as opposed to other similar conditions), there will be loss of uptake in the posterior putamen. This can be an asymmetric finding. Colloquially speaking the appearance of a these areas on a normal patient resembles a comma and on a patient with Parkinson's disease they become more like full stops.

Wilson disease

Wilson disease is a disorder of copper metabolism. It causes white matter atrophy and T2 hyperintensities predominantly affecting the basal ganglia and thalami.

prompt: What is the most likely type of malignancy?
explanation:
Calcification within lymph node metastases of thyroid cancer can occur with both medullary and papillary thyroid cancer although is more common with papillary thyroid cancer. When performing an USS of a lymph node in the context of a thryoid malignancy it is challenging to determine if there is metastatic involvement or not. The presence of calciifcaiton should raise the suspicion of involvement however this is not always present. The loss of normal hilar morphology is a more reliable sign as node becomes taken over by tumour cells and the lymph node hilum becomes destroyed.

Medullary

Medullary thryoid cancer is associated with MEN II syndrome. Calcification within the tumour is a common feature. Spread to adjacent lymph nodes is common and may show calcification. This cancer does not respond to I-131.

Follicular

Calcification is not a feature which would typically be seen with follicular thyroid cancer. The tumour can take up pertechnate but not simple radio-iodine. Cytology alone does not differentiate benign from malignant and frozen section analysis must be performed to make the diagnosis. This cancer most commonly spreads via the haaematogenous route.

Anaplastic

This cancer usually arises in ederly patients or those who have had radiation therapy. It grows rapidly and aggressively with lymphatic spread.

Papillary

This is the most common subtype of thyroid cancer. Microcalcification and cystic components are common.

Lymphoma

This usually affects older patients and can have a variety of appearances. It is usually nodular and diffuse, and rarely appears cystic.

explanation:
Tullio phenomenon – this refers to vertigo and nystagmus induced by loud noises. It is caused by superior semicircular canal dehiscence which is best demonstrated on coronal CT slices.

Fistulisation of the lateral semicircular canal (known by some as the Clint Eastwood sign owing to the shape of the canals resembling a pistol) is a documented complication of cholesteatomas and an important negative when reporting a cholesteatoma.

Meniere disease is an idiopathic condition of the inner ear structures giving rise to symptoms principally of vertigo and tinnitus. Radiologically the vestibular aqueduct is seen to be either small or not visible.

Cholesteatomas (Acquired or congenital) are histolologically epidermoid cysts. They are seen as a middle ear mass formed by desquamated epithelium of the middle ear. They can cause erosion of the ossicles, scutum and other parts of the middle ear.

prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Functional imaging in dementia

Tc99m-HMPAO SPECT and 18F-FDG PET produce very similar patterns when used to image patients with cognitive decline however the latter is considered to have a greater sensitivity and specificity and is therefore preferred.

Two structures bear particular importance in the imaging of dementia; the precuneus and the cingulate gyrus. Both are best appreciate on sagittal views.

Precuneus: The precuneus is located on the medial surface of each hemisphere, in the posterior parietal lobe. It has functions in motor planning, working memory and also connections to the visual pathways.

The cingulate gyrus: The cinculate gyrus is also located on the medial side of each hemisphere and runs anteroposteriorly just above the corpus callosum. The cingulate gyrus has complex functions to do with learning, emotional response and memory.

Alzheimer disease

The radiological findings of this well known disease are diffuse sulcal and ventricular enlargement. There is a disproportionate effect to the anterior temporal lobes, hippocampi and sylvian fissures with sparing of the sensorimotor and visual cortices, thalami and cerebellum. Functional studies (Tc-HMPAO SPECT or F-18 FDG PET) show reduced uptake in the precuneus, posterior cingulate gyrus, frontal and temporoparietal lobes but with characteristic sparing of the sensorimotor cortex and basal ganglia bilaterally. Importantly there is also sparing of the occipital lobes, which helps differentiate it from Lewy body dementia where the occipital lobes are involved. Other differences between the two conditions are seen with specific dopamine transporter agent imaging techniques

Lewy body dementia

A core clinical feature to this dementia is the fluctuant nature of the symptoms. Parkinsonian features can also develop although these are usually subsequent to the memory decline. Visual hallucinations are also a feature.  Radiologically there is a generalised decrease in cerebral volume (sparing the hippocampi). Temporo-parietal hypoperfusion on HMPAO Tc99m SPECT scanning is indicative of Lewy body dementia. Involvement of the occipital cortex, which is typically spared in Alzheimers disease, sets the two apart from one another on PET studies. The cingulate island sign has also been ascribed to Lewy body dementia, where there is preservation of metabolism in the  mid-posterior cingulate gyrus. If present, this is said to be specific for Lewy body dementia.

Vascular dementia

Technically vascular dementia presents as a step-wise decline due to the finite number of small vascular insults that take place. The imaging features should be fairly familiar to candidates from day to day reporting. There are multifocal bilateral white matter changes which can be seen on CT when severe.  Inclusion of susceptibility weighted sequences on an MRI scan allows detection of microhaemorrhages suggestive of a parallel diagnosis of cerebral amyloid angiopathy where present.

Korsakoff syndrome

This presents as a triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia and is attributable to thiamine deficiency. There is  high T2 signal in the thalami, periaqueductal region and mammillothalamic tract. This is usually in relation to chronic alcohol excess but can is caused by thiamine deficiency from any cause.

Pick disease

When there is disproportionate atrophy of the frontal and temporal lobes in an unusually young patient Pick disease should be suspected. This can sometimes be described as enlargement of the frontal horns but the concept is the same; volume loss of the frontal and temporal lobes. Functional studies show reduced uptake in the frontal lobes and anterior cingulate gyri.

Parkinson's disease

Generalised cerebral atrophy occurs with Parkinson's disease but is a highly non-specific feature. There are, however, radiological findings in the midbrain which although subtle, are far more specific. Parkinson's disease occurs when there is neuronal loss in the substantia nigra, specifically the pars compacta of the substantia nigra. On a T2 weighted MRI image this appears as blurring of the intermediate signal intensity line which separates the two adjacent low intensity structures (these are the pars reticulata of the substantia nigra and the red nucleus).

A DAT scan (Dopamine Active Transfer) can be performed to confirm the diagnosis. This uses the radiopharmaceutical I-123 Ioflupane to image dopamine transporters in the brain. These are present in the highest concentrations in the putamina and caudate nuclei. In patients with true Parkinson's disease (as opposed to other similar conditions), there will be loss of uptake in the posterior putamen. This can be an asymmetric finding. Colloquially speaking the appearance of a these areas on a normal patient resembles a comma and on a patient with Parkinson's disease they become more like full stops.

prompt: What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Arachnoiditis

The giveaway feature here is ‘clumping of the nerve roots’. At other times this may be describes as ‘empty thecal sac sign’ where the nerve roots are so adherent to the posterior aspect of the space that they become next to invisible. Arachnoiditis can occur secondary to surgery, meningitis, subarachnoid haemorrhage, myelography and can also be idiopathic in origin.

Disc sequestration

This is the term used to describe the finding when a part of the disc material has completely separated itself from its parent disc and is seen free within the canal.

Post-op fibrosis

MRI scans are often performed to look for post-op fibrosis or scar tissue and to differentiate it from recurrent disc pathology. The important imaging feature in such cases is enhancement Scar tissue will show enhancement with contrast whereas disc material will not.

CSF leak

Although this would be a valid concern post-operatively the usual presentation is of positional headaches and most of the time there is nothing to see on imaging.

prompt: What is the most likely cause?
options: Right sided middle cerebral artery aneurysm
explanation:
This is an anatomy question. To point to the answer you have to know where those cranial nerves can all be affected by one pathology.

Cavernous sinus meningioma

Although meningiomas are usually benign, they do undergo interval growth and there comes a point where they can then cause mass-effect derived symptoms.

Intracranial aneurysm

A cavernous sinus aneurysm could conceivably cause the symptoms described, with an ICA aneurysm far more likely to do so in this instance than an MCA one but it would have to be an ipsilateral one, not a contralateral one.

Brainstem infarction

Brainstem infarctions can give rise to all sorts of constellations of symptoms which all have eponymous names. They are worth a cursory glance and lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenburg syndrome) is worth learning in reasonable detail. The giveaway feature of brainstem infarctions is the fact that ipsilateral palsy and contralateral sensory loss.

prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The classical feature of a cavernoma (aka cavernous haemangioma) on MRI is the ‘popcorn’ appearance caused by a bright lobulated centre surrounded by a rim of hypointensity. Haemosiderin deposition causes the blooming artefact on susceptibility weighted sequences. It is perhaps slightly counterintuitive that there can be no enhancement on post-contrast CT scans, given the vascular nature of these lesions, however when we consider that flow within the lesion may be very slow then this makes a little more sense. Another important distinguishing feature from other lesions is the fact that, unlike metastases, there is no mass effect or oedema from these lesions, despite the fact that they can often present with seizures.

Cerebral amyloid angiopathy gives rise to micro-haemorrhages at the grey-white matter junction which are well seen as blooming artefact on susceptibility weighted sequences.

Post-contrast sequences for recurrent cholesteatomas require a delay of around 45 minutes from giving the contrast to acquiring images as the granulation tissue is slow to take up contrast. This has obvious down-sides to any modern day busy MRI schedule. However since the management of post-operative granulation tissue and post-operative fluid is largely identical, namely expectant, it is not important to differentiate the one from the other. Thus findings on diffusion weighted sequences are the most important thing in post-operative cholesteatoma imaging.

Cholesteatoma

Cholesteatomas (Acquired or congenital) are histolologically epidermoid cysts. On imaging the finding of non-dependant soft tissue and bony erosion within the middle ear is typical for a cholesteatoma.

There are two types of acquired cholesteatoma:

Pars flaccida (80%) – classically erodes the scutum and extends superiorly

Pars tensa (20%) – classically erodes the ossicles, extending medially

These refer to the two parts of the tympanic membrane from which they arise.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

In due course, if left unattended, a cholesteatoma will expand to fill the entire middle ear. Prior to this point they can be seen as non-dependant soft tissue within the middle ear. Dependant soft tissue within the middle ear suggests the presence of fluid or pus and the diagnosis of a middle ear infection. Once a cholesteatoma has filled the middle ear completely however no gas remains from which to discern dependency.

There are a number of theories as to how cholesteatomas arise. One theory is that following a perforation of the tympanic membrane entry of desquamated stratified keratinised squamous epithelium from the external auditory canal into the middle ear is permitted. There it adheres to the tympanic membrane and proliferates unrelentingly causing a soft tissue mass to form and eventually leading to bony erosion of the ossicles, scutum and/or other parts of the middle ear.

A congenital cholesteatoma behaves in a similar manner but is present from birth due to an aberrant location of a tiny island of keratinised squamous epithelium.

Cholesterol granuloma

A cholesterol granuloma occurs as a sequela of recurrent bouts of otitis media. Haemorrhage within the middle ear leads to the formation of granulation tissue. On imaging this is seen as non-specification of the middle ear on CT. Bony changes can occur chronically with bony expansion, or displacement and even destruction of the ossicles. The signals characteristics on MRI are therefore important to distinguish it from a cholesteatoma. Whereas a cholesteatoma on MRI is isointense to brain parenchyma on T1, a cholesterol granuloma will show high signal in the middle ear on T1 due to the paramagnetic effects of methaemoglobin. On clinical examination the ENT surgeon may report a bulging blue tympanic membrane. This is classical. Dehiscence of the jugular bulb is an important differential diagnosis to exclude as this will also give a blue tympanic membrane on examination but the management is radically different!

Aberrant internal carotid artery

An aberrant internal carotid artery can cause a pulsatile mass in the middle ear. The question usually asked on this topic is slightly different and to do with the persistent stapedial artery and consequential aplastic foramen spinosum (anatomically – ‘the heel of the high-heeled shoe’). The stapedial artery in such cases arises from the internal carotid artery and runs through the stapes, becoming the middle meningeal artery (which usually arises from the external carotid artery and courses through the foramen spinosum).

prompt: Which of the following is NOT a likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which is NOT a likely diagnosis.

The differential diagnosis for orbital pathology is heavily anatomically based.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

Globe lesions are situated within the eyeball itself.

Retinoblastoma

Melanoma

Retinal detachment

Outside the globe there are three conditions which are included in all of the other orbital compartments namely sarcoidosis, pseudotumours and lymphoproliferative lesions.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

Lymphoproliferative disorders include leukaemias, lymphomas, and less aggressive collections of lymphoid tissue. The term is used particularly in head and neck radiology where histological diagnosis of such entities is key. Some masses on a CT scan can have a 'typical' appearance for a lymphoma but are actually only benign lymphoid hyperplastic tissue and thus the term lymphoproliferative disorder covers both entities accurately.

IgG4 related diseases are one of Radiology’s newest entities. They comprise a constellation of fibrotic conditions affecting virtually every part of the body, mediated by a subclass of Immunoglobulin called IgG4. Where one condition exists others may also be present. The more common of these include:

Orbital pseudotumour

Fibrosing mediastinitis

Reidel thyroiditis

Autoimmune pancreatitis

Sclerosing mesenteritis

Retroperitoneal fibrosis

There is a defined differential for ‘lesions which cross the corpus callosum’: GBM, lymphoma, infarction, trauma, radiation, metastases, MS. Although not well described here the ‘T2 changes’ could be oedema relating to the mass.

PML (progressive multifocal leucoencephalopathy) is an HIV related condition caused by the JC virus which is classically described as having asymmetrical high T2 signal but there isn’t anything else in the question which points to this.

Gliomatosis cerebri is a horrible tumour seen as generalised high T2 signal involving at least three lobes but is usually found in younger patients than this.

An anaplastic astrocytoma is a main player in the differential diagnosis for ‘lesions which cross the corpus callosum’ but is more prevalent in younger or middle aged patients.

Thus the answer for this question comes down to lymphoma or GBM. Both can be low on T1 but central necrosis is a classical finding in GBM and there is often significant oedema. By contrast lymphoma is usually iso or hypointense relative to the cortex.

Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease

There are three types of this prion transmitted disease; the one linked to the BSE (bovine spongiform encephalopathy) epidemic of the late 1980s and 1990s, a rare familial variant, and finally a sporadic version which accounts for the vast majority of the cases. Clinically there is a rapidly progressive dementia with ataxia and myoclonus which should be the give-away feature even before imaging features are discussed.  On MRI, the reported finding is of high T2/FLAIR signal in the basal ganglia bilaterally and symmetrically (particularly the putamen). The pulvinar sign is often described in association with cJD which describes high FLAIR signal in the pulvinar thalamic nuclei (called the hockey stick sign). Strangely the signal changes are a rare cause of restriction of diffusion, seen as bright areas on DWI. Important negatives for this condition are the lack of enhancement with contrast and the lack of white matter involvement (since the white matter is protected by its myelin sheath).

prompt: Which of the following is NOT a complication of this condition? Select ONE answer only.
options: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord
explanation:
A post-traumatic vertebral artery dissection classically presents as a third nerve palsy and cerebellar signs. The ‘sickle sign’ or ‘fried egg’ sign refers to the appearance of T1 fat saturated sequences where a slice transverse through the vessel shows hyperintensity in a crescenteric or circumferential shape to the wall of the affected vessel. Unlike large vessel dissections the anatomy here is usually too small to see a dissection flap.

Subacute combined degeneration

This is a curious condition which can be subtle to detect. A deficiency of vitamin B12 (usually caused by malabsorption) leads to degeneration within the dorsal columns of the cord. The dorsal columns carry nerves responsible for position and vibration sense and as such patients present with loss of these senses as well as sensory ataxia (balance significantly deteriorates when the patients’ eyes are shut thereby excluding visual stabilisation as opposed to sensory stabilisation), and hyperreflexia.

On an MRI scan there will be (if the resolution allows), a longitudinal line of high T2 signal within the cord on sagittal sequences, and often a characteristic 'inverted-V' shape of high T2 signal on axial sequences. In some cases, the 'V' is clearly seen and in others it is harder to appreciate and the finding is more of high T2 signal bilaterally and symmetrically in the region of the posterior columns.

Image sourced from WikipediaCourtesy of Chiara Briani CC BY-SA 3.0

Spinal cord infarction

The vascular supply to the spinal cord is derived largely from the vertebral arteries or intercostal arteries with one longitudinal running anterior spinal cord artery and two small longitudinally running posterior spinal cord arteries.

The artery of Adamkiewicz is a particularly large segmental artery supplying the anterior spinal artery from around the level of T9. It is responsible for most of the spinal cord blood supply for the lumbar spinal cord. Damage during aortic surgery or trauma can result in spinal cord infarction.

Usually any vascular insult results in a reasonably rapid onset of symptoms. Spinal cord infarctions are no exception. Often more than one vertebral level is affected.

An MRI will show T2 hyperintensity of at least the central grey matter (if not the whole cross-section of the cord) due to oedema. As with intracranial infarctions there will be restriction of diffusion on the DWI sequences.

Particularly in the thoracic spine, the adjacent vertebral body may also lose its blood supply and undergo infarction.

Lateral Medullary Syndrome (Wallenburg syndrome)

This is caused by either a vertebral artery occlusion or PICA occlusion and is one of those syndromes that is far more common in exams than in real life. There is a short list of slightly unusual symptoms any combination of which, in the exam context, should make you suspicious for this syndrome:

Cerebellar involvement – DANISH mnemonic

Autonomic dysfunction – ipsilateral Horners syndrome, hiccoughs

Sensory symptoms – symptoms of sensory loss are commonplace in the stroke world but in this syndrome it is specifically loss of pain and temperature sensation in the ipsilateral face and contralaterally in the rest of the body. Patients can also experience ipsilateral stabbing pains; pain symptoms are highly unusual in the stroke world and usually point to a different diagnosis.

Ipsilateral bulbar symptoms – dysphagia, dysarthria etc.

prompt: NextWhich of the following is a pitfall of sagittal sinus thrombosis imaging? Select ONE answer only.
options: Dense triangle sign on unenhanced CT
Empty delta sign on post contrast CT
High intensity in the sinus on T1
explanation:
The empty delta sign is a post-contrast CT finding. Bilateral haemorrhages can be a secondary consequence to a sagittal sinus thrombosis which may point towards the diagnosis but the thrombosis itself is recognised by the empty delta sign on post-contrast CT.

Dense triangle sign pertains to the acute thrombus as it appears on an unenhanced CT scan.

On an MRI, static blood within the sagittal sinus gives rise to low signal on T1, although the thrombus itself is likely to be high in signal (if subacute in nature). Normally the sagittal sinus will appear as a flow void on T1w. Blooming artefact can be seen on T2* gradient echo sequences and is a strong indicatory of the diagnosis. Confusion can arise with time-of-flight 3D reformatted images and great care should be taken not to overdiagnose flow artefactas thrombosis. Careful reference should always be made to the source images and where there is doubt a CT venogram may be of more use.

The associated infarctions can often be haemorrhagic and parasagittal haemorrhages are very specific for a sagittal sinus thrombosis, but subarachnoid haemorrhage is not likely to be related.

prompt: Which of the following is the most likely explanation?
explanation:
Cavum septum pellucidum

This is a normal finding in all preterm infants, and common in most term infants, but persists in around 10-20% of adults. It is also known as the 5th ventricle. It is a triangular shaped CSF space in between the anterior horns of the lateral ventricles.

Cavum vergae

This is a cavity posterior to the columns of fornix. It is essentially a posterior continuation of a cavum septum pellucidum.

Cavum Velum interpositium

This is present if the quadrigeminal cistern is seen to extend above the third ventricle to the foramen of Monro, but remains bound by the thalamus laterally.

Holoprosencephaly

This is a developmental abnormality where there is incomplete separation of the two cerebral hemispheres. It can be classified into lobar, semilobar and alobar forms.

Lobar: Nearly normal. Septum pellucidum is absent.

Semilobar:Variable cleavage with a partially formed falx, and a rudimentary third ventricle.

Alobar:The most severe form with no cleavage at all. The falx and third ventricle are absent. The cerebral hemispheres and thalami are fused. There is a large single ‘lateral’ ventricle.

Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP)

Atrophy of the midbrain produces a characteristic ‘hummingbird’ sign of the brainstem and midbrain (also known at the penguin sign). The size of the midbrain can be compared to that of the pons and a ratio of <0.15 is a reliable sign of PSP.

prompt: What would be the best test to demonstrate this acutely?
explanation:
The available answers in this question are deliberately limited. In some centres CT perfusion is used to detect reversible acute ischaemia but this answer is not given. Unenhanced CT is the first test a patient suspected to have an acute infarction should undergo but this is largely to rule out haemorrhage should the patient be a candidate for thrombolysis therapy. The question, however, actually asks which test should be performed to detect the infarction and hence the answer is DWI. DWI is far superior to an unenhanced CT in confirming the presence of an acute infarction (except in the brainstem and medulla where there is a high false negative rate within the first 24hours). A DAT scan is a nuclear medicine test used in the differential diagnosis of Parkinsonism.

prompt: Which of the following is NOT a cause of optic atrophy.
explanation:
Optic atrophy is difficult to pick up on an MRI scan unless you are specifically looking for it. On a T2 weighted coronal sequence (particularly a CISS, heavily T2 weighted sequence) scrolling through the optic nerves you may be able to appreciate that there is too much CSF surrounding the optic nerve, particularly if it is a unilateral finding.

Myasthenia Gravis is a muscular condition where there is increased fatiguability of all muscles. The effect can be seen with the ocular muscles particularly well. The optic nerves are unaffected.

Glaucoma occurs when the pressures within the eye are greater than normal. This increased pressure damages the optic nerve and, without treatment, can lead to irreversible optic neuropathy and thereafter optic atrophy.

Optic neuritis is inflammation of the optic nerve and can occur in the context of multiple sclerosis, or in isolation. Like glaucoma, it can progress to neuropathy and atrophy.

Neuromyelitis optica is a specific condition, with similarities to multiple sclerosis, where there is optic neuritis. Usually patients have enlarged optic nerves but chronic damage leads to optic atrophy.

stem: A 55-year-old lady with a worsening headache has an MRI scan which shows enlargement of optic nerve. On the post-contrast sequences there is linear peripheral enhancement with central non-enhancement.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The differentiation between a meningioma and an orbital pseudotumour is useful to know. The tram-track sign refers to enhancement of the optic nerve sheath post-contrast. Confusingly though some question writers talk about ‘tram-track calcification’. All the answers given are technically differential diagnoses however sarcoidosis in the context of the tram-track sign is limited to a sparse couple of case reports in the literature. Optic neuritis can sometimes be seen as high T2 signal within the optic nerve as opposed to post-contrast enhancement. Involvement of the optic nerve in cases of orbital lymphoma is rare too but can produce a tram-track appearance. Orbital pseudotumour can affect any part of the eye (as differentiating from Grave disease). That being said the optic nerve is not usually involved. The other possibility which has not been provided is an optic nerve glioma. Characteristically this causes kinking or buckling of the optic nerve which a meningioma does not.

She undergoes a CT scan of her head which shows calcified lesions, each having a thin rim of low attenuation around them. A pelvis x-ray shows soft tissue calcification around the hip.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The information provided in this vignette is confusing since once calcified, the lesions usually do not demonstrate perilesional oedema (low attenuation). However, the presence of soft tissue calcification around the pelvis region suggests that this is the diagnosis being alluded to.

Neurocysticercosis

Cysticercosis is caused by a tapeworm native to low income countries and carried by pigs. It is the most common parasitic infection involving the central nervous system and the central nervous system is itself commonly affected during the disease process; around 90% of cases show CNS involvement. The larva disseminate via the suparachnoid and intraventricular system and consequentially the meninges are most frequently affected, being involved in around 40% of cases, with particular involvement of the basal cisterns. Parenchymal involvement occurs in around a fifth of cases. The larval cells (termed cysticerci) also migrate to large skeletal muscle and, following destruction, become calcified and visible on plain radiographs as 'rice-grain' calcification. The long axis of the foci of calcification is usually orientated along the muscle fibres in which they are situated.

Parasitic stage

Features

Larval

Small foci of oedema

Vesicular

Small CSF cysts without surrounding oedema but containing a 2-3mm mural nodule (cyst with a dot)

Colloidal vesicular

Ring enhancing cyst with proteinaceous content

Focal seizures

Nodular granular stage

Cyst shrinks and becomes isointense to brain on T1, hypointense on T2

Calcified stage

Small focal calcifications appearing 1-10 years following acute infection

Rice-like muscle calcification

Seizures or asymptomatic

Cavernoma

The classical feature of a cavernoma (aka cavernous haemangioma) on MRI is the ‘popcorn’ appearance caused by a bright lobulated centre surrounded by a rim of hypointensity. Haemosiderin deposition causes the blooming artefact on susceptibility weighted sequences. It is perhaps slightly counterintuitive that there can be no enhancement on post-contrast CT scans, given the vascular nature of these lesions, however when we consider that flow within the lesion may be very slow then this makes a little more sense. Another important distinguishing feature from other lesions is the fact that, unlike metastases, there is no mass effect or oedema from these lesions, despite the fact that they can often present with seizures. Associated cutaneous manifestations of multiple cavernomas include cafe au lait spots and cherry angiomas, neither of which calcify.

Neurofibromatosis

Type 2 neurofibromatosis (MISME) is characterised by multiple meningiomas, schwannomas and ependymomas. In theory multiple calcified meningiomas each with a rim of surrounding oedema could be present. Neurofibromatosis is also in the differential diagnosis for soft tissue calcification though this relates to curvilinear calcifications related to plexiform neurofibromas (ie type 1 neurofibromatosis).

Osteosarcoma metastases

Osteosarcoma can cause soft tissue calcification, and within the lungs is a classic cause for calcified lung metastases however brain metastases (from all causes) rarely calcify. In the few cases reported in the literature the calcification is more globular than peripheral/rim calcification.

Dermatomyositis

This is a classic cause of soft tissue calcification with striking 'sheets' of calcification occurring in severe cases. Intracranial calcification is not a feature however.

stem: A 40-year-old man presents with a unilateral ptosis and unilateral inferolateral deviation of gaze (third nerve palsy).
prompt: Where would an aneurysm be to cause these symptoms?
explanation: The third cranial nerve runs parallel to the posterior communicating artery and dives under the posterior cerebral artery. The association between PCOM or PCA pathology and third nerve palsy signs is classical. If a patient has a painful ptosis, aPCOM aneurysm should be considered. It will be an ipsilateral pathology because the Oculomotor nerve is post-ganglionic at this point.

stem: A 70-year-old man undergoes an MRI scan as part of a memory impairment work up. This shows a mass in the left cavernous sinus. Among other features there is evidence of narrowing of the ICA within the cavernous sinus.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
It is meningiomas which can classically constrict the lumen of the ICA without invading it. Pituitary adenomas and metastases are likely to demonstrate invasion rather than compression. The classical demographic for a cavernous haemangioma is a 50-year-old woman which goes against this being the answer if you hadn’t already pinpointed meningioma. stem: A gentleman is seen in a neurology outpatient clinic with complaints of progressive memory loss and some movement problems. He subsequently undergoes an MRI scan of his brain. You suspect he may have a neurodegenerative condition.
prompt: Which of the following findings is correctly matched to its condition?
options: Blurring of structures in the midbrain - Alzheimer disease
Disproportionate involvement of the hippocampi - Parkinson's disease
Sparing of the hippocampi - Lewy body dementia
explanation:
Lewy body dementia

A core clinical feature to this dementia is the fluctuant nature of the symptoms. Parkinsonian features can also develop although these are usually subsequent to the memory decline. Visual hallucinations are also a feature.  Radiologically there is a generalised decrease in cerebral volume (sparing the hippocampi). Temporo-parietal hypoperfusion on HMPAO Tc99m SPECT scanning is indicative of Lewy body dementia. Involvement of the occipital cortex, which is typically spared in Alzheimers disease, sets the two apart from one another on PET studies. The cingulate island sign has also been ascribed to Lewy body dementia, where there is preservation of metabolism in the  mid-posterior cingulate gyrus. If present, this is said to be specific for Lewy body dementia.

Huntington disease

There are relatively few radiological manifestations of Huntington disease. The usual one described is atrophy of the heads of the caudate nuclei with consequential prominence of the adjacent lateral ventricle frontal horns with a ‘box’ like appearance. Various studies have been done to quantify the extent of this atrophy.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease

There are three types of this prion transmitted disease; the one linked to the BSE (bovine spongiform encephalopathy) epidemic of the late 1980s and 1990s, a rare familial variant, and finally a sporadic version which accounts for the vast majority of the cases. Clinically there is a rapidly progressive dementia with ataxia and myoclonus which should be the give-away feature even before imaging features are discussed.  On MRI, the reported finding is of high T2/FLAIR signal in the basal ganglia bilaterally and symmetrically (particularly the putamen). The pulvinar sign is often described in association with cJD which describes high FLAIR signal in the pulvinar thalamic nuclei (called the hockey stick sign). Strangely the signal changes are a rare cause of restriction of diffusion, seen as bright areas on DWI. Important negatives for this condition are the lack of enhancement with contrast and the lack of white matter involvement (since the white matter is protected by its myelin sheath).

Alzheimer disease

The radiological findings of this well known disease are diffuse sulcal and ventricular enlargement. There is a disproportionate effect to the anterior temporal lobes, hippocampi and sylvian fissures with sparing of the sensorimotor and visual cortices, thalami and cerebellum.

Parkinson's disease

Generalised cerebral atrophy occurs with Parkinson's disease but is a highly non-specific feature. There are, however, radiological findings in the midbrain which although subtle, are far more specific. Parkinson's disease occurs when there is neuronal loss in the substantia nigra, specifically the pars compacta of the substantia nigra. On a T2 weighted MRI image this appears as blurring of the intermediate signal intensity line which separates the two adjacent low intensity structures (these are the pars reticulata of the substantia nigra and the red nucleus).

A DAT scan (Dopamine Active Transfer) can be performed to confirm the diagnosis. This uses the radiopharmaceutical I-123 Ioflupane to image dopamine transporters in the brain. These are present in the highest concentrations in the putamina and caudate nuclei. In patients with true Parkinson's disease (as opposed to other similar conditions), there will be loss of uptake in the posterior putamen. This can be an asymmetric finding. Colloquially speaking the appearance of a these areas on a normal patient resembles a comma and on a patient with Parkinson's disease they become more like full stops.

explanation:
Demyelination

Demyelination can occur due to multiple sclerosis, ADEM or as an idiopathic process.

Acute idiopathic transverse myelitis is a specific diagnosis of exclusion however. There is inflammation of the spinal cord leading to bilateral motor, sensory and autonomic dysfunction. On imaging there is expansion of the central portion of the cord extending over multiple vertebral levels. The inflamed portion returns high signal on T2 weighted sequences. This occurs most commonly in the thoracic spine and importantly, should involve at least two thirds of the cross sectional area of the cord at the affected level. This is in contrast to a multiple sclerosis plaque which involves under half of the cross sectional area of the cord.

Multiple sclerosis can affect the spinal cord. Lesions tend to be smaller usually confined to 1-2 vertebral levels and affecting less than half of the cross sectional area of the cord. There may be mild focal expansion of the cord, but this is a far less prominent feature than it is with idiopathic transverse myelitis. 90% of patients will have other intracranial lesions. The lesions of MS also return high T2 signal, like their intracranial counterparts. The cervical cord is most commonly affected.

ADEM (acute disseminated encephalomyelitis) is an autoimmune condition which occurs days-weeks following a viral infection. It largely affects the white matter of the brain but the spinal cord can also be affected.  Grey matter, particularly the basal ganglia are also often involved. It can occur at any age, but it is usually young children who are affected. Patients usually respond very well to steroid therapy and fortunately, most (90%) cases resolve without any residual deficit. On imaging, the affected areas return high T2 signal.

stem: A 32-year-old woman who delivered a healthy baby two days previously in an uncomplicated normal vaginal delivery has an MRI pituitary which shows an area of high T1 signal in the suprasellar and sellar region.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This patient has haemorrhaged into the pituitary gland (as evidenced by the high T1 signal). Sheehan syndrome is consequent on obstetric hypovolaemia which is excluded by the description of an uncomplicated normal vaginal delivery. It is therefore more likely that she has undergone spontaneous pituitary apoplexy (and that the pregnancy is a red herring) ie bleeding into a macroadenoma.

Pituitary apoplexy

Pathologically, pituitary apoplexy is infarction which can take place with or without haemorrhage. Over half of patients have an underlying macroadenoma; haemorrhage into a pre-existing macroadenoma is the usual presentation. 'All' patients present with a headache and panhypopituitarism. Visual impairment is also common as the pituitary enlarges and impacts on the chiasm. On a CT scan there will be a sellar/suprasellar mass (ie pituitary enlargement). Hyperdensity is caused by the underlying haemorrhage, if present. On an MRI, the pituitary can be seen to be enlarged with T1 hyperintensity (specifically in the subacute phases). In the chronic phase however, the pituitary will be involuted and small, even appearing as an 'empty sella'.

Sheehan syndrome is pituitary apoplexy due to hypovolaemic shock and can be consequential to delivery. At the time of apoplexy, the predominant issue for the patient is the systemic hypovolaemia for which aggressive management is usually already being pursued. In the early days following the delivery, the first hypopituitary issues to manifest is usually any or all of hyponatraemia, diabetes insipidus or hypothyroidism. At this time the MRI findings can vary from a normal appearing pituitary through to the classic pituitary apoplexy appearances of an enlarged pituitary with high T1 signal. Patients can also present many months or years later with panhypoituitarism at which time an MRI will usually show an empty sella.

stem: A 40-year-old lady is brought into A&E with neurological problems. She undergoes a CT scan which shows multiple lesions and you suspect she may have neurocysticercosis.
prompt: Which of the following features would NOT be consistent with this diagnosis?
options: Soft tissue calcification around the thigh
explanation:
Neurocysticercosis

Cysticercosis is caused by a tapeworm native to low income countries and carried by pigs. It is the most common parasitic infection involving the central nervous system and the central nervous system is itself commonly affected during the disease process; around 90% of cases show CNS involvement. The larva disseminate via the suparachnoid and intraventricular system and consequentially the meninges are most frequently affected, being involved in around 40% of cases, with particular involvement of the basal cisterns. Parenchymal involvement occurs in around a fifth of cases. The larval cells (termed cysticerci) also migrate to large skeletal muscle and, following destruction, become calcified and visible on plain radiographs as 'rice-grain' calcification. The long axis of the foci of calcification is usually orientated along the muscle fibres in which they are situated.

Parasitic stage

Features

Larval

Small foci of oedema

Vesicular

Small CSF cysts without surrounding oedema but containing a 2-3mm mural nodule (cyst with a dot)

Colloidal vesicular

Ring enhancing cyst with proteinaceous content. The contents never enhance, being derived from the tapeworm, not the host human.

Focal seizures

Nodular granular stage

Cyst shrinks and becomes isointense to brain on T1, hypointense on T2

Calcified stage

Small focal calcifications appearing 1-10years following acute infection

Rice-like muscle calcification

Seizures or asymptomatic

stem: A 45-year-old man is involved in a high-speed road traffic accident. He sustains a significant head injury and a CT head is performed. This shows intracranial blood within the fissures at the vertex, crossing suture lines, but which does not cross the midline.
prompt: Which of the following would best explain these findings? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Blood being present within the fissures suggests subarachnoid origin.

The learning point here is how a haemorrhage deals with the sutures. Extradural (aka epidural) haematomas do cross the midline but do not cross suture lines as this is where the dura is attached to the skull. Subdural haematomas on the other hand do not cross the midline but do extend along the falx, dipping down and affecting both sides of the falx cerebri on the coronal views for example. Combined haematomas (ie extradural and subdural) are possible but on balance the question seems to imply that it is one haematoma rather than two with separate properties for each.

A subarachnoid haemorrhage can be seen as high density on CT within the small fissures on the surface of the brain, as well as into the larger fissures such as the interhemispheric fissure. Obviously very small subarachnoid haemorrhages can be very hard to spot on CT scans and a high index of suspicion is required.

This question comes down to two answers: Medullary or papillary thyroid cancer.

Calcification within lymph node metastases of thyroid cancer can occur with both medullary and papillary thyroid cancer although is more common with papillary thyroid cancer. When performing an USS of a lymph node in the context of a thryoid malignancy it is challenging to determine if there is metastatic involvement or not. The presence of calciifcaiton should raise the suspicion of involvement however this is not always present. The loss of normal hilar morphology is a more reliable sign as node becomes taken over by tumour cells and the lymph node hilum becomes destroyed.

Medullary thyroid cancer - 10% – can have a familial pattern and/or association with other endocrine malignancies. Medullary thyroid cancer usually demonstrates granular calcification and nodal spread in 50% of cases.

Papillary thyroid cancer - 65% - Punctate calcification and regional lymph nodes in 40% of patients and is of a low reflectivity on ultrasound. Anaplastic thyroid cancer is usually in an older age range.

Anaplastic thyroid cancer - 1% - can be ruled out as it affects an older age range. Secondary hyperparathyroidism can be ruled out because it doesn’t explain the malignant looking lymph nodes (or the thyroid mass). Thyroid lymphoma does not typically demonstrate calcification.

stem: A 64-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department by his worried wife. She describes a sudden collapse at home and on examination it is evident that he has loss of power and sensation below T7 on the left, with pain and temperature loss on the contralateral side. An urgent MRI is requested which shows high T2 signal in the T7 vertebral body and high signal of cord at T7. There is no significant adjacent disc disease.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Brown-Sequard syndrome

This is a specific finding where damage to the dorsal columns leads to ipsilateral loss of touch sensation and contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation due to damage to the lateral spinothalamic tracts (contralateral since these ascend after having crossed). There is also ipsilateral motor function loss.

Causes of Brown-Sequard syndrome

Traumatic:

Penetrating injury

Mechanical trauma e.g. RTA

Iatrogenic injury

Compression e.g. disc herniation

Spinal cord tumour

Vascular:

Aortic aneurysm repair complication

Vertebral artery dissection

Spinal cord haemorrhage

Spinal cord infarction

The vascular supply to the spinal cord is derived largely from the vertebral arteries or intercostal arteries with one longitudinal running anterior spinal cord artery and two small longitudinally running posterior spinal cord arteries.

The artery of Adamkiewicz is a particularly large segmental artery supplying the anterior spinal artery from around the level of T9. It is responsible for most of the spinal cord blood supply for the lumbar spinal cord. Damage during aortic surgery or trauma can result in spinal cord infarction.

Usually any vascular insult results in a reasonably rapid onset of symptoms. Spinal cord infarctions are no exception. Often more than one vertebral level is affected.

An MRI will showT2 hyperintensity of at least the central grey matter (if not the whole cross-section of the cord) due to oedema. As with intracranial infarctions there will be restriction of diffusion on the DWI sequences.

Particularly in the thoracic spine, the adjacent vertebral body may also lose its blood supply and undergo infarction.

Demyelination

Acute idiopathic transverse myelitis is a specific diagnosis of exclusion however. On imaging there is expansion of the central portion of the cord extending over multiple vertebral levels.

Multiple sclerosis can affect the spinal cord. Lesions tend to be smaller usually confined to 1-2 vertebral levels and affecting less than half of the cross-sectional area of the cord.

Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis) largely affects the white matter of the brain but the spinal cord can also be affected. On imaging, the affected areas return high T2 signal and there is characteristic sparing of the grey matter.

Spondylitis

Infection of the spine, termed spondylitis, is usually considered as either pyogenic or tuberculous (with a couple of notable exceptions). There is some overlap in the features of the two:

Tuberculous spondylodiscitis

Staphylococcal spondylodiscitis

Calcification (almost pathognomonic)

No calcification

Involvement of the posterior elements

Posterior elements spared

Insidious onset

More acute onset

Less loss of disc space

More loss of disc space

Gibbus deformity (angular kyphosis)

No gibbus deformity

Multiple levels involved

One level involved

Lateral Medullary Syndrome (Wallenburg syndrome)

This is caused by either a vertebral artery occlusion or PICA occlusion and is one of those syndromes that is far more common in exams than in real life.

Subacute combined degeneration

On an MRI scan there will be (if the resolution allows), a longitudinal line of high T2 signal within the cord on sagittal sequences, and often a characteristic 'inverted-V' shape of high T2 signal on axial sequences. In some cases, the 'V' is clearly seen and in others it is harder to appreciate, and the finding is more of high T2 signal bilaterally and symmetrically in the region of the posterior columns.

stem: A 78-year-old man undergoes an MRI after a routine asymptomatic screening ear exam shows an intact blue tympanic membrane. The scan shows a middle ear mass which is homogeneously high on T1 and T2.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A cholesterol granuloma should be at the top of the list when a blue tympanic membrane is mentioned. The features described in the question are classical for a cholesterol granuloma – the other notable feature not provided is the absence of pulsatile tinnitus which helps distinguish it from a glomus tympanicum. A cholesterol granuloma contains both cholesterol crystals and blood products (hence is bright on T1) whereas a cholesteatoma is isointense to brain parenchyma on T1 and can apparently be seen clinically as a whitish mass behind the tympanic membrane.

An aberrant internal carotid artery can cause a pulsatile mass in the middle ear. The question usually asked on this topic is slightly different and to do with the persistent stapedial artery and consequential aplastic foramen spinosum (anatomically – ‘the heel of the high-heeled shoe’). The stapedial artery in such cases arises from the internal carotid artery and runs through the stapes, becoming the middle meningeal artery (which usually arises from the external carotid artery and courses through the foramen spinosum).

Haemangiomas of the middle ear have been described but are largely confined to case reports in the literature.

topic: A cholesterol granuloma should be at the top of the list when a blue tympanic membrane is mentioned. The features described in the question are classical for a cholesterol granuloma – the other notable feature not provided is the absence of pulsatile tinnitus which helps distinguish it from a glomus tympanicum. A cholesterol granuloma contains both cholesterol crystals and blood products (hence is bright on T1) whereas a cholesteatoma is isointense to brain parenchyma on T1 and can apparently be seen clinically as a whitish mass behind the tympanic membrane.
stem: An aberrant internal carotid artery can cause a pulsatile mass in the middle ear. The question usually asked on this topic is slightly different and to do with the persistent stapedial artery and consequential aplastic foramen spinosum (anatomically – ‘the heel of the high-heeled shoe’). The stapedial artery in such cases arises from the internal carotid artery and runs through the stapes, becoming the middle meningeal artery (which usually arises from the external carotid artery and courses through the foramen spinosum). He is found to have focal neurology and undergoes imaging. prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Neurocysticercosis

Cysticercosis is caused by a tapeworm native to low income countries and carried by pigs. Cysts calcify over time. In the skeletal muscle these can be seen on plain radiographs as ‘rice grain’ calcifications. CNS infection with cysticercosis is termed neurocysticercosis and is well described in the literature.

Cytomegalovirus – this is a neonatal infection or one of the immunocompromised. Periventricular cysts and calcifications develop.

Cryptococcus

This is an opportunistic yeast-like fungus which therefore requires a degree of immunocompromise, typically AIDS. The cryptococcomas are non-enhancing low density lesions in the basal ganglia. A granulomatous meningitis can also occur. They can be differentiated from VR spaces on FLAIR where VR spaces will suppress (being CSF in content) whereas the mucoid cryptococcomas will not.

Metastatic chondrosarcoma or osteosarcoma – Metastases from osteosarcomas can show calcification (this can present as a pneumothorax secondary to lung metastases). Chondrosarcomas are cartilaginous forming tumours although rings and arcs of calcification are a feature.

stem: A 54-year-old man collapses while playing golf. On arrival at the Emergency Department the blood pressure in his arms is found to be different. He is thought to have suffered a stroke and undergoes carotid Doppler study. The sonographer believes he may have subclavian steal syndrome.
prompt: Which of the following findings would be expected if this were the case? Select ONE answer only.
options: Filling defect in the left subclavian artery and monophasic flow in the axillary artery
Filling defect in the left subclavian vein and biphasic flow in the axillary vein
Flow reversal in the left carotid vein and triphasic flow in the jugular vein
Flow reversal in the left vertebral artery and monophasic flow in the left axillary artery
Flow reversal in the left vertebral vein and biphasic flow in the left axillary vein
explanation:
Subclavian steal syndrome occurs when blood supplying the arm (usually the left arm) travels via the ipsilateral vertebral artery in order to bypass a proximal obstruction of the subclavian artery. The distal subclavian artery ‘steals’ blood from the vertebral artery circulation. This gives rise to two different categories of symptoms:

Arm - weaker pulses, numbness, paraesthesia, fingertip necrosis

Brain - syncope, ischaemic symptoms

The most likely cause of subclavian steal would be atherosclerosis. Takayasu aortitis and aortic dissections can also cause subclavian steal but would not be at the top of a differential list without further prompts from the history.

stem: You are reviewing a CT of a 71-year-old man who has an acquired cholesteatoma.
prompt: Which of the following is NOT correct? Select ONE answer only.
options: The Prussak space is found behind the superior part of the tympanic membrane
The head of the malleus is situated in the epitympanum
The malleus is connected to the tympanic membrane
The stapes is connected to the round window of the cochlea
The stapes is situated in the mesotympanum
explanation:
Please note that the question asks for the answer that is NOT correct.

The anatomy of the middle ear is complex but important and contains a number of specific anatomical terms.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

The epitympanum, also known as the attic, is the superior portion above the highest point of the tympanic membrane. It contains the head of the malleus and the short crus of the incus (These give the appearance of an ice-cream cone on an axial CT).

Image © Medical Exam Prep

The Prussak space is found within the epitympanum and is a tiny space at the top of the tympanic membrane, just behind the scutum. Its clinical relevance is that it is the usual origin for pars flaccida cholesteatomas.

The aditus ad antrum connects the epitympanum to the mastoid antrum and thence the mastoid air cells.

The tegmen mastoidium (tegmen means roof) is the point at which the mastoid air cells meet the temporal lobe of the brain.

The tegmen tympani is the point at which the upper most extent of the epitympanum reaches the temporal lobe of the brain.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

The mesotympanum is the space posterior to the tympanic membrane and contains the body of the incus, the manubrium (connected to the tympanic membrane) and the anterior process of the malleus and the stapes. The stapes is connected to the incus as well as the oval window of the cochlea. There is also a round window placed more inferiorly which bulges to allow compression waves transmitted from the stapes to the oval window to travel through the cochlea.

The hypotympanum is a far less significant space than either the epitympanum or the mesotympanum. It begins at the inferior most extent of the tympanic membrane. The Eustachian tube opens into the hypotympanum anteriorly.

prompt: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
There are two anatomical areas of the brain which are particular important in the field of neurodegenerative nuclear medicine.

The cingulate gyrus - next to the corpus callosum

The precuneus - between the cingulate sulcus and the parieto-occipital sulcus

Image © Medical Exam Prep

Huntington’s disease

There are relatively few radiological manifestations of Huntington disease. The usual one described is atrophy of the heads of the caudate nuclei with consequential prominence of the adjacent lateral ventricle frontal horns with a ‘box’ like appearance. Various studies have been done to quantify the extent of this atrophy. On functional studies there can be low activity in the caudate nucleus head and putamen.

Pick's disease is also called frontotemporal dementia

As the name would suggest, the main abnormalities are seen in the frontal and temporal lobes, including the anterior part of the cingulate gyrus. These areas show low metabolism on PET studies. The posterior part of the cingulate gyrus and the precuneus are spared.

Alzheimer's disease

Neuronal loss with Alzheimer's disease occurs first in the mesial temporal lobe which can be seen as cerebral volume loss there on an MRI scan. To assess this region the scan should be viewed on a coronal sequence through the level of the pons, where the hippocampi can be seen clearly. Although medial temporal lobe atrophy is not remotely specific for Alzheimer's disease, it is almost always present. Early changes in metabolism can be seen in the posterior part of the cingulate gyrus and the precuneus on PET studies, as well as in the posterior temporal and parietal lobes. Classically there is sparing of specific areas such as the anterior cingulate gyrus the basal ganglia, and the occipital lobes.

Parkinson's disease

Generalised cerebral atrophy occurs with Parkinson's disease but is a highly non-specific feature. There are, however, radiological findings in the midbrain which although subtle, are far more specific. Parkinson's disease occurs when there is neuronal loss in the substantia nigra, specifically the pars compacta of the substantia nigra. On a T2 weighted MRI image this appears as blurring of the intermediate signal intensity line which separates the two adjacent low intensity structures (these are the pars reticulata of the substantia nigra and the red nucleus).

A DAT scan (Dopamine Active Transfer) can be performed to confirm the diagnosis. This uses the radiopharmaceutical I-123 Ioflupane to image dopamine transporters in the brain. These are present in the highest concentrations in the putamina and caudate nuclei. In patients with true Parkinson's disease (as opposed to other similar conditions), there will be loss of uptake in the posterior putamen. This can be an asymmetric finding. Colloquially speaking the appearance of these areas on a normal patient resembles a comma and on a patient with Parkinson's disease they become more like full stops.

prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Optic nerve sheath meningioma

Like meningiomas elsewhere, the signal characteristics on T1 and T2 weighted sequences can be unimpressive. Signal from T2 weighted sequences may be more hyperintense, if anything. On the post-contrast sequences however there is usually strikingly strong enhancement and lesions may show a typical dural tail along the lesser sphenoid wing. Around a third to half of optic nerve sheath meningiomas demonstrate calcification and some of these will show the stereotypical 'tram-track' type calcification. Sparing of the distal portion of the nerve immediately posterior to the globe is also typical.

Also like other meningiomas elsewhere in the brain, local hyperostosis can occur. This is better appreciated with CT.

About 10% of patients with optic nerve sheath meningiomas have Neurofibromatosis type 2 and in these patients presentation tends to be in childhood. Otherwise the peak age for presentation is between 40s and 50s although there is wide variability.

Optic nerve glioma

This usually affects the whole optic nerve in a fusiform way. The vignette draws attention to some sparing of the optic nerve immediately posterior to the globe which makes optic nerve sheath meningioma more likely.

prompt: What normal venous structure is she describing?
explanation:
Basal vein of Rosenthal

This deep vein passes lateral to the midbrain and eventually drains into the vein of Galen.

Vein of Labbe

Large draining vein connecting the transverse sinus and the superficial middle vein.

Vein of Trolard

Usually smaller than the vein of Labbe. Connects the superficial middle vein and sagittal sinus. A larger vein of Labbe is associated with a smaller vein of Trolard and vice versa.

Vein of Galen

The confluence of the internal cerebral veins results in the vein of Galen.

Straight sinus

Drains the inferior sagittal sinus into (usually) the confluence of sinuses.

explanation:
There is an association between adult polycystic kidney disease (APCKD) and berry aneurysms. The man has had a subarachnoid haemorrhage from a ruptured aneurysm.

Moyamoya disease is progressive occlusion/arteritis of the distal ICA causing the formation of a large network of tiny collateral vessels seen on angiogram as a ‘puff of smoke’. It is predominantly found in children or young adults.
