stem: A man is admitted with left sided weakness and facial droop which began 8 hours previously.
prompt: Which of the following would be a contraindication to thrombolysis with alteplase?
options: The fact that this began 8 hours ago
explanation:
Practices vary locally however the usual quoted time frame is 4.5 hours following onset of symptoms. 8 hours is much beyond this.

A normal CT head is often the case for patients who are thrombolysed. There is a time lag before infarcted tissue becomes radiologically apparent. Loss of the insular ribbon sign refers to loss of grey-white matter differentiation at the insular cortex and is often seen with MCA territory infarctions. It forms part of the assessment of the ASPECTS score whereby 10 specific parts of the MCA territory are reviewed. Patients with more than two of these areas involved who are thrombolysed have been shown to have poorer outcomes than those not thrombolysed so whilst insular ribbon involvement on its own is not a contraindication it can contribute to the overall picture.

stem: A 70-year-old man undergoes an MRI scan of the base of his skull. He has previously undergone surgery for a left sided cholesteatoma and the surgeon is concerned there may be a recurrence. Within the surgical cavity on the left there is a mass which enhances on the post-contrast sequences but doesn’t restrict diffusion.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Cholesteatomas are difficult to manage as they have a high recurrence rate. Imaging has a significant role to play in the management of recurrent cholesteatomas; distinguishing recurrence from post-operative granulation tissue or fluid is important.

Diagnosis

Post-contrast sequences for recurrent cholesteatomas require a delay of around 45 minutes from giving the contrast to acquiring images as the granulation tissue is slow to take up contrast. This has obvious down-sides to any modern day busy MRI schedule. However since the management of post-operative granulation tissue and post-operative fluid is largely identical, namely expectant, it is not important to differentiate the one from the other. Thus findings on diffusion weighted sequences are the most important thing in post-operative cholesteatoma imaging.

Cholesteatoma

Cholesteatomas (Acquired or congenital) are histolologically epidermoid cysts. On imaging the finding of non-dependant soft tissue and bony erosion within the middle ear is typical for a cholesteatoma.

There are two types of acquired cholesteatoma:

Pars flaccida (80%) – classically erodes the scutum and extends superiorly

Pars tensa (20%) – classically erodes the ossicles, extending medially

These refer to the two parts of the tympanic membrane from which they arise.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

In due course, if left unattended, a cholesteatoma will expand to fill the entire middle ear. Prior to this point they can be seen as non-dependant soft tissue within the middle ear. Dependant soft tissue within the middle ear suggests the presence of fluid or pus and the diagnosis of a middle ear infection. Once a cholesteatoma has filled the middle ear completely however no gas remains from which to discern dependency.

There are a number of theories as to how cholesteatomas arise. One theory is that following a perforation of the tympanic membrane entry of desquamated stratified keratinised squamous epithelium from the external auditory canal into the middle ear is permitted. There it adheres to the tympanic membrane and proliferates unrelentingly causing a soft tissue mass to form and eventually leading to bony erosion of the ossicles, scutum and/or other parts of the middle ear.

A congenital cholesteatoma behaves in a similar manner but is present from birth due to an aberrant location of a tiny island of keratinised squamous epithelium.

Cholesterol granuloma

A cholesterol granuloma occurs as a sequela of recurrent bouts of otitis media. Haemorrhage within the middle ear leads to the formation of granulation tissue. On imaging this is seen as opacification of the middle ear on CT. Bony changes can occur chronically with bony expansion, or displacement and even destruction of the ossicles. The signals characteristics on MRI are therefore important to distinguish it from a cholesteatoma. Whereas a cholesteatoma on MRI is isointense to brain parenchyma on T1, a cholesterol granuloma will show high signal in the middle ear on T1 due to the paramagnetic effects of methaemoglobin. On clinical examination the ENT surgeon may report a bulging blue tympanic membrane. This is classical. Dehiscence of the jugular bulb is an important differential diagnosis to exclude as this will also give a blue tympanic membrane on examination but the management is radically different!

stem: A 40-year-old man is brought to A&E following a road traffic incident. He is found to have sustained a vertebral artery dissection.
prompt: Which of the following is NOT a complication of this condition?
options: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord
explanation:
A post-traumatic vertebral artery dissection classically presents as a third nerve palsy and cerebellar signs. The ‘sickle sign’ or ‘fried egg’ sign refers to the appearance of T1 fat saturated sequences where a slice transverse through the vessel shows hyperintensity in a crescenteric or circumferential shape to the wall of the affected vessel. Unlike large vessel dissections the anatomy here is usually too small to see a dissection flap.

Subacute combined degeneration

This is a curious condition which can be subtle to detect. A deficiency of vitamin B12 (usually caused by malabsorption) leads to degeneration within the dorsal columns of the cord. The dorsal columns carry nerves responsible for position and vibration sense and as such patients present with loss of these senses as well as sensory ataxia (balance significantly deteriorates when the patients eyes are shut thereby excluding visual stabilisation as opposed to sensory stabilisation), and hyperreflexia.

On an MRI scan there will be (if the resolution allows), a longitudinal line of high T2 signal within the cord on sagittal sequences, and often a characteristic 'inverted-V' shape of high T2 signal on axial sequences. In some cases the 'V' is clearly seen and in others it is harder to appreciate and the finding is more of high T2 signal bilaterally and symmetrically in the region of the posterior columns.

Spinal cord infarction

The vascular supply to the spinal cord is derived largely from the vertebral arteries or intercostal arteries with one longitudinal running anterior spinal cord artery and two small longitudinally running posterior spinal cord arteries.

The artery of Adamkiewicz is a particularly large segmental artery supplying the anterior spinal artery from around the level of T9. It is responsible for most of the spinal cord blood supply for the lumbar spinal cord. Damage during aortic surgery or trauma can result in spinal cord infarction.

Usually any vascular insult results in a reasonably rapid onset of symptoms. Spinal cord infarctions are no exception. Often more than one vertebral level is affected.

An MRI will showT2 hyperintensity of at least the central grey matter (if not the whole cross-section of the cord) due to oedema. As with intracranial infarctions there will be restriction of diffusion on the DWI sequences.

Particularly in the thoracic spine, the adjacent vertebral body  may also lose its blood supply and undergo infarction.

Lateral Medullary Syndrome (aka Wallenburg syndrome)

This is caused by either a vertebral artery occlusion or PICA occlusion and is one of those syndromes that is far more common in exams than in real life. There is a short list of slightly unusual symptoms any combination of which, in the exam context, should make you suspicious for this syndrome:

Cerebellar involvement – DANISH mnemonic as per medical school

Autonomic dysfunction – ipsilateral Horners syndrome, hiccoughs

Sensory symptoms – symptoms of sensory loss are common place in the stroke world but in this syndrome it is specifically loss of pain and temperature sensation in the contralateral face. Patients can also experience ipsilateral stabbing pains; pain symptoms are highly unusual in the stroke world and usually point to a different diagnosis.

Ipsilateral bulbar symptoms – dysphagia, dysarthria etc.

stem: You are reviewing an MRI scan of a 21-year-old woman's brain who has recently been diagnosed with Neurofibromatosis type 2.
prompt: Which of the following is a feature of Neurofibromatosis type 2? Select ONE answer only.

stem: You are reviewing a CT of a 74-year-old man who has an acquired cholesteatoma.
prompt: Which of the following is correct? Select ONE answer only.
options: The Eustachian tube opens into the hypotympanum
The Prussak space is found behind the inferior part of the tympanic membrane
The head of the malleus is situated in the mesotympanum
The short crus of the incus is situated in the mesotympanum
The stapes is connected to the malleus
explanation:
The anatomy of the middle ear is complex but important and contains a number of specific anatomical terms.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

The epitympanum, also known as the attic, is the superior portion above the highest point of the tympanic membrane. It contains the head of the malleus and the short crus of the incus (These give the appearance of an ice-cream cone on an axial CT).

Image © Medical Exam Prep

The Prussak space is found within the epitympanum and is a tiny space at the top of the tympanic membrane, just behind the scutum. Its clinical relevance is that it is the usual origin for pars flaccida cholesteatomas.

The aditus ad antrum connects the epitympanum to the mastoid antrum and thence the mastoid air cells.

The tegmen mastoidium (tegmen means roof) is the point at which the mastoid air cells meet the temporal lobe of the brain.

The tegmen tympani is the point at which the upper most extent of the epitympanum reaches the temporal lobe of the brain.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

The mesotympanum is the space posterior to the tympanic membrane and contains the body of the incus, the manubrium (connected to the tympanic membrane) and the anterior process of the malleus and the stapes. The stapes is connected to the incus as well as the oval window of the cochlea. There is also a round window placed more inferiorly which bulges to allow compression waves transmitted from the stapes to the oval window to travel through the cochlea.

The hypotympanum is a far less significant space than either the epitympanum or the mesotympanum. It begins at the inferior most extent of the tympanic membrane. The Eustachian tube opens into the hypotympanum anteriorly.

stem: A 73-year-old lady with a presentation of progressive memory loss undergoes an 18F-FDG PET study. There is low metabolism in the posterior part of the cingulate gyrus as well as the precuneus. The occipital lobes are notably spared.
prompt: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
There are two anatomical areas of the brain which are particular important in the field of neurodegenerative nuclear medicine.

The cingulate gyrus - next to the corpus callosum

The precuneus - between the cingulate sulcus and the parieto-occipital sulcus

Image © Medical Exam Prep

Alzheimer's disease

Neuronal loss with Alzheimer's disease occurs first in the mesial temporal lobe which can be seen as cerebral volume loss there on an MRI scan. To assess this region the scan should be viewed on a coronal sequence through the level of the pons, where the hippocampi can be seen clearly. Although medial temporal lobe atrophy is not remotely specific for Alzheimer's disease, it is almost always present. Early changes in metabolism can be seen in the posterior part of the cingulate gyrus and the precuneus on PET studies, as well as in the posterior temporal and parietal lobes. Classically there is sparing of specific areas such as the anterior cingulate gyrus the basal ganglia, and the occipital lobes.

Huntington’s disease

There are relatively few radiological manifestations of Huntington disease. The usual one described is atrophy of the heads of the caudate nuclei with consequential prominence of the adjacent lateral ventricle frontal horns with a ‘box’ like appearance. Various studies have been done to quantify the extent of this atrophy. On functional studies there can be low activity in the caudate nucleus head and putamen.

Pick's disease is also called frontotemporal dementia

As the name would suggest, the main abnormalities are seen in the frontal and temporal lobes, including the anterior part of the cingulate gyrus. These areas show low metabolism on PET studies. The posterior part of the cingulate gyrus and the precuneus are spared.

Parkinson's disease

Generalised cerebral atrophy occurs with Parkinson's disease but is a highly non-specific feature. There are, however, radiological findings in the midbrain which although subtle, are far more specific. Parkinson's disease occurs when there is neuronal loss in the substantia nigra, specifically the pars compacta of the substantia nigra. On a T2 weighted MRI image this appears as blurring of the intermediate signal intensity line which separates the two adjacent low intensity structures (these are the pars reticulata of the substantia nigra and the red nucleus).

A DAT scan (Dopamine Active Transfer) can be performed to confirm the diagnosis. This uses the radiopharmaceutical I-123 Ioflupane to image dopamine transporters in the brain. These are present in the highest concentrations in the putamina and caudate nuclei. In patients with true Parkinson's disease (as opposed to other similar conditions), there will be loss of uptake in the posterior putamen. This can be an asymmetric finding. Colloquially speaking the appearance of these areas on a normal patient resembles a comma and on a patient with Parkinson's disease they become more like full stops.

NextA 45-year-old man with known HIV presents with deteriorating memory problems and word finding difficulties. He undergoes an MRI scan which shows bilateral symmetrical gross white matter high signal on T2 and FLAIR. The radiologist notes sparing of the subcortical U-fibres.
prompt: What is the most likely explanation?
explanation:
HIV encephalopathy

Separating HIV encephalitis from PML can challenging in real life. HIV encephalitis causes bilateral symmetrical white matter changes, seen as high T2 signal (The T1 sequences can be normal). There is also sparing of the subcortical U-fibres.

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML)

This is a JC virus mediated phenomenon which causes asymmetrical patchy white matter changes. These can be bilateral. The testable feature is involvement of the cortical U-fibres which separates it from HIV encephalopathy where the U-fibres are spared.

Cryptococcus

This is an opportunistic yeast-like fungus which therefore requires a degree of immunocompromise, typically AIDS. The cryptococcomas are non-enhancing low density lesions in the basal ganglia. These show as high signal on T2 sequences. A granulomatous meningitis can also occur. They can be differentiated from VR spaces on FLAIR where VR spaces will suppress (being CSF in content) whereas the mucoid cryptococcomas will not.

Toxoplasmosis

Toxoplasmosis is a more common finding in AIDS patients than lymphoma is, by a large margin. On MRI it is seen as multiple ring enhancing lesions, which can show haemorrhage particularly following treatment. One of the stronger differentiators between toxoplasmosis and lymphoma is the SPECT findings. This is sometimes termed ‘hypometabolic’ meaning the lesions do not demonstrate SPECT uptake. The table below gives some general features of the two conditions. There is however considerable overlap in the imaging features despite these broad trends.

stem: A 27-year-old man who had been previously well visits his GP after falling over for apparently no reason at work. His GP also establishes a history of positional headaches. He is referred for a CT scan which shows a well-defined hyperdense spherical lesion in the anterosuperior portion of the third ventricle. The bony windows are normal.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The clinical history of positional headaches and intermittent ataxia is classical for a colloid cyst which can act in a ‘ball + valve’ type mechanism with intermittent CSF obstruction through the third ventricle. The hyperdensity on CT is caused by its proteinaceous content as opposed to calcification, hence it is not seen on bony windows. Of the other answers given a meningioma would need a dural base. Ependymomas are more often found in the paediatric cohort and do not give the intermittent symptoms described here. A cavum veli interpositum cyst are largely asymptomatic normal variants and imaging characteristics would follow CSF. A basilar artery aneurysm is an interesting differential diagnosis here but would not be found in the anatomical location provided.

stem: NextA 70-year-old man much troubled by tinnitus undergoes an MRI scan of the base of his skull. The ossicles are disrupted by a middle ear mass which is bulging the tympanic membrane. It is high in signal on T1 and T2 weighted sequences.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Cholesterol granuloma

A cholesterol granuloma occurs as a sequela of recurrent bouts of otitis media. Haemorrhage within the middle ear leads to the formation of granulation tissue. On imaging this is seen as non-specification of the middle ear on CT. Bony changes can occur chronically with bony expansion, or displacement and even destruction of the ossicles. The signals characteristics on MRI are therefore important to distinguish it from a cholesteatoma. Whereas a cholesteatoma on MRI is isointense to brain parenchyma on T1, a cholesterol granuloma will show high signal in the middle ear on T1 due to the paramagnetic effects of methaemoglobin. On clinical examination the ENT surgeon may report a bulging blue tympanic membrane. This is classical. Dehiscence of the jugular bulb is an important differential diagnosis to exclude as this will also give a blue tympanic membrane on examination but the management is radically different!

Cholesteatoma

Cholesteatomas (Acquired or congenital) are histolologically epidermoid cysts. On imaging the finding of non-dependant soft tissue and bony erosion within the middle ear is typical for a cholesteatoma.

There are two types of acquired cholesteatoma:

Pars flaccida (80%) – classically erodes the scutum and extends superiorly

Pars tensa (20%) – classically erodes the ossicles, extending medially

These refer to the two parts of the tympanic membrane from which they arise.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

In due course, if left unattended, a cholesteatoma will expand to fill the entire middle ear. Prior to this point they can be seen as non-dependant soft tissue within the middle ear. Dependant soft tissue within the middle ear suggests the presence of fluid or pus and the diagnosis of a middle ear infection. Once a cholesteatoma has filled the middle ear completely however no gas remains from which to discern dependency.

There are a number of theories as to how cholesteatomas arise. One theory is that following a perforation of the tympanic membrane entry of desquamated stratified keratinised squamous epithelium from the external auditory canal into the middle ear is permitted. There it adheres to the tympanic membrane and proliferates unrelentingly causing a soft tissue mass to form and eventually leading to bony erosion of the ossicles, scutum and/or other parts of the middle ear.

A congenital cholesteatoma behaves in a similar manner but is present from birth due to an aberrant location of a tiny island of keratinised squamous epithelium.

Cholesteatomas are difficult to manage as they have a high recurrence rate. Imaging has a significant role to play in the management of recurrent cholesteatomas; distinguishing recurrence from post-operative granulation tissue or fluid is important.

Post-contrast sequences for recurrent cholesteatomas require a delay of around 45 minutes from giving the contrast to acquiring images as the granulation tissue is slow to take up contrast. This has obvious down-sides to any modern day busy MRI schedule. However since the management of post-operative granulation tissue and post-operative fluid is largely identical, namely expectant, it is not important to differentiate the one from the other. Thus findings on diffusion weighted sequences are the most important thing in post-operative cholesteatoma imaging.

Aberrant internal carotid artery

An aberrant internal carotid artery can cause a pulsatile mass in the middle ear. The question usually asked on this topic is slightly different and to do with the persistent stapedial artery and consequential aplastic foramen spinosum (anatomically – ‘the heel of the high-heeled shoe’). The stapedial artery in such cases arises from the internal carotid artery and runs through the stapes, becoming the middle meningeal artery (which usually arises from the external carotid artery and courses through the foramen spinosum).

prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?

High T1 signal can be caused by:

Melanin, protein, contrast agents, fat, methaemaglobin (subacute haemorrhage).

He is otherwise fit and well, and has been scanned under the NICE guidelines for the management of head injuries. There is no intracranial haemorrhage but you notice a midline destructive lesion involving the clivus. There are bony fragments within it and it is displacing the basilar artery posteriorly.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Chordoma

These tumours are chiefly found in either the clivus or the sacrum. In the clivus they arise from the synchondrosis (primary cartilaginous joint) between the occipital bone inferiorly and the sphenoid bone superiorly. This is a midline joint and consequently the resultant chordoma is classically midline in nature. This helps to distinguish it from a chondrosarcoma which can appear very similar.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

Chordomas are aggressive, lobulated tumours which cause destruction of surrounding bone but lobulated mass effect on the pons with so-called 'thumbprinting' of the pons. Adjacent vascular structures, if not frankly invaded, are displaced. Posterior displacement of the basilar artery is a useful finding. Within the mass there are often calcific fragments representing either sequestered bone or dystrophic tumoral calcifications, or both. On an MRI scan the mass will be isointense to brain parenchyma on T1 and usually high in signal on T2. Most enhance with contrast.

Chondrosarcoma

In some cases there can be a lot of overlap between clival chondrosarcomas and clival chordomas. If a mass is determindly off-midline however, a chondrosarcoma is far more likely. These arise from tiny remnants of cartilage in the synchondrosis between the petrous temporal bone laterally and the occipital bone medially. Patients may present with cranial neuropathies which would be less usual for a chordoma when the nerves traversing the petrous temporal bone are affected. The abducens (CN VI) nerve is most often affected and CN III, V, VII and VIII may also be involved.

Intralesional calcifications take the form of the classic 'arcs and rings' seen with chondrosarcomas elsewhere in the body. On an MRI scan the signal characteristics can be similar to a chordoma with isointensity on T1 to brain parenchyma and high T2 signal. Chondrosarcomas are also likely to enhance with contrast.

Skull base metastasis and multiple myeloma

A myelomatous or metastatic process must always be kept in the differential diagnosis for a skull base mass however this would be less usual (although obviously not impossible) in a patient without a known primary site or known disease. On an MRI scan there will be loss of the high T1 marrow signal, as with other aggressive bony lesions, however the T2 signal is usually low or isointense.

explanation: Medulloblastomas are the most common posterior fossa tumours in children and the imaging features here are characteristic. The distinguishing feature from an ependymoma is the hypointense rim on the post-contrast sequences. Cavernous angiomas are also described as having a hypointense rim but this would be on the T2 sequences as opposed to the post contrast T1 sequences and the other features given are not applicable. On CT medulloblastomas are usually (90%) slightly higher in attenuation than the adjacent parenchyma; they are highly cellular tumours and appear very dense.

stem: Which of the following would not help differentiate between benign intracranial hypertension and sagittal sinus thrombosis on imaging?
prompt: Select one answer only.
explanation:
Benign intracranial hypertension is now, more correctly, referred to as idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

The lateral ventricles in idiopathic intracranial hypertension are described as ‘pinched’ and in sagittal sinus thrombosis the development of cerebral oedema secondary to infarction can also compress the lateral ventricles, a finding in approximately a third of cases.

In contrast to this, prominent temporal horns, suggestive of developing hydrocephalus can be seen in sagittal sinus thrombosis due to decreased CSF absorption.

Ventricular bleeds might be seen in sagittal sinus thrombosis in the neonatal age group.

Bilateral haemorrhages in the context of sagittal sinus thrombosis are caused by venous infarction.

Delta sign is seen in sagittal sinus thrombosis; high T1 signal in a triangular shape within the sagittal sinus is the MRI (or non enhanced CT) finding. On post contrast sequences the same pathology can give the empty-delta sign.

Papilloedema can be seen with both conditions and newer MRI techniques are being developed around this sign, thought to be a useful marker of raised intracranial pressure.

stem: A 40-year-old lady is brought into the Emergency Department with neurological problems. She undergoes a CT scan which shows multiple lesions and you suspect she may have neurocysticercosis.
prompt: Which of the following features would NOT be consistent with this diagnosis? Select ONE option only.
options: Soft tissue calcification around the thigh
explanation:
Neurocysticercosis

Cysticercosis is caused by a tapeworm native to low income countries and carried by pigs. It is the most common parasitic infection involving the central nervous system and the central nervous system is itself commonly affected during the disease process; around 90% of cases show CNS involvement. The larva disseminate via the suparachnoid and intraventricular system and consequentially the meninges are most frequently affected, being involved in around 40% of cases, with particular involvement of the basal cisterns. Parenchymal involvement occurs in around a fifth of cases. The larval cells (termed cysticerci) also migrate to large skeletal muscle and, following destruction, become calcified and visible on plain radiographs as 'rice-grain' calcification. The long axis of the foci of calcification is usually orientated along the muscle fibres in which they are situated.

Parasitic stage

Features

Larval

Small foci of oedema

Vesicular

Small CSF cysts without surrounding oedema but containing a 2-3mm mural nodule (cyst with a dot)

Colloidal vesicular

Ring enhancing cyst with proteinaceous content

Focal seizures

Nodular granular stage

Cyst shrinks and becomes isointense to brain on T1, hypointense on T2

Calcified stage

Small focal calcifications appearing 1-10 years following acute infection

Rice-like muscle calcification

Seizures or asymptomatic

stem: You are reviewing an MRI scan of a 45-year-old woman's brain who has recently been diagnosed with orbital lymphoma.
prompt: Which of the following is NOT a feature of orbital lymphoma? Select ONE answer only.
options: Most commonly involves the lacrimal gland
explanation:
Please note the question asks which option is NOT a feature.

Orbital lymphoproliferative disorders

Lymphoproliferative disorders include leukaemias, lymphomas, and less aggressive collections of lymphoid tissue. The term is used particularly in head and neck radiology where histological diagnosis of such entities is key. Some masses on a CT scan can have a 'typical' appearance for a lymphoma but are actually only benign lymphoid hyperplastic tissue and thus the term lymphoproliferative disorder covers both entities accurately.

There is a huge spectrum of imaging appearances, ranging from well defined, heterogenous mildly enhancing masses to poorly defined, homogeneous, avidly enhancing masses. There is also significant overlap with the imaging features of other non-lymphomatous orbital lesions.

Findings may be bilateral or unilateral although most cases of primary lymphoma are unilateral and most cases of benign disease are bilateral. Proptosis is common owing to simple mass effect posterior to the globe.

Typically orbital lymphoma is seen as a hyperdense mass with contrast enhancement on CT but they may be isodense.

stem: A 25-year-old lady who is 20 weeks pregnant with known pre-eclampsia develops sudden onset cortical blindness.
prompt: Where is the most likely area of concern on MRI scanning?
explanation:
Bilateral occipital haemorrhages are the classical imaging finding for PRES (posterior reversible leukoencephalopathy syndrome). Classically PRES presents as a visual disturbance in a pregnant or post-partum patient with pre-eclampsia and CT shows haemorrhages in the posterior fossa. The main underlying pathological process is vasogenic oedema. Technically PRES is not exclusive to pregnancy or the post-partum period, and often with a history (implied or provided) of pre-eclampsia. Other causes such as SLE or immunosuppression are also technically feasible. Cortical blindness is the classical symptom.

Sagittal sinus thrombosis would be a possible differential diagnosis and without any additional information as to the imaging findings it would only be the classical nature of the vignette described which would make PRES a better answer over sagittal sinus thrombosis.

stem: A 50-year-old woman has an USS thyroid which shows a solid looking region in the left thyroid lobe with punctuate echogenic foci. There are associated malignant looking lymph nodes in the left cervical chain. You suspect she has a thyroid malignancy and grade the scan as U5.
prompt: Which of the following regarding thyroid cancer is NOT correct? Select ONE answer only.
options: Anaplastic thyroid cancers usually arise in elderly patients
Calcification in a thyroid mass is most suggestive of papillary thyroid cancer
Calcification within a lymph node is most suggestive of papillary thyroid cancer
Medullary thyroid cancer can show familial inheritance patterns
Medullary thyroid cancer is the most common type of thyroid cancer
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which answer is NOT correct.

Calcification and thyroid cancers:

Calcification of a malignant thyroid mass is most suggestive of a Papillary thyroid cancer, which is also by far the most common of the thyroid cancers, however medullary thyroid cancers can also give lesional calcification.

Medullary thyroid cancer - 10% – can have a familial pattern and/or association with other endocrine malignancies. Medullary thyroid cancer usually demonstrates granular calcification and nodal spread in 50% of cases.

Papillary thyroid cancer - 65% - Punctate calcification and regional lymph nodes in 40% of patients and is of a low reflectivity on ultrasound. Anaplastic thyroid cancer is usually in an older age range.

Anaplastic thyroid cancer - 1% - can be ruled out as it affects an older age range.

Secondary hyperparathyroidism can be ruled out because it doesn’t explain the malignant looking lymph nodes (or the thyroid mass).

Thyroid lymphoma does not typically demonstrate calcification.

stem: You are reviewing a case series on the teaching files of cholesteatomas.
prompt: Which of the following is the area LEAST likely to be involved?
explanation:
Certainly the ossicles, lateral semicircular canal (Known by some as the Clint Eastwood sign) and lateral epitympanic wall (i.e. scutum) are often involved. Of the ossicles, the long process, lenticular process of the incus and the head of the stapes are commonly involved. The tegmen tympani is the roof of the middle ear and is also often involved. It can be seen superior to the ‘ice cream cone’ on coronal images. The tegmen mastoidium is the roof of the mastoid and is seen laterally to the tegmen tympani.

There are two types of acquired cholesteatoma:

Pars flaccid – classically erodes the scutum

Pars tensa – classically erodes the ossicles

stem: You are reviewing the HMPAO images from a patient who presented to his GP with a gradual decline in memory.
prompt: Which of the following findings is correctly matched to its diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
options: Involvement of the occipital lobes - Lewy body dementia
Reduced uptake in the precuneus and cingulate gyrus - Pick disease
Reduced uptake of the frontal lobes - Alzheimer's disease
Susceptibility artefact bilaterally but asymmetrically - Parkinson's disease
Temporoparietal hypoperfusion bilaterally and symmetrically - Vascular dementia
explanation:
Functional imaging in dementia

Tc99m-HMPAO SPECT and 18F-FDG PET produce very similar patterns when used to image patients with cognitive decline however the latter is considered to have a greater sensitivity and specificity and is therefore preferred.

Two structures bear particular importance in the imaging of dementia; the precuneus and the cingulate gyrus. Both are best appreciated on sagittal views.

Precuneus: The precuneus is located on the medial surface of each hemisphere, in the posterior parietal lobe. It has functions in motor planning, working memory and also connections to the visual pathways.

The cingulate gyrus: The cinculate gyrus is also located on the medial side of each hemisphere and runs anteroposteriorly just above the corpus callosum. The cingulate gyrus has complex functions to do with learning, emotional response and memory.

Alzheimer's disease

The radiological findings of this well-known disease are diffuse sulcal and ventricular enlargement. There is a disproportionate effect to the anterior temporal lobes, hippocampi and sylvian fissures with sparing of the sensorimotor and visual cortices, thalami and cerebellum. Functional studies (Tc-HMPAO SPECT or F-18 FDG PET) show reduced uptake in the precuneus, posterior cingulate gyrus, frontal and temporoparietal lobes but with characteristic sparing of the sensorimotor cortex and basal ganglia bilaterally. Importantly there is also sparing of the occipital lobes, which helps differentiate it from Lewy body dementia where the occipital lobes are involved. Other differences between the two conditions are seen with specific dopamine transporter agent imaging techniques

Lewy body dementia

There is a generalised decrease in cerebral volume (sparing the hippocampi). Temporo-parietal hypoperfusion on HMPAO Tc99m SPECT scanning is indicative of Lewy body dementia. Involvement of the occipital cortex, which is typically spared in Alzheimer’s disease, sets the two apart from one another on PET studies. The cingulate island sign has also been ascribed to Lewy body dementia, where there is preservation of metabolism in the mid-posterior cingulate gyrus. If present, this is said to be specific for Lewy body dementia.

Vascular dementia

Technically vascular dementia presents as a step-wise decline due to the finite number of small vascular insults that take place. The imaging features should be fairly familiar to candidates from day to day reporting. There are multifocal bilateral white matter changes which can be seen on CT when severe. Inclusion of susceptibility weighted sequences on an MRI scan allows detection of microhaemorrhages suggestive of a parallel diagnosis of cerebral amyloid angiopathy where present.

NextNeurodegenerative Disease

A 58-year-old man presents with rapidly progressive dementia and myoclonus. An MRI study demonstrates increased T2 signal in the thalamus with a ‘hockey-stick’ appearance on the FLAIR images. 18F-FDG PET confirms reduced metabolism in this region.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Autoimmune encephalitis

Familial Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease

Hypoglycaemic encephalopathy

Leigh’s disease

Variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease

explanation:
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease

CJD is a prion disease with the sporadic form being most common (85-90%). Familial disease accounts for just 10% of cases. Variant CJD gives the classical ‘Hockey stick’ high signal seen in the thalamus.

Autoimmune encephalitis can be paraneoplastic phenomenon and usually affects the limbic system with high T2 signal and restricted diffusion.

Leigh’s disease

Leigh’s disease is a rare mitochondrial disease. Imaging findings include peri-aqueductal high T2 signal, similar to Wernicke’s disease, but Leigh's disease is seen in children. Patients usually have a raised serum lactate.

explanation:
For a detailed explanation of DWI please use a more robust text than what follows. Readers should be warned that this is a very light glossing over of the concepts only.

Diffusion weighted imaging is the summation of both diffusion and T2 effects. The images must be interpreted in the light of findings on the corresponding ADC map which gives diffusion effects only. The more ‘unrestricted’ the water molecules in a given substance are, the more diffusion takes place during the slice acquisition and the faster the dephasing of the magnetism. There are multiple ADC maps with increasing B-values to see how this dephasing responds. Usually you can pick out a DWI image because the CSF is black (aide memoire ‘Dark Water Imaging’).

Restriction of diffusion is a binary entity – things either restrict or they do not. The things that restrict diffusion are relatively limited in number and you would be well advised to learn them thoroughly for day to day practice as well as for the exams.

Cytotoxic oedema – failure of the cellular membrane ion pumps leads to an increase in intracellular (restricted) water

Acute infarction

As a stroke ages the DWI increases due to the T2 effect and the ADC becomes less dark from shine through. At approximately weeks 1-4 the ADC undergoes pseudonormalisation where restricted diffusion is matched by vasogenic oedema which is not restricted. Chronic infarctions do not restrict diffusion

Hypercellularity – Limiting the ability of extracellular water to diffuse

Some gliomas

Lymphoma

High viscosity

Abscess

Acute demyelination – a complex mechanism involving glutamate

ADEM

Acute MS

Elevated protein

Epidermoid cysts (technically due to waxy content as opposed to protein)

Subacute blood

T2 shine through – this is a pseudofinding of a bright lesion on the DWI image with a corresponding high signal area on the ADC map.

stem: A 38-year-old man with ataxia undergoes an MRI scan. There is haemosiderin deposition over the cerebellum with concurrent cerebellar atrophy. You also see a circular area of T2 hypointensity.
prompt: What is the most likely explanation for his symptoms?
explanation:
Superficial siderosis

In this case an AVM has been clumsily described as the T2 hypointense rim, and chronic haemorrhage from it has caused the siderosis. It is the siderosis which has affected the cerebellum and caused the ataxia. Superficial siderosis occurs when there is deposition of haemosiderin over the pial and ependymal surfaces. This is often thought to be secondary to recurrent subarachnoid haemorrhage (for which there is a further differential besides the presence of an AVM). On MRI there is blooming artefact on the susceptibility weighted images and low signal in particular on the T2 weighted sequences. If only limited in extent it can be particularly well demonstrated in the cerebellum where it is associated with atrophy in long-standing cases. Classically the siderosis coating the cranial nerves causes a sensorineural hearing loss.

Friedrich ataxia

This rare condition usually presents in childhood. There is loss of myelination from the posterior and lateral columns of the spinal cord. On MRI therefore there is ‘cervicomedullary junction thinning’; the upper spinal cord appears very thin, despite returning normal signal. Cerebellar atrophy is associated.

Ataxia telangiectasia

This autosomal recessive syndrome can usually be recognised by the strange combination of cerebellar ataxia, pulmonary infections, immunodeficiency and cancers (lymphoma or leukaemia in children, breast and bowel cancer in adults). The cerebellar atrophy is striking.

Cavernous haemangioma

The classical feature of a cavernoma (aka cavernous haemangioma) on MRI is the ‘popcorn’ appearance caused by a bright lobulated centre surrounded by a rim of hypointensity. Haemosiderin deposition causes the blooming artefact on susceptibility weighted sequences. It is perhaps slightly counterintuitive that there can be no enhancement on post-contrast CT scans, given the vascular nature of these lesions, however when we consider that flow within the lesion may be very slow then this makes a little more sense. Another important distinguishing feature from other lesions is the fact that, unlike metastases, there is no mass effect or oedema from these lesions, despite the fact that they can often present with seizures.

Multisystem atrophy

Cerebellar atrophy is a feature of this condition but otherwise the information provided doesn’t fit. The classical imaging feature described in this condition is the ‘hot cross bun’ sign where there is T2 hyperintensity in the shape of a cross at the level of the pons.

stem: A 76-year-old man is admitted with cerebellar ataxia, and corticospinal tract involvement.
prompt: Which of the following is LEAST in-keeping with a diagnosis of Lateral Medullary Syndrome? Select ONE answer only.
options: Contralateral pain and temperature loss to the face
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which answer is LEAST in-keeping with the diagnosis.

Lateral Medullary Syndrome (Wallenburg syndrome)

This is caused by either a vertebral artery occlusion or PICA occlusion.

This is a classic scenario for an exam question and is one of those syndromes that is far more common in the exam world than in the real world. There is a short list of slightly unusual symptoms any combination of which, in the exam context, should make you suspicious about this syndrome:

Cerebellar involvement – DANISH mnemonic as per medical school

Autonomic dysfunction – ipsilateral Horner’s syndrome, hiccoughs

Sensory symptoms – symptoms of sensory loss are common place in the stroke world but in this syndrome it is specifically loss of pain and temperature sensation in the ipsilateral face and contralaterally to the rest of the body. Patients can also experience ipsilateral stabbing pains; pain symptoms are highly unusual in the stroke world and usually point to a different diagnosis.

Ipsilateral bulbar symptoms – dysphagia, dysarthria etc.

stem: A 50-year-old woman has an USS thyroid which shows a mixed cystic and solid region in the left lobe with low reflectivity overall. There are associated malignant looking lymph nodes in the left cervical chain.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis
explanation:
This question comes down to two answers: Medullary or papillary thyroid cancer.

Papillary thyroid cancer – is of low reflectivity on ultrasound and 40% have lymph node involvement at presentation. Classically there is calcification but this is not an exclusive finding Papillary carcinoma also accounts for approximately 65% of thyroid carcinoma whereas medullary carcinoma accounts for <10%. Medullary thyroid cancer – can have a familial pattern and/or association with other endocrine malignancies. Demonstrates granular calcification and nodal spread in 50% of cases.

Anaplastic thyroid cancer is usually in an older age range.

Neither De Quervain thyroiditis or Hashimoto would explain the malignant lymph nodes.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents acutely unwell. Of note in her medical history she has been taking the oral contraceptive pill. She undergoes a CT scan which shows high density of the superior sagittal sinus. An MRI is requested for follow-up.
prompt: Which of the following findings would be unusual in this condition? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
The empty delta sign is a post-contrast CT finding. Bilateral haemorrhages can be a secondary consequence to a sagittal sinus thrombosis which may point towards the diagnosis but the thrombosis itself is recognised by the empty delta sign on post-contrast CT.

Dense triangle sign pertains to the acute thrombus as it appears on an unenhanced CT scan.

On an MRI, static blood within the sagittal sinus gives rise to low signal on T1, although the thrombus itself is likely to be high in signal (if subacute in nature). Normally the sagittal sinus will appear as a flow void on T1w. Blooming artefact can be seen on T2* gradient echo sequences and is a strong indicatory of the diagnosis. Confusion can arise with time-of-flight 3D reformatted images and great care should be taken not to overdiagnose flow artefactas thrombosis. Careful reference should always be made to the source images and where there is doubt a CT venogram may be of more use.

The associated infarctions can often be haemorrhagic and parasagittal haemorrhages are reasonably common and very specific for a sagittal sinus thrombosis, but subarachnoid haemorrhage is less common (though does occur).

stem: A 64-year-old man is brought to A&E by his worried wife. She describes a sudden collapse at home and on examination it is evident that he has loss of power and sensation below T7 on the left, with pain and temperature loss on the contralateral side. An urgent MRI is requested which shows high T2 signal in the T7 vertebral body and high signal of cord at T7. There is no significant adjacent disc disease.
prompt: Which of the following is NOT a cause of Brown-Sequard syndrome?
options: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which is NOT a cause of Brown-Sequard syndrome.

Brown-Sequard syndrome

This is a specific finding where damage to the dorsal columns leads to ipsilateral loss of touch sensation and contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation due to damage to the lateral spinothalamic tracts (contralateral since these ascend after having crossed). There is also ipsilateral motor function loss.

Causes of Brown-Sequard syndrome

Traumatic

Penetrating injury

Mechanical trauma e.g. RTA

Iatrogenic injury

Compression e.g disc herniation

Spinal cord tumour

Vascular/Infarction

Aortic aneurysm repair complication

Vertebral artery dissection

Spinal cord haemorrhage

Spinal cord infarction

The vascular supply to the spinal cord is derived largely from the vertebral arteries or intercostal arteries with one longitudinal running anterior spinal cord artery and two small longitudinally running posterior spinal cord arteries.

The artery of Adamkiewicz is a particularly large segmental artery supplying the anterior spinal artery from around the level of T9. It is responsible for most of the spinal cord blood supply for the lumbar spinal cord. Damage during aortic surgery or trauma can result in spinal cord infarction.

Usually any vascular insult results in a reasonably rapid onset of symptoms. Spinal cord infarctions are no exception. Often more than one vertebral level is affected.

An MRI will showT2 hyperintensity of at least the central grey matter (if not the whole cross-section of the cord) due to oedema. As with intracranial infarctions there will be restriction of diffusion on the DWI sequences.

Particularly in the thoracic spine, the adjacent vertebral body  may also lose its blood supply and undergo infarction.

Subacute combined degeneration

This is a curious condition which can be subtle to detect. A deficiency of vitamin B12 (usually caused by malabsorption) leads to degneration within the dorsal columns of the cord. The dorsal columns carry nerves responsible for position and vibration sense and as such patients present with loss of these senses as well as sensory ataxia (balance significantly deteriorates when the patients eyes are shut thereby excluding visual stabilisation as opposed to sensory stabilisation), and hyperreflexia.

On an MRI scan there will be (if the resolution allows), a longitudinal line of high T2 signal within the cord on sagittal sequences, and often a characterisitc 'inverted-V' shape of high T2 signal on axial sequences. In some cases the 'V' is clearly seen and in others it is harder to appreciate and the finding is more of high T2 signal bilaterally and symmetrically in the region of the posterior columns.

stem: A 76-year-old man, known to have dementia, undergoes an MRI scan of his head which shows multifocal haemorrhages. His blood pressure is normal, with a normal cholesterol.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA)

The prevalence of cerebral amyloid angiopathy is high. It is present in at least a third of the over 60s. Deposition of beta-amyloid protein is the cause and results in microhaemorrhage formation. The pattern of microhaemorrhage formation is slightly different from that of chronic hypertensive encephalopathy (outlined below), with involvement of the cortical/subcortical regions but sparing of the deep white matter and basal ganglia. An elderly patient who presents with a large intracerebral haemorrhage despite a lack of trauma or hypertension should be suspected of having CAA. As with the microhaemorrhages of chronic hypertensive encephalopathy those of CAA are best demonstrated as blooming artefact on either T2* weighted sequences or susceptibility weighted images. Appearances can be quite striking.

Chronic hypertensive encephalopathy

This is slightly different from vascular dementia as the pathological process relates to microhaemorrhage formation secondary to hypertension as opposed to vasculopathy with micro-infarction. The key areas affected are those of end arteries such as the thalamic and lenticulostriate perforators; ie the thalamus, pons, caudate nucleus and internal capsule. These are best demonstrated as blooming artefact on either T2* weighted sequences or susceptibility weighted images.

Lewy body dementia

A core clinical feature to this dementia is the fluctuant nature of the symptoms. Parkinsonian features can also develop although these are usually subsequent to the memory decline. Visual hallucinations are also a feature. Radiologically there is a generalised decrease in cerebral volume (sparing the hippocampi). Temporo-parietal hypoperfusion on HMPAO Tc99m SPECT scanning is indicative of lewy body dementia.

Alzheimer disease

The radiological findings of this well known disease are diffuse sulcal and ventricular enlargement. There is a disproportionate effect to the anterior temporal lobes, hippocampi and sylvian fissures with sparing of the sensorimotor and visual cortices, thalami and cerebellum.

Pick disease

When there is disproportionate atrophy of the frontal and temporal lobes in an unusually young patient Pick disease should be suspected. This can sometimes be described as enlargement of the frontal horns but the concept is the same; volume loss of the frontal and temporal lobes.

A 9mm pituitary lesion showing hypoinentsity on T1 without enhancement

A mass showing hyperintensity to grey matter and a small dural tail

A well defined mass projecting into the interpeduncular cistern with no enhancement

A medical student examines her and presents to the consultant that she has bitemporal hemianopia. After the consultant examines her he requests an MRI scan which shows a pituitary macroadenoma.
prompt: What are the likely findings on MRI that lead to the diagnosis?
options: A 9mm pituitary lesion showing hypoinentsity on T1 without enhancement
A mass showing hyperintensity to grey matter and a small dural tail
A pituitary lesion causing expansion of the sella and suprasellar cistern, homogeneous enhancement
A well defined mass projecting into the interpeduncular cistern with no enhancement
Expansion of the left cavernous sinus by a region demonstrating significant susceptibility weighted artefact with consequential impaction on the optic nerves bilaterally
explanation:
A pituitary macroadenoma by definition is greater than 10mm in size. Aneurysms of the basilar tip are found in the same region and can cause blooming on susceptibility weighting, most usually when there has been haemorrhage.

Projection into the interpeduncular cistern is not a very specific description but hypothalamic hamartomas do not show enhancement with gadolinium. The patient is also outside of the usual age range for these hamartomas.

A dural tail is a giveaway feature for a meningioma.

stem: A 36-year-old man complains of painless facial swelling and is referred for an ultrasound scan. The scan shows bilateral parotid swelling with cysts and cervical lymph node enlargement. There is no necrosis within the lymph nodes.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
HIV parotitis

This occurs in around 5% of patients with HIV. There is diffuse lymphocytosis with enlargement of the cervical lymph nodes and hypoechoic/cystic areas seen in bilaterally enlarged parotid glands. The whole of the gland is affected.

Warthin tumour

A Warthin tumour is a differential diagnosis for a painless parotid lump and has an association with smokers. Different sources describe different imaging characteristics. A Warthin tumour usually presents as bilateral asymptomatic masses or possibly multiple unilateral masses.

Due to late encapsulation of the parotid gland within an embryo lymphoid tissue becomes contained within the parotid gland and it is from this lymphoid tissue that Warthin tumours arise.

Sjogren's syndrome

This can cause parotid swelling and is usually unilateral when it does. It would give a cystic appearance. You would however expect the usual xerostomia and xerophthalmia too. In advanced disease there is sialectasis which is better appreciated either on a sialogram or an MRI than ultrasound.

Mumps

Mumps is usually caused by a paramyxovirus and leads to diffuse tender enlargement of the parotid glands. This can be bilateral or unilateral. The diagnosis is usually evident clinically and requires no imaging.

topic: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord
stem: A 64-year-old man is brought to A&E by his worried wife. He became unwell at home and examination findings are concerning for a problem with his spinal cord. An MRI is performed and you suspect there may be subacute combined degeneration of the cord.
prompt: Which of the following is most suggestive of this diagnosis?
options: High T2 signal extending over three vertebral levels
High T2 signal in the adjacent vertebral body
Inverted-V shape of high T2 signal in the posterior columns
explanation:
Subacute combined degeneration

This is a curious condition which can be subtle to detect. A deficiency of vitamin B12 (usually caused by malabsorption) leads to degeneration within the dorsal columns of the cord. The dorsal columns carry nerves responsible for position and vibration sense and as such patients present with loss of these senses as well as sensory ataxia (balance significantly deteriorates when the patients eyes are shut thereby excluding visual stabilisation as opposed to sensory stabilisation), and hyperreflexia.

On an MRI scan there will be (if the resolution allows), a longitudinal line of high T2 signal within the cord on sagittal sequences, and often a characteristic 'inverted-V' shape of high T2 signal on axial sequences. In some cases the 'V' is clearly seen and in others it is harder to appreciate and the finding is more of high T2 signal bilaterally and symmetrically in the region of the posterior columns.

Spinal cord infarction

The vascular supply to the spinal cord is derived largely from the vertebral arteries or intercostal arteries with one longitudinal running anterior spinal cord artery and two small longitudinally running posterior spinal cord arteries.

The artery of Adamkiewicz is a particularly large segmental artery supplying the anterior spinal artery from around the level of T9. It is responsible for most of the spinal cord blood supply for the lumbar spinal cord. Damage during aortic surgery or trauma can result in spinal cord infarction.

Usually any vascular insult results in a reasonably rapid onset of symptoms. Spinal cord infarctions are no exception. Often more than one vertebral level is affected.

An MRI will showT2 hyperintensity of at least the central grey matter (if not the whole cross-section of the cord) due to oedema. As with intracranial infarctions there will be restriction of diffusion on the DWI sequences.

Particularly in the thoracic spine, the adjacent vertebral body  may also lose its blood supply and undergo infarction.

explanation:
Trauma is the most common cause of subarachnoid haemorrhage and intracranial aneurysms are the most common cause, by a large margin, in non-traumatic cases.

Invasive angiogram

stem: You are reviewing the HMPAO images from a patient who presented to his GP with a gradual decline in memory. You suspect the patient may have Alzheimer disease.
prompt: Which of the following would support this diagnosis?
options: Reduced uptake in the precuneus and cingulate gyrus
Reduced uptake of the frontal lobes
explanation:
Functional imaging in dementia

Tc99m-HMPAO SPECT and 18F-FDG PET produce very similar patterns when used to image patients with cognitive decline however the latter is considered to have a greater sensitivity and specificity and is therefore preferred.

Two structures bear particular importance in the imaging of dementia; the precuneus and the cingulate gyrus. Both are best appreciate on sagittal views.

Precuneus: The precuneus is located on the medial surface of each hemisphere, in the posterior parietal lobe. It has functions in motor planning, working memory and also connections to the visual pathways.

The cingulate gyrus: The cinculate gyrus is also located on the medial side of each hemisphere and runs anteroposteriorly just above the corpus callosum. The cingulate gyrus has complex functions to do with learning, emotional response and memory.

Alzheimer disease

The radiological findings of this well known disease are diffuse sulcal and ventricular enlargement. There is a disproportionate effect to the anterior temporal lobes, hippocampi and sylvian fissures with sparing of the sensorimotor and visual cortices, thalami and cerebellum. Functional studies (Tc-HMPAO SPECT or F-18 FDG PET) show reduced uptake in the precuneus, posterior cingulate gyrus, frontal and temporoparietal lobes but with characteristic sparing of the sensorimotor cortex and basal ganglia bilaterally. Importantly there is also sparing of the occipital lobes, which helps differentiate it from Lewy body dementia where the occipital lobes are involved. Other differences between the two conditions are seen with specific dopamine transporter agent imaging techniques

Lewy body dementia

A core clinical feature to this dementia is the fluctuant nature of the symptoms. Parkinsonian features can also develop although these are usually subsequent to the memory decline. Visual hallucinations are also a feature.  Radiologically there is a generalised decrease in cerebral volume (sparing the hippocampi). Temporo-parietal hypoperfusion on HMPAO Tc99m SPECT scanning is indicative of Lewy body dementia. Involvement of the occipital cortex, which is typically spared in Alzheimers disease, sets the two apart from one another on PET studies. The cingulate island sign has also been ascribed to Lewy body dementia, where there is preservation of metabolism in the  mid-posterior cingulate gyrus. If present, this is said to be specific for Lewy body dementia.

Vascular dementia

Technically vascular dementia presents as a step-wise decline due to the finite number of small vascular insults that take place. The imaging features should be fairly familiar to candidates from day to day reporting. There are multifocal bilateral white matter changes which can be seen on CT when severe.  Inclusion of susceptibility weighted sequences on an MRI scan allows detection of microhaemorrhages suggestive of a parallel diagnosis of cerebral amyloid angiopathy where present.

stem: You are reviewing a CT of a 74-year-old man who has an acquired cholesteatoma.
prompt: Which of the following is correct? Select ONE answer only.
options: The Eustachian tube opens into the mesotympanum
The Prussak space is found behind the inferior part of the tympanic membrane
The head of the malleus is situated in the epitympanum
The short crus of the incus is situated in the mesotympanum
The stapes is connected to the malleus
explanation:
The anatomy of the middle ear is complex but important and contains a number of specific anatomical terms.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

The epitympanum, also known as the attic, is the superior portion above the highest point of the tympanic membrane. It contains the head of the malleus and the short crus of the incus (These give the appearance of an ice-cream cone on an axial CT).

Image © Medical Exam Prep

The Prussak space is found within the epitympanum and is a tiny space at the top of the tympanic membrane, just behind the scutum. Its clinical relevance is that it is the usual origin for pars flaccida cholesteatomas.

The aditus ad antrum connects the epitympanum to the mastoid antrum and thence the mastoid air cells.

The tegmen mastoidium (tegmen means roof) is the point at which the mastoid air cells meet the temporal lobe of the brain.

The tegmen tympani is the point at which the upper most extent of the epitympanum reaches the temporal lobe of the brain.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

The mesotympanum is the space posterior to the tympanic membrane and contains the body of the incus, the manubrium (connected to the tympanic membrane) and the anterior process of the malleus and the stapes. The stapes is connected to the incus as well as the oval window of the cochlea. There is also a round window placed more inferiorly which bulges to allow compression waves transmitted from the stapes to the oval window to travel through the cochlea.

The hypotympanum is a far less significant space than either the epitympanum or the mesotympanum. It begins at the inferior most extent of the tympanic membrane. The Eustachian tube opens into the hypotympanum anteriorly.

The neurologist notes a family history of similar issues. She goes on to have an MRI scan which shows low T2 signal in the globus pallidi bilaterally.
prompt: What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
This question draws on the classic differential diagnosis of ‘basal ganglia signal changes’.

Poisoning

Impairment of mitochondrial function in the highly metabolically active basal ganglia classically causes high T2/FLAIR signal in a bilateral symmetrical fashion but the T1 is usually low in signal. Methanol, cyanide, and carbon monoxide can all cause this.

Neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation aka hallervorden-Spatz syndrome

The classic radiological feature which comes up here is the ‘eye of the tiger’ sign where there is low T2 signal in the globus pallidus due to iron accumulation. Confusingly the patient can go on to develop high T2 signal in these areas as gliosis develops. The typical patient will be a young woman with a family history of movement disorders presenting with rigidity or bradykinesia.

Behcet syndrome

Behcet syndrome is classically described as a triad of oral and genital ulcers associated with one of several ocular manifestations. Its effect on the CNS tends to be as meningoencephalitis or venous sinus thrombosis. In the basal ganglia, in some patients, it can cause lesions with low T1 signal and high T2 signal.

Toxoplasmosis

Infections derived from intrauterine transmission cause periventricular calcifications affecting the basal ganglia. Otherwise, in AIDS related toxoplasmosis the findings are more of multiple ring enhancing lesions.

Toxoplasmosis is a more common finding in AIDS patients than lymphoma is, by a large margin. On MRI it is seen as multiple ring enhancing lesions, which can show haemorrhage particularly following treatment. One of the stronger differentiators between toxoplasmosis and lymphoma is the SPECT findings. This is sometimes termed ‘hypometabolic’ meaning the lesions do not demonstrate SPECT uptake. The table below gives some general features of the two conditions. There is however considerable overlap in the imaging features despite these broad trends.

Lymphoma

A ring solitary ring enhancing lesion in the context of an AIDS patient should raise lymphoma as a strong possibility. Multiple lesions can and do occur however, making the distinction from toxoplasmosis challenging. Lymphoma is also part of the differential diagnosis for lesions that cross the corpus callosum and this can be a feature that separates it from toxoplasmosis, although is not a feature of exclusion. Similarly if haemorrhage has been seen associated with the lesion this is more a feature of toxoplasmosis but absence of haemorrhage does not exclude toxoplasmosis.

stem: An elderly man is admitted following a fall. His CT head shows multiple highly attenuating lesions. There is no lesional haemorrhage.
prompt: What is next most appropriate investigation?
explanation:
This question is contraversial given modern day NHS practices. Assuming that the question is driving at malignant melanoma metastases (dense lesions without haemorrhage), none of the other answers would be relevant however in usual practice this kind of patient would almost certainly get a CT CAP at the very least. However, we have to ask what the potential diagnosis is meant to be behind each of the proffered answers. A CXR or a CT chest and liver would be for the investigation of lung cancer, some of which can cause haemorrhagic metastases. A Renal ultrasound would be the investigation for a potential RCC, also potentially causing haemorrhagic metastases. Colonoscopy would be for investigation of suspected colon cancer. Mucinous adenocarcinoma of the colon can cause calcified metastases and the question is irritatingly ambiguous in this regard but on balance the description fits better with dense metastases from malignant melanoma rather than calcified metastases.

stem: NextMRI head findings An imaging set of a young man in his 20s is being reviewed for teaching purposes. He has chronic liver disease and high signal in his basal ganglia on T1W.
prompt: Which of the following would best explain these findings?
explanation:
Wilson disease

Wilson disease is a disorder of copper metabolism affecting the liver. It causes white matter atrophy and T2 hyperintensities predominantly affecting the basal ganglia and thalami. T1 signal is also high in these areas, owing to the paramagnetic effects of the copper, differentiating it from many of the other basal ganglia disorders. There is a classical feature of ‘sparing of the red nucleus’ leading to an appearance known as the giant panda sign at the level of the pons.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

Central pontine myelinolysis

This occurs when there are osmotic shifts following rapid correction of electrolyte disturbances. The classical scenarios given are usually alcoholics or liver transplant patients. There is asymmetrical noninflammatory demyelination of the pons which appears as high T2 signal in not only the pons but also the basal ganglia and thalami. The T1 signal is far less affected.

Carbon monoxide poisoning

Impairment of mitochondrial function in the highly metabolically active basal ganglia classically causes high T2/FLAIR signal (especially in the medial portion of the globus pallidus, but also in the remainder of the basal ganglia too) in a bilateral symmetrical fashion but the T1 is usually low in signal.

Huntington disease

There are relatively few radiological manifestations of Huntington disease. The usual one described is atrophy of the heads of the caudate nuclei with consequential prominence of the adjacent lateral ventricle frontal horns with a ‘box’ like appearance. Various studies have been done to quantify the extent of this atrophy.

Fabry disease

Fabry disease is caused by an X-linked inborn error of metabolism. On an MRI brain there is often evidence of small vessel ischaemic change, particularly affecting posterior circulation territories, and high T1 signal in the basal ganglia thought to be caused by mineral deposition. It is associated with end stage renal failure but not liver disease per se.

explanation:
Embryologically the thyroid originates from the foramen caecum at the posterior aspect of the tongue and migrates inferiorly to its usual position along the thyroglossal duct. Where there is failure of this migration thyroid tissue can be found at any point along the path of the thyroglossal duct. Although not classically described as cystic in nature, this answer is the best of the choices provided.

A dermoid cyst classically contains fluid, fat and calcium as well as being a midline structure. They can be found in the floor of the mouth but are usually more complex in morphology than straiqhtforwardly cystic.

A thornwaldt cyst is a midline congenital pouch found in the nasopharynx of young adults. It presents as halitosis or a foul taste in the mouth.

A thyroglossal duct cyst would not demonstrate any enhancement unless it were inflamed.

A branchial cleft cyst would not enhance, and are not midline structures.

She refers him to a Neurology consultant. An MRI scan shows high signal in the region of the sella on T1 and T1 fat saturated sequences.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Pituitary apoplexy

Pathologically, pituitary apoplexy is infarction which can take place with or without haemorrhage. Over half of patients have an underlying macroadenoma; haemorrhage into a pre-existing macroadenoma is the usual presentation. 'All' patients present with a headache and panhypopituitarism. Visual impairment is also common as the pituitary enlarges and impacts on the chiasm. On a CT scan there will be a sellar/suprasellar mass (ie pituitary enlargement). Hyperdensity is caused by the underlying haemorrhage, if present. On an MRI, the pituitary can be seen to be enlarged with T1 hyperintensity (specifically in the subacute phases). In the chronic phase however, the pituitary will be involuted and small, even appearing as an 'empty sella'.

Sheehan syndrome is pituitary apoplexy due to hypovolaemic shock and can be consequential to delivery. At the time of apoplexy, the predominant issue for the patient is the systemic hypovolaemia for which aggressive management is usually already being pursued. In the early days following the delivery, the first hypopituitary issues to manifest is usually any or all of hyponatraemia, diabetes insipidus or hypothyroidism. At this time the MRI findings can vary from a normal appearing pituitary through to the classic pituitary apoplexy appearances of an enlarged pituitary with high T1 signal. Patients can also present many months or years later with panhypoituitarism at which time an MRI will usually show an empty sella.

Rathke cleft cyst

The location of this lesion, if it can be appreciated, is the giveaway feature; between the anterior and posterior pituitary, even in the absence of any other features which would be noted on the scan but which have not been provided and which would usually be used to eliminated any further doubt as to the diagnosis. Rathke's cleft cyst is classically hyperbright on T2. The lack of symptoms is also a key feature which points away from several of the other diagnoses given. Microadenomas are below 10mm in size, but 80% return low signal on T1 weighted sequences. Craniopharyngiomas are usually lobulated, often contain cystic and calcified areas. Pathologically the appearance of the cholesterol-rich components gives rise to a classical 'machinery oil' type appearance of craniopharyngiomas.

Craniopharyngioma

Craniopharyngiomas was previously thought to have a bimodal age distribution with a peaks at around age 12 and age 50. The two different age distributions actually represent different tumour types with overlapping features. In children these are adamantinomatous craniopharyngiomas and in adults they are papillary craniopharyngiomas. Both present with symptoms attributable to their sella/suprasella location. In children this includes growth retardation due to compression of the hypothalamus. Calcification is more common in the paediatric group. Avid enhancement post-gadolinium is a good differentiating feature from Rathke cleft cysts which will only show mural enhancement. Adenomas enhance variably. Adenomas can also show cystic degeneration.

explanation:
On balance nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (NSF) seems to fit best as the itchiness of the rash described fits better than it does for sarcoid. Dyspnoea has been described in NSF patients but is by no means a prominent feature though. The question writer has however, gone to the trouble of telling us that the patient has had an MRI scan which adds to the weight of evidence for NSF. On the other hand there is no suggestion that the patient has a poor renal function to predispose him or her to NSF (except possibly a post-iodiniated contrast nephropathy following the CT scan, despite the lack of clarity regarding time frames in this regard).

NSF

Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis is a very nasty condition which develops a few weeks or months after a patient has received Gadolinium in patients with acute or chronic renal failure, in particular post liver or kidney transplant patients (NB. hepatorenal syndrome). No particular therapy for it has been found to be effective. Dyspnoea has been described in association with NSF in some literature.

Sarcoidosis

Erythema nodosum is a well described manifestation of sarcoidosis but is usually described as tender erythematous nodules.

The thoracic manifestations of sarcoid are legion and shortness of breath could well be a symptom.

Neurosarcoid classically affects the cranial nerves but mass lesions can occur.

SLE

The cutaneous manifestations of SLE are not usually itchy and the brain parenchyma is not often involved (with the exception of haemorrhage or abscess formation), although neuropsychiatric symptoms do occur.

Whipple disease

Whipple disease causes malabsorption. Tropical sprue also causes malabsorption and is associated with dermatitis herpetiformis but otherwise is unrelated to the scenario described.

Extrinsic allergic alveolitis

This is a thoracic condition caused by an excessive immune response to an inhaled antigen.

stem: A 32-year-old lady with pre-eclampsia who delivered 2 days ago by normal vaginal delivery develops sudden cortical blindness. She has been receiving treatment for pre-eclampsia both before and after delivery. She is taken for a scan.
prompt: What are the expected imaging features?
options: Enlarged pituitary with high T1 and low T2 signal
Ischaemic changes to both occipital lobes
Low attenuation and loss of grey/white matter differentiation in both occipital lobes
explanation:
This is not a straightforward question; the answers given in this question are deliberately confusing but this question is ultimately aimed at PRES (posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome). Although the pathophysiology of PRES is not fully understood, in imaging terms it is specifically the subcortical white matter which is involved and shows ischemic changes (low attenuation on CT and high T2/FLAIR on MRI). Loss of grey/white matter differentiation implies territorial infarction with cytotoxic oedema as opposed to the vasogenic (and reversible) oedema of PRES where the grey/white matter junction is preserved. Given this, we can choose the answer given over the other option mentioning the occipital lobes. Around 10% of patients with PRES also have intraparenchymal haemorrhage.

Classically PRES presents as a visual disturbance in a pregnant or post-partum patient with pre-eclampsia and CT shows haemorrhages in the posterior fossa. The main underlying pathological process is vasogenic oedema. Technically PRES is not exclusive to pregnancy or the post-partum period, and often with a history (implied or provided) of pre-eclampsia. Other causes such as SLE or immunosuppression are also technically feasible. Cortical blindness is the classical symptom.

Sheehan syndrome is pituitary apoplexy due to hypovolaemic shock and can be consequential to delivery. At the time of apoplexy, the predominant issue for the patient is the systemic hypovolaemia for which aggressive management is usually already being pursued. In the early days following the delivery, the first hypopituitary issues to manifest is usually any or all of hyponatraemia, diabetes insipidus or hypothyroidism. At this time the MRI findings can vary from a normal appearing pituitary through to the classic pituitary apoplexy appearances of an enlarged pituitary with high T1 signal. Patients can also present many months or years later with panhypoituitarism at which time an MRI will usually show an empty sella.
