stem: A 50-year-old man is seen in a neurology outpatient clinic with complaints of progressive memory loss and some movement problems. He subsequently undergoes an MRI scan of his brain. There is high T2 and high FLAIR signal in the basal ganglia bilaterally. You notice that the abnormal areas also show restriction of diffusion.
prompt: What is the SINGLE most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease

There are three types of this prion transmitted disease; the one linked to the BSE (bovine spongiform encephalopathy) epidemic of the late 1980s and 1990s, a rare familial variant, and finally a sporadic version which accounts for the vast majority of the cases. Clinically there is a rapidly progressive dementia with ataxia and myoclonus which should be the give-away feature even before imaging features are discussed. On MRI, the reported finding is of high T2/FLAIR signal in the basal ganglia bilaterally and symmetrically (particularly the putamen). The pulvinar sign is often described in association with cJD which describes high FLAIR signal in the pulvinar thalamic nuclei (called the hockey stick sign). Strangely the signal changes are a rare cause of restriction of diffusion, seen as bright areas on DWI. Important negatives for this condition are the lack of enhancement with contrast and the lack of white matter involvement (since the white matter is protected by its myelin sheath).

Image © Medical Exam Prep

Huntington disease

There are relatively few radiological manifestations of Huntington disease. The usual one described is atrophy of the heads of the caudate nuclei with consequential prominence of the adjacent lateral ventricle frontal horns with a ‘box’ like appearance. Various studies have been done to quantify the extent of this atrophy.

Lewy body dementia

A core clinical feature to this dementia is the fluctuant nature of the symptoms. Parkinsonian features can also develop although these are usually subsequent to the memory decline. Visual hallucinations are also a feature. Radiologically there is a generalised decrease in cerebral volume (sparing the hippocampi). Temporo-parietal hypoperfusion on HMPAO Tc99m SPECT scanning is indicative of Lewy body dementia. Involvement of the occipital cortex, which is typically spared in Alzheimers disease, sets the two apart from one another on PET studies. The cingulate island sign has also been ascribed to Lewy body dementia, where there is preservation of metabolism in the mid-posterior cingulate gyrus. If present, this is said to be specific for Lewy body dementia.

Alzheimer's disease

The radiological findings of this well known disease are diffuse sulcal and ventricular enlargement. There is a disproportionate effect to the anterior temporal lobes, hippocampi and sylvian fissures with sparing of the sensorimotor and visual cortices, thalami and cerebellum.

Parkinson's disease

Generalised cerebral atrophy occurs with Parkinson's disease but is a highly non-specific feature. There are, however, radiological findings in the midbrain which although subtle, are far more specific. Parkinson's disease occurs when there is neuronal loss in the substantia nigra, specifically the pars compacta of the substantia nigra. On a T2 weighted MRI image this appears as blurring of the intermediate signal intensity line which separates the two adjacent low intensity structures (these are the pars reticulata of the substantia nigra and the red nucleus).

stem: A 78-year-old man undergoes an MRI after a routine asymptomatic screening ear exam shows a blue tympanic membrane. The scan shows a middle ear mass which is homogeneously high on T1 and T2.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A cholesterol granuloma should be at the top of the list when a blue tympanic membrane is found. The features described in the question are classical for a cholesterol granuloma – the other notable feature not provided is the absence of pulsatile tinnitus which helps distinguish it from a glomus tympanicum. A cholesterol granuloma contains both cholesterol crystals and blood (hence is bright on T1) whereas a cholesteatoma is isointense to brain parenchyma on T1 and can apparently be seen clinically as a whitish mass behind the tympanic membrane. Meningiomas are hypo or isointense on T1.

prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Cryptococcus

This is an opportunistic yeast-like fungus which therefore requires a degree of immunocompromise, typically AIDS. The cryptococcomas are non-enhancing low density lesions in the basal ganglia. These show as high signal on T2 sequences. A granulomatous meningitis can also occur. They can be differentiated from VR spaces on FLAIR where VR spaces will suppress (being CSF in content) whereas the mucoid cryptococcomas will not.

Toxoplasmosis

Toxoplasmosis is a more common finding in AIDS patients than lymphoma is, by a large margin. On MRI it is seen as multiple ring enhancing lesions, which can show haemorrhage particularly following treatment. One of the stronger differentiators between toxoplasmosis and lymphoma is the SPECT findings. This is sometimes termed ‘hypometabolic’ meaning the lesions do not demonstrate SPECT uptake. The table below gives some general features of the two conditions. There is however considerable overlap in the imaging features despite these broad trends.

Lymphoma

A ring solitary ring enhancing lesion in the context of an AIDS patient should raise lymphoma as a strong possibility. Multiple lesions can and do occur however, making the distinction from toxoplasmosis challenging. Lymphoma is also part of the differential diagnosis for lesions that cross the corpus callosum and this can be a feature that separates it from toxoplasmosis, although is not a feature of exclusion. Similarly if haemorrhage has been seen associated with the lesion this is more a feature of toxoplasmosis but absence of haemorrhage does not exclude toxoplasmosis.

HIV encephalopathy

Separating HIV encephalitis from PML can challenging in real life. HIV encephalitis causes bilateral symmetrical white matter changes, seen as high T2 signal (The T1 sequences can be normal). There is also sparing of the subcortical U-fibres.

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML)

This is a JC virus mediated phenomenon which causes asymmetrical patchy white matter changes. These can be bilateral. The testable feature is involvement of the cortical U-fibres which separates it from HIV encephalopathy where the U-fibres are spared.

stem: A 40-year-old lady is brought into A&E with neurological problems. She undergoes a CT scan which shows multiple lesions and you suspect she may have neurocysticercosis.
prompt: Which of the following features would be consistent with this diagnosis?
options: Comma shaped calcification in the paraspinal muscles
Sheets of calcification over major joints
Thick serpiginous calcification adjacent to the ankle joint
Thin serpiginous calcification in the web spaces of the hand
explanation:
Neurocysticercosis

Cysticercosis is caused by a tapeworm native to low income countries and carried by pigs. It is the most common parasitic infection involving the central nervous system and the central nervous system is itself commonly affected during the disease process; around 90% of cases show CNS involvement. The larva disseminate via the suparachnoid and intraventricular system and consequentially the meninges are most frequently affected, being involved in around 40% of cases, with particular involvement of the basal cisterns. Parenchymal involvement occurs in around a fifth of cases. The larval cells (termed cysticerci) also migrate to large skeletal muscle and, following destruction, become calcified and visible on plain radiographs as 'rice-grain' calcification. The long axis of the foci of calcification is usually orientated along the muscle fibres in which they are situated.

Parasitic stage

Features

Larval

Small foci of oedema

Vesicular

Small CSF cysts without surrounding oedema but containing a 2-3mm mural nodule (cyst with a dot)

Colloidal vesicular

Ring enhancing cyst with proteinaceous content. The contents never enhance, being derived from the tapeworm, not the host human.

Focal seizures

Nodular granular stage

Cyst shrinks and becomes isointense to brain on T1, hypointense on T2

Calcified stage

Small focal calcifications appearing 1-10years following acute infection

Rice-like muscle calcification

Seizures or asymptomatic

Other parasitic calcifications within soft tissues:

Armillifer - comma shaped, found within the muscles of the trunk

Loa loa - serpiginous thread, found in the web spaces of the hand

Guinea worm - thicker serpiginous, especially around the lower limbs

Dermatomyositis characteristically causes sheet-like calcification, often overlying large joints.

topic: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord
stem: A 64-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department by his worried wife. He became unwell at home and examination findings suggest a problem with his spinal cord. An MRI is performed, and you suspect there may be subacute combined degeneration of the cord.
prompt: Which of the following is most suggestive of this diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
options: High T2 signal extending over three vertebral levels
High T2 signal in the adjacent vertebral body
Inverted-V shape of high T2 signal in the posterior columns
explanation:
Subacute combined degeneration

This is a curious condition which can be subtle to detect. A deficiency of vitamin B12 (usually caused by malabsorption) leads to degeneration within the dorsal columns of the cord. The dorsal columns carry nerves responsible for position and vibration sense and as such patients present with loss of these senses as well as sensory ataxia (balance significantly deteriorates when the patients’ eyes are shut thereby excluding visual stabilisation as opposed to sensory stabilisation), and hyperreflexia.

On an MRI scan there will be (if the resolution allows), a longitudinal line of high T2 signal within the cord on sagittal sequences, and often a characteristic 'inverted-V' shape of high T2 signal on axial sequences. In some cases, the 'V' is clearly seen and in others it is harder to appreciate and the finding is more of high T2 signal bilaterally and symmetrically in the region of the posterior columns.

Image sourced from WikipediaCourtesy of Chiara Briani CC BY-SA 3.0

Spinal cord infarction

The vascular supply to the spinal cord is derived largely from the vertebral arteries or intercostal arteries with one longitudinal running anterior spinal cord artery and two small longitudinally running posterior spinal cord arteries.

The artery of Adamkiewicz is a particularly large segmental artery supplying the anterior spinal artery from around the level of T9. It is responsible for most of the spinal cord blood supply for the lumbar spinal cord. Damage during aortic surgery or trauma can result in spinal cord infarction.

Usually any vascular insult results in a reasonably rapid onset of symptoms. Spinal cord infarctions are no exception. Often more than one vertebral level is affected.

An MRI will show T2 hyperintensity of at least the central grey matter (if not the whole cross-section of the cord) due to oedema. As with intracranial infarctions there will be restriction of diffusion on the DWI sequences.

Particularly in the thoracic spine, the adjacent vertebral body may also lose its blood supply and undergo infarction.

stem: A 70-year-old man with a high Hba1c and poorly controlled hypertension undergoes a CT scan of his head. This shows multiple fluid density spaces in both basal ganglia. A subsequent MRI shows no restriction in diffusion.
prompt: Which of the following best explains these findings?
explanation:
In day to day reporting would be second nature to diagnose these. Both VR spaces and lacunar infarctions could be described in this manner however the history of diabetes and hypertension shifts the balance more towards lacunar infarctions. Chronic infarctions do not restrict diffusion.

Cryptococcus

This is an opportunistic yeast-like fungus which therefore requires a degree of immunocompromise, typically AIDS. The cryptococcomas are non-enhancing low density lesions in the basal ganglia. A granulomatous meningitis can also occur. They can be differentiated from VR spaces on FLAIR where VR spaces will suppress (being CSF in content) whereas the mucoid cryptococcomas will not.

Neurocysticercosis

A CNS infection caused by a tapeworm native to low income countries and carried by pigs. Cysts calcify over time. The cysts are classically described as a ‘cyst with a dot’.

Lyme disease

Lyme disease is caused by the bacterium Borrelia burdorferi which is carried by ticks. Neurological findings are cranial or peripheral neuropathies and meningitis. On MRI there can be areas of high T2 signal and the condition is known as an MS mimic.

NextCarotid doppler findings

A 54-year-old man collapses while playing golf. On arrival in A+E the blood pressure in his arms is found to be different. He is thought to have suffered a stroke and undergoes carotid Doppler study. This shows reversal of flow in his left vertebral artery with biphasic flow in his left axillary and brachial arteries. The right is normal.

What is the diagnosis?

Coarctation repair complication

History of Blalock-Taussig surgery

Subclavian steal syndrome

Takayasu aortitis

Thoracic aortic dissection

prompt: What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
The key to this question is ‘reversal of flow in the vertebral artery’. Subclavian steal syndrome occurs when blood supplying the arm (usually the left arm) travels via the ipsilateral vertebral artery in order to bypass a proximal obstruction of the subclavian artery. The distal subclavian artery ‘steals’ blood from the vertebral artery circulation. This gives rise to two different categories of symptoms:

Arm -  weaker pulses, numbness, paraesthesia, fingertip necrosis

Brain - syncope, ischaemic symptoms

The most likely cause of subclavian steal would be atherosclerosis. Takayasu aortitis can indeed cause subclavian steal but would not be at the top of a differential list without further prompts from the history. Likewise thoracic aortic dissection can also cause steal and would be a reasonable guess but subclavian steal as an answer is more accurate.

Blalock-Taussig surgery is performed in the management of Tetralogy of Fallot and is included as a differential here simply because the subclavian artery is (or used to be, prior to the advent of synthetic grafting) ligated during the procedure.

Similarly complications following repair of an aortic coarctation can also lead to subclavian steal.

stem: You are reviewing the images from a patient being investigated for primary hyperparathyroidism. The CT and MRI images are in off-site storage and the retrieval system is broken.
prompt: Which of the following would be the best options to chose instead?
explanation:
The question is asking how is best to locate a suspected ectopic parathyroid adenoma. The traditional answer used to be a Sestamibi scan (Tc99m MIBI). Prior to this technetium-thallium subtraction imaging used to be the best test.

In recent years PET/CT has entered into the debate and C-11 Methionine PET/CT is now considered to have a role in parathyroid adenoma localisation. The available evidence currently suggests that PET/CT be used as an adjunct to traditional localisation methods where results from those have proven inconclusive. Sestamibi is still the first-line investigation in the NHS but how is ‘best’ defined? This is a contentious area and the authors strongly suggest you to do your own research into this particular topic.

In the author’s experience however, if PET is given as an option to choose instead of Sestamibi, it is probably because the question writers are of a mind that it is better. Of course if PET is not even an option then the correct answer would be sestamibi.

Octreotide scanning is done for the localisation of neuroendocrine tumours; it is a somatostatin analogue.

MIBG scanning is also done for the localisation of neuroendocrine tumours.

stem: A 76-year-old man presents with Vernet syndrome. He undergoes an urgent MRI scan of his head which shows an irregular mass causing significant bony erosion, and extending into the middle ear. There is low signal on T1 and high signal on T2 with marked enhancement post-contrast. There are both flow voids and foci of hyperintensity within the mass.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Vernet syndrome is the name for a collection of symptoms caused by pathology at the jugular foramen and consequentially affecting cranial nerves IX, X and XI ie. Loss of taste to the posterior third of the tongue, vocal cord paralysis, dysphasia, weakness of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius.

There is a differential diagnosis for such pathology the identification of which will depend on the further imaging features provided. This question could easily be asked in a way to point to any of the other diagnoses provided.

A jugular foramen metastasis will be destructive and infiltrating with possible enlargement or pathological enhancement of the nerve roots and obliteration of normal fat planes. No particular history of a primary malignancy has been offered though.

A paraganglioma (or glomus jugulare tumour) is the most common cause of Vernet syndrome. This will cause infiltration of the connective tissue planes following the path of least resistance. There can be a moth eaten pattern of temporal bone destruction with associated ossicular destruction and consequential hearing loss. A so-called ‘salt and pepper’ appearance is classical.

A neural sheath tumour (ie a schwannoma or neurofibroma) will cause smooth scalloping of the adjacent bone.

A meningioma will have classical meningioma features (Extra-axial mass appearing isodense on CT with avid enhancement post-contrast, variable signal characteristics on MRI with avid enhancement post-contrast). Bony hyperostosis may be seen.

A PNET in this area would more usually present as a progressive bulbar palsy and appears as a destructive mass causing irregular bony destruction.

stem: A 6-month-old girl undergoes an MRI scan under sedation for investigation of severe developmental delay. The scan shows multiple periventricular calcifications.
prompt: What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
A lack of information is as fustrating in practice questions as it is in the exam. In these situations it is important to use any information you have been provided.

CMV

This is by far the most common TORCH infection (almost twice as common as all the others put together). Periventricular calcification is the most common finding. It is also commonly associated with polymicrogyria.

HSV

Haemorrhagic infarction is a prominent feature of HSV, with subsequent encephalomalacia. It is usually HSV-2 rather than HSV-1.

Rubella

Focal high signal in the white matter is the most common finding.

Toxoplasmosis

Toxoplasmosis is a reasonable suggestion if there is hydrocephalus with the calcifications. Toxoplasmosis is the second most common TORCH infection after CMV.

HIV

Frontal predominant atrophy is the main feature with basal ganglia calcification.

prompt: What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
The presence of hydrocephalus is key in this question, which should steer you away from the most common TORCH (CMV) and towards toxoplasmosis. The key features of the TORCH infections are below:

stem: A 45-year-old man with known HIV presents with deteriorating memory problems and word finding difficulties. He undergoes an MRI scan which shows bilateral white matter high signal on T2 and FLAIR. The radiologist notes sparing of the subcortical U-fibres.
prompt: Which of the following would make PML more likely than HIV encephalopathy? Select ONE answer only.
options: High T2 signal in white matter
Low T2 signal in white matter
explanation:
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML)

This is a JC virus mediated phenomenon which causes asymmetrical patchy white matter changes. These can be bilateral. The testable feature is involvement of the cortical U-fibres which separates it from HIV encephalopathy where the U-fibres are spared. Other differentiating features are that PML usually causes asymmetrical changes whereas those of HIV encephalopathy are usually symmetrical and that cortical atrophy is a feature of HIV encephalopathy but not PML.

HIV encephalopathy

Separating HIV encephalopathy from PML can challenging in real life. HIV encephalopathy causes bilateral symmetrical white matter changes, seen as high T2 signal (The T1 sequences can be normal). There is also sparing of the subcortical U-fibres. Another feature which separates it from PML is the presence of notable cerebral atrophy. This is not a feature of PML and if present should be attributed to a second pathology.

HIV encephalopathy

PML

No cerebral atrophy

Symmetrical changes

prompt: Select one answer only.

Distinguishing between Graves eye disease and IgG4 related orbital disease (previously termed pseudotumour, which is now considered a separate entity, albeit with overlapping features) should be relatively simple.

Graves eye disease starts with one muscle involved but can progress to involve others too. The mnemonic for remembering the order in which the eye muscles are affected in Graves eye disease is: I’m Slow (Inferior, Medial, Superior, Lateral). Otherwise the following table compares the features of the two conditions.

IgG4 related disease is a relatively newly developed concept with a number of radiological avenues.

stem: A 54-year-old male presents with disinhibition and ataxia. An MRI scan demonstrates optic nerve atrophy, subcortical white matter necrosis and hemorrhagic putaminal necrosis.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Methanol poisoning

Optic nerve atrophy, subcortical white matter necrosis and hemorrhagic putaminal necrosis are classical findings.

Carbon monoxide poisoning

T2 bright signal in the globus pallidus is the usual finding.

Marchiafava-Bignami syndrome

This is often seen in alcoholic patients. There is swelling and T2 bright signal affecting the corpus callosum, involving the central fibres but sparing the dorsal and ventral fibres. This is known as the sandwich sign.

Lead toxicity

This does not cause any classical neurological findings, but results in bands of increased density at the metaphyses.

Iron overload

Iron accumulation in the brain causes signal drop out in the basal ganglia.

stem: A 58-year-old man presents with a painless cheek swelling. He has a long history of smoking. On ultrasound this is shown to be a cystic parotid mass. On MRI there are multiple areas of High T1 signal.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Warthin tumours are associated with smoking. They also have a male preponderance.

A Thornwaldt cyst is a midline congenital pouch found in the nasopharynx of young adults. It presents as halitosis or a foul taste in the mouth.

Sjogren syndrome can cause parotid swelling and is usually unilateral when it does. It would give a cystic appearance. You would however expect the usual xerostomia and xerophthalmia too and there isn’t a particular association with smoking.

HIV parotitis does give cystic parotid enlargement but it is usually bilateral and involves the whole gland diffusely rather than focally.

Squamous cell carcinoma – When these arise from the scalp and other nearby areas they can metastasize via the lymph nodes and the parotid lymph nodes represent a very common location for nodal metastasis in these cases however they are less likely to be cystic.

stem: A 43-year-old man with anosmia undergoes an MRI scan. This shows a central, subfrontal well defined tumour with bilateral oedema adjacent to it.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Approximately 10% of meningiomas occur at the olfactory groove. Although usually benign, meningiomas can cause oedema when they become larger.

Pick disease is frontotemporal atrophy presenting as dementia at a young age.

Juvenile angiofibromas are tumours of the soft tissues of the soft tissues of the nasopharynx.

CADASIL (Cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy) The typical patient is a youngish adult (30-50s) with recurrent TIAs/strokes, and/or psychiatric symptoms such as depression, psychosis. The classical area affected is the anterior temporal lobes and external capsules.

A glioblastoma multiforme (Grade IV astrocytoma) is sometimes referred to as a butterfly glioma due to its crossing of the corpus callosum. On the scan the distinction between this and a meningioma should be straightforward depending on whether there were features consistent with either an intra-axial or extra-axial mass. This question is ambiguous in this regard though.

prompt: Regarding the subarachnoid cisterns, which of the following is correct?
options: The ambient cistern is lateral to the cerebellum
The ambient cistern is posterolateral to the midbrain
The interpeduncular cistern is posterior to the midbrain
The quadrigeminal cistern is anterior to the midbrain
The quadrigeminal cistern is lateral to the cerebellum
explanation:
The quadrigeminal cistern sits behind the midbrain, just above the cerebellum. The ambient cisterns run around the posterolateral aspect of the midbrain on either side joining to the interpeduncular cistern and is essentially an extension of the quadrigeminal cistern.

stem: 80-year-old man is found to have a mass involving the corpus callosum. Broadly speaking the mass is low on T1 and high on T2. There is avid homogeneous contrast enhancement and T2 changes in periventricular regions.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
There is a defined differential for ‘lesions which cross the corpus callosum’ for which there is a defined differential: GBM, lymphoma, infarction, trauma, radiation, metastases, MS. Although not well described here the ‘T2 changes’ could be oedema relating to the mass.

PML (progressive multifocal leucoencephalopathy) is an HIV related condition caused by the JC virus which is classically described as having asymmetrical high T2 signal but there isn’t anything else in the question which points to this.

Gliomatosis cerebri is a horrible tumour seen as generalised high T2 signal involving at least three lobes but is usually found in younger patients than this.

An anaplastic astrocytoma is a main player in the differential diagnosis for ‘lesions which cross the corpus callosum’ but is more prevalent in younger or middle aged patients.

Thus the answer for this question comes down to lymphoma or GBM. Both can be low on T1 and high on T2 (although lymphoma is more usually low on T2) but homogeneous contrast enhancement makes the answer more likely to be lymphoma.

He has also started making sudden movements which he says he cannot control. He is examined and referred onto a neurologist when the GP finds myoclonus. He undergoes an MRI scan which shows high signal in the putamina, caudate nuclei and frontal lobes.  There is no enhancement with contrast.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Huntington disease

He undergoes an MRI scan which shows high signal in the putamina, caudate nuclei and frontal lobes.  There is no enhancement with contrast.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease

There are three types of this prion transmitted disease; the one linked to the BSE (bovine spongiform encephalopathy) epidemic of the late 1980s and 1990s, a rare familial variant, and finally a sporadic version which accounts for the vast majority of the cases. Clinically there is a rapidly progressive dementia with ataxia and myoclonus which should be the give-away feature even before imaging features are discussed.  On MRI, the reported finding is of high T2/FLAIR signal in the basal ganglia bilaterally and symmetrically (particularly the putamen). The pulvinar sign is often described in association with cJD which describes high FLAIR signal in the pulvinar thalamic nuclei (called the hockey stick sign). Strangely the signal changes are a rare cause of restriction of diffusion, seen as bright areas on DWI. Important negatives for this condition are the lack of enhancement with contrast and the lack of white matter involvement (since the white matter is protected by its myelin sheath).

Image © Medical Exam Prep

Huntington disease

There are relatively few radiological manifestations of Huntington disease. The usual one described is atrophy of the heads of the caudate nuclei with consequential prominence of the adjacent lateral ventricle frontal horns with a ‘box’ like appearance. Various studies have been done to quantify the extent of this atrophy.

Parkinson's disease

Generalised cerebral atrophy occurs with Parkinson's disease but is a highly non-specific feature. There are, however, radiological findings in the midbrain which although subtle, are far more specific. Parkinson's disease occurs when there is neuronal loss in the substantia nigra, specifically the pars compacta of the substantia nigra. On a T2 weighted MRI image this appears as blurring of the intermediate signal intensity line which separates the two adjacent low intensity structures (these are the pars reticulata of the substantia nigra and the red nucleus).

A DAT scan (Dopamine Active Transfer) can be performed to confirm the diagnosis. This uses the radiopharmaceutical I-123 Ioflupane to image dopamine transporters in the brain. These are present in the highest concentrations in the putamina and caudate nuclei. In patients with true Parkinson's disease (as opposed to other similar conditions), there will be loss of uptake in the posterior putamen. This can be an asymmetric finding. Colloquially speaking the appearance of a these areas on a normal patient resembles a comma and on a patient with Parkinson's disease they become more like full stops.

Wilson disease

Wilson disease is a disorder of copper metabolism. It causes white matter atrophy and T2 hyperintensities predominantly affecting the basal ganglia and thalami.

stem: A 76-year-old man is admitted with stroke. His wife said his symptoms started exactly 2 hours ago. Thrombolysis is being considered.
prompt: What is the first line of investigation?
explanation:
A large role of acute imaging in stroke is to rule out haemorrhage, and acute haemorrhage is better seen on CT than on MRI.

MRI + DWI has a 20-30% false negative rate within the first 24 hours of symptoms. The only other answer which may be given could be CT perfusion which is often performed in stroke centres. An infarction will obviously cause an increase in the (mean transit time) MTT and is the most sensitive parameter for detecting a stroke. The cerebral blood volume map is used to determine reversibility as it will be severely reduced in frank ischaemia but may be normal or increased in the potentially salvageable penumbra. If there is only a modest reduction in cerebral blood volume but a marked loss of cerebral blood flow this would also indicate potential reversibility.

stem: You are reviewing the MRI brain of a patient with known Alzheimer’s disease.
prompt: Which of the following is NOT part of the limbic system? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which answer is NOT part of the limbic system.

The limbic system

The limbic system is a complex network of connections between a number of important different regions of the brain. It has roles in emotion, learning, memory, affective disorders and some dementias to name but a few.

Components of the limbic system:

Cortical structures

The olfactory cortex

Parahippocampal gyrus

Hippocampus

Cingulate gyrus

Subcallosal gyrus

Subcortical structures

Amygdala

Septum pellucidum

Hypothalamus

Anterior thalamic nuclei

Mamillary bodies

Two structures bear particular importance in the imaging of dementia; the precuneus and the cingulate gyrus. Both are best appreciated on sagittal views.

Precuneus: The precuneus is located on the medial surface of each hemisphere, in the posterior parietal lobe. It has functions in motor planning, working memory and also connections to the visual pathways.

The cingulate gyrus: The cinculate gyrus is also located on the medial side of each hemisphere and runs anteroposteriorly just above the corpus callosum. The cingulate gyrus has complex functions to do with learning, emotional response and memory.

stem: A 54-year-old man undergoes an MRI spine which shows serpiginous structures outside the cord.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Spinal dural AVFs often present with insidious pain, weakness and sensory loss. Serpiginous flow voids over the surface of the cord are the main described feature on MRI.

Superficial siderosis

Superficial siderosis occurs when there is deposition of haemosiderin over the pial and ependymal surfaces. This is often thought to be secondary to recurrent subarachnoid haemorrhage (for which there is a further differential besides the presence of an AVM). On MRI there is blooming artefact on the susceptibility weighted images and low signal in particular on the T2 weighted sequences. If only limited in extent it can be particularly well demonstrated in the cerebellum where it is associated with atrophy in long-standing cases. Classically the siderosis coating the cranial nerves causes a sensorineural hearing loss.

A spinal AVM is classically an intramedullary lesion. There are some confusing subtypes where a spinal dural AVF is actually counted as a type I spinal AVM. An AVM is also described as having a ‘nidus’ of affected vessels whereas an AVF is more of a single connection between the arterial and venous systems.

Strongyloides is a roundworm infection prevalent to developing countries. The worms themselves are a matter of millimetres long.

topic: Spinal dural AVFs often present with insidious pain, weakness and sensory loss. Serpiginous flow voids over the surface of the cord are the main described feature on MRI.
stem: Superficial siderosis Superficial siderosis occurs when there is deposition of haemosiderin over the pial and ependymal surfaces. This is often thought to be secondary to recurrent subarachnoid haemorrhage (for which there is a further differential besides the presence of an AVM). On MRI there is blooming artefact on the susceptibility weighted images and low signal in particular on the T2 weighted sequences. If only limited in extent it can be particularly well demonstrated in the cerebellum where it is associated with atrophy in long-standing cases. Classically the siderosis coating the cranial nerves causes a sensorineural hearing loss. A spinal AVM is classically an intramedullary lesion. There are some confusing subtypes where a spinal dural AVF is actually counted as a type I spinal AVM. An AVM is also described as having a ‘nidus’ of affected vessels whereas an AVF is more of a single connection between the arterial and venous systems. Strongyloides is a roundworm infection prevalent to developing countries. The worms themselves are a matter of millimetres long. prompt: Which of the following sequences would be best for detecting inactive demyelinating plaques?
explanation:
In fact the demyelinating lesions seen on sagittal FLAIR sequences may be characteristic but that does not necessarily mean they are the ‘best’ at depicting demyelinating plaques. ‘Best’ is an ambiguous term in any case as it does not differentiate between the most specific and the most sensitive test.

Some general take home points are these:

Both contrast enhancement and restriction of diffusion can be used to identity acute lesions.

FLAIR is particularly good for periventricular lesions where picking the lesions out against the CSF signal of the lateral ventricles is hardest

Corpus callosal lesions seen on sagittal FLAIR sequences are ‘classical’

Axial T2 is ‘better’ than FLAIR for posterior fossa lesions

STIR sequences are good for spinal cord lesions

T1 pre-contrast sequences add very little information

Multiple sclerosis

The imaging characteristics of multiple sclerosis should definitely be learnt, as much for real life radiology as for the exams. This is an idiopathic demyelinating disease with oedematous perivascular inflammation in the acute stage progressing to demyelination with proliferation of the astroglia in the chronic phase. There are oblong elliptical plaques of high T2 signal at the callososeptal interface.

Other highly testable features:

Involvement of the middle cerebellar peduncle is specific to multiple sclerosis when attempting to differentiate it from small vessel ischaemic changes

Lesions can cross the midline

Axial T2 sequences are better than FLAIR for posterior fossa lesions

Acute lesions can enhance with contrast, classically in an ‘incomplete ring’

Thalamic involvement is rare and suggests the possibility of ADEM instead

prompt: Which of the following is a likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
The differential diagnosis for orbital pathology is heavily anatomically based.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

Globe lesions are situated within the eyeball itself.

Retinoblastoma

Melanoma

Retinal detachment

Outside the globe there are three conditions which are included in all of the other orbital compartments namely sarcoidosis, pseudotumours and lymphoproliferative lesions.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

Lymphoproliferative disorders include leukaemias, lymphomas, and less aggressive collections of lymphoid tissue. The term is used particularly in head and neck radiology where histological diagnosis of such entities is key. Some masses on a CT scan can have a 'typical' appearance for a lymphoma but are actually only benign lymphoid hyperplastic tissue and thus the term lymphoproliferative disorder covers both entities accurately.

IgG4 related diseases are one of Radiology’s newest entities. They comprise a constellation of fibrotic conditions affecting virtually every part of the body, mediated by a subclass of Immunoglobulin called IgG4. Where one condition exists others may also be present. The more common of these include:

Orbital pseudotumour

Fibrosing mediastinitis

Reidel thyroiditis

Autoimmune pancreatitis

Sclerosing mesenteritis

Retroperitoneal fibrosis

stem: A 31-year-old lady who delivered by vaginal delivery 2 years ago following a pregnancy complicated by pre-eclampsia complains of secondary amenorrhoea. Her GP thinks she might be suffering from pre-eclampsia due to an occult pregnancy but a serum pregnancy test is negative. She is taken for a scan.
prompt: What are the expected imaging features?
options: A moderate volume of sub-arachnoid blood
Haemorrhage into enlarged pituitary lobe and ischaemic changes in both occipital lobes on CT
Homogeneous enlargement of the pituitary showing high T1 and low T2 on MRI
Low attenuation and loss of grey/white matter differentiation in both occipital lobes
explanation:
Sheehan syndrome is consequent on obstetric hypovolaemia. Pre-eclampsia certainly increases the risk of peri-partum haemorrhage and with little further information provided, Sheehan syndrome is a viable option. Chronically, the pituitary of a patient with Sheehan syndrome becomes atrophic to the point of radiological invisibility (empty sella).

Pituitary apoplexy

Pathologically, pituitary apoplexy is infarction which can take place with or without haemorrhage. Over half of patients have an underlying macroadenoma; haemorrhage into a pre-existing macroadenoma is the usual presentation. 'All' patients present with a headache and panhypopituitarism. Visual impairment is also common as the pituitary enlarges and impacts on the chiasm. On a CT scan there will be a sellar/suprasellar mass (ie pituitary enlargement). Hyperdensity is caused by the underlying haemorrhage, if present. On an MRI, the pituitary can be seen to be enlarged with T1 hyperintensity (specifically in the subacute phases). In the chronic phase however, the pituitary will be involuted and small, even appearing as an 'empty sella'.

Sheehan syndrome is pituitary apoplexy due to hypovolaemic shock and can be consequential to delivery. At the time of apoplexy, the predominant issue for the patient is the systemic hypovolaemia for which aggressive management is usually already being pursued. In the early days following the delivery, the first hypopituitary issues to manifest is usually any or all of hyponatraemia, diabetes insipidus or hypothyroidism. At this time the MRI findings can vary from a normal appearing pituitary through to the classic pituitary apoplexy appearances of an enlarged pituitary with high T1 signal. Patients can also present many months or years later with panhypoituitarism at which time an MRI will usually show an empty sella.

Sheehan syndrome is pituitary apoplexy due to hypovolaemic shock and can be consequential to delivery. The visual field problems can be caused by pressure effects on the optic chiasm. The answer given describes the classical appearance for Sheehan syndrome in the acute setting. The answer ‘haemorrhage into enlarged pituitary lobe’ would be an arguable second best answer however the occipital lobe changes are not related to Sheehan syndrome but again this would be in the acute setting. Of the answers offered, pituitary atrophy is the most likely finding in the chronic setting.

stem: A 78-year-old man undergoes a CT scan of his head. There is an avidly enhancing tubular mass within the left middle ear. You also notice that the foramen spinosum is aplastic.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: An aberrant internal carotid artery can cause a pulsatile mass in the middle ear. This condition can be found either with or without a persistent stapedial artery and consequential aplastic foramen spinosum (anatomically – ‘the heel of the high-heeled shoe’). The stapedial artery in such cases arises from the internal carotid artery and runs through the stapes, becoming the middle meningeal artery (which usually arises from the external carotid artery and courses through the foramen spinosum).

stem: A 76-year-old man is admitted with cerebellar ataxia, and corticospinal tract involvement.
prompt: Which of the following is most in-keeping with a diagnosis of Lateral Medullary Syndrome? Select ONE answer only.
options: Contralateral pain and temperature loss to the face
explanation:
Lateral Medullary Syndrome (Wallenburg syndrome)

This is caused by either a vertebral artery occlusion or PICA occlusion.

This is a classic scenario for an exam question and is one of those syndromes that is far more common in the exam world than in the real world. There is a short list of slightly unusual symptoms any combination of which, in the exam context, should make you suspicious for this syndrome:

Cerebellar involvement – DANISH mnemonic as per medical school

Autonomic dysfunction – ipsilateral Horner’s syndrome, hiccoughs

Sensory symptoms – symptoms of sensory loss are common place in the stroke world but in this syndrome it is specifically loss of pain and temperature sensation in the ipsilateral face and contralaterally to the rest of the body. Patients can also experience ipsilateral stabbing pains prior to the sensory loss; pain symptoms are highly unusual in the stroke world and usually point to a different diagnosis.

Ipsilateral bulbar symptoms – dysphagia, dysarthria etc.

stem: A 50-year-old man is seen in a neurology outpatient clinic with complaints of progressive memory loss and some movement problems. He subsequently undergoes an MRI scan of his brain. You suspect he may have a neurodegenerative condition.
prompt: Which of the following findings is INCORRECTLY matched to its condition? Select ONE answer only.
options: Blurring of structures in the midbrain - Parkinson's disease
Disproportionate involvement of the hippocampi – Alzheimer’s disease
Sparing of the hippocampi - Lewy body dementia
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which finding is INCORRECTLY matched.

Huntington disease

There are relatively few radiological manifestations of Huntington disease. The usual one described is atrophy of the heads of the caudate nuclei with consequential prominence of the adjacent lateral ventricle frontal horns with a ‘box’ like appearance. Various studies have been done to quantify the extent of this atrophy.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease

There are three types of this prion transmitted disease; the one linked to the BSE (bovine spongiform encephalopathy) epidemic of the late 1980s and 1990s, a rare familial variant, and finally a sporadic version which accounts for the vast majority of the cases. Clinically there is a rapidly progressive dementia with ataxia and myoclonus which should be the give-away feature even before imaging features are discussed. On MRI, the reported finding is of high T2/FLAIR signal in the basal ganglia bilaterally and symmetrically (particularly the putamen). The pulvinar sign is often described in association with cJD which describes high FLAIR signal in the pulvinar thalamic nuclei (called the hockey stick sign). Strangely the signal changes are a rare cause of restriction of diffusion, seen as bright areas on DWI. Important negatives for this condition are the lack of enhancement with contrast and the lack of white matter involvement (since the white matter is protected by its myelin sheath).

Lewy body dementia

A core clinical feature to this dementia is the fluctuant nature of the symptoms. Parkinsonian features can also develop although these are usually subsequent to the memory decline. Visual hallucinations are also a feature. Radiologically there is a generalised decrease in cerebral volume (sparing the hippocampi). Temporo-parietal hypoperfusion on HMPAO Tc99m SPECT scanning is indicative of Lewy body dementia. Involvement of the occipital cortex, which is typically spared in Alzheimer's disease, sets the two apart from one another on PET studies. The cingulate island sign has also been ascribed to Lewy body dementia, where there is preservation of metabolism in the mid-posterior cingulate gyrus. If present, this is said to be specific for Lewy body dementia.

Alzheimer's disease

The radiological findings of this well known disease are diffuse sulcal and ventricular enlargement. There is a disproportionate effect to the anterior temporal lobes, hippocampi and sylvian fissures with sparing of the sensorimotor and visual cortices, thalami and cerebellum.

Parkinson's disease

Generalised cerebral atrophy occurs with Parkinson's disease but is a highly non-specific feature. There are, however, radiological findings in the midbrain which although subtle, are far more specific. Parkinson's disease occurs when there is neuronal loss in the substantia nigra, specifically the pars compacta of the substantia nigra. On a T2 weighted MRI image this appears as blurring of the intermediate signal intensity line which separates the two adjacent low intensity structures (these are the pars reticulata of the substantia nigra and the red nucleus).

stem: Following a finding of an enlarged level II cervical lymph node detected clinically, a 65-year-old man undergoes an FNA which demonstrates metastatic squamous cell carcinoma. A CT scan is otherwise normal as is mediastinoscopy.
prompt: What is the next best management plan for the patient?
options: Watch and wait for 3 months then repeat CT
Watch and wait for 6 months then repeat CT
explanation: The patient has a proven SCC and every effort must be made to identify the primary source. PET/CT can be very helpful in such cases and is the recommended management. Expectant management is inappropriate in the face of a malignant FNA result.

stem: You are reviewing the HMPAO images from a patient who presented to his GP with a gradual decline in memory. The scan shows reduced flow to precuenus and cingulate gyrus.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Functional imaging in dementia

Tc99m-HMPAO SPECT and 18F-FDG PET produce very similar patterns when used to image patients with cognitive decline however the latter is considered to have a greater sensitivity and specificity and is therefore preferred.

Two structures bear particular importance in the imaging of dementia; the precuneus and the cingulate gyrus. Both are best appreciated on sagittal views.

Precuneus: The precuneus is located on the medial surface of each hemisphere, in the posterior parietal lobe. It has functions in motor planning, working memory and also connections to the visual pathways.

The cingulate gyrus: The cinculate gyrus is also located on the medial side of each hemisphere and runs anteroposteriorly just above the corpus callosum. The cingulate gyrus has complex functions to do with learning, emotional response and memory.

Alzheimer's disease

The radiological findings of this well-known disease are diffuse sulcal and ventricular enlargement. There is a disproportionate effect to the anterior temporal lobes, hippocampi and sylvian fissures with sparing of the sensorimotor and visual cortices, thalami and cerebellum. Functional studies (Tc-HMPAO SPECT or F-18 FDG PET) show reduced uptake in the precuneus, posterior cingulate gyrus, frontal and temporoparietal lobes but with characteristic sparing of the sensorimotor cortex and basal ganglia bilaterally. Importantly there is also sparing of the occipital lobes, which helps differentiate it from Lewy body dementia where the occipital lobes are involved. Other differences between the two conditions are seen with specific dopamine transporter agent imaging techniques

Lewy body dementia

There is a generalised decrease in cerebral volume (sparing the hippocampi). Temporo-parietal hypoperfusion on HMPAO Tc99m SPECT scanning is indicative of Lewy body dementia. Involvement of the occipital cortex, which is typically spared in Alzheimer’s disease, sets the two apart from one another on PET studies. The cingulate island sign has also been ascribed to Lewy body dementia, where there is preservation of metabolism in the mid-posterior cingulate gyrus. If present, this is said to be specific for Lewy body dementia.

Pick disease

When there is disproportionate atrophy of the frontal and temporal lobes in an unusually young patient Pick disease should be suspected. This can sometimes be described as enlargement of the frontal horns but the concept is the same; volume loss of the frontal and temporal lobes. Functional studies show reduced uptake in the frontal lobes and anterior cingulate gyri.

prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Cryptococcus

This is an opportunistic yeast-like fungus which therefore requires a degree of immunocompromise, typically AIDS. The cryptococcomas are typically non-enhancing low density lesions in the basal ganglia (some show variable enhancement  but enhancement depends on host immunity however most cases occur in immunosuppressed patients). These show as high signal on T2 sequences. A granulomatous meningitis can also occur. They can be differentiated from VR spaces on FLAIR where VR spaces will suppress (being CSF in content) whereas the mucoid cryptococcomas will not.

Toxoplasmosis

Toxoplasmosis is a more common finding in AIDS patients than lymphoma is, by a large margin. On MRI it is seen as multiple ring enhancing lesions, which can show haemorrhage particularly following treatment. One of the stronger differentiators between toxoplasmosis and lymphoma is the SPECT findings. This is sometimes termed ‘hypometabolic’ meaning the lesions do not demonstrate SPECT uptake. The table below gives some general features of the two conditions. There is however considerable overlap in the imaging features despite these broad trends.

A ring solitary ring enhancing lesion in the context of an AIDS patient should raise lymphoma as a strong possibility. Multiple lesions can and do occur however, making the distinction from toxoplasmosis challenging. Lymphoma is also part of the differential diagnosis for lesions that cross the corpus callosum and this can be a feature that separates it from toxoplasmosis, although is not a feature of exclusion. Similarly if haemorrhage has been seen associated with the lesion this is more a feature of toxoplasmosis but absence of haemorrhage does not exclude toxoplasmosis.

HIV encephalopathy

Separating HIV encephalitis from PML can challenging in real life. HIV encephalitis causes bilateral symmetrical white matter changes, seen as high T2 signal (The T1 sequences can be normal). There is also sparing of the subcortical U-fibres.

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML)

This is a JC virus mediated phenomenon which causes asymmetrical patchy white matter changes. These can be bilateral. The testable feature is involvement of the cortical U-fibres which separates it from HIV encephalopathy where the U-fibres are spared.
