The table below gives some general features of the two conditions. There is however considerable overlap in the imaging features despite these broad trends. Toxoplasmosis Lymphoma Number of lesions Multiple lesions Single lesion (can be multiple) Predilection/involvement of Basal ganglia Corpus callosum DWI Range of appearances Restricts Thallium SPECT Negative Avid MRS choline Decreased Increased MR perfusion Decreased rCBV Increased rCBV Lymphoma A ring solitary ring enhancing lesion in the context of an AIDS patient should raise lymphoma as a strong possibility. Multiple lesions can and do occur however, making the distinction from toxoplasmosis challenging. Lymphoma is also part of the differential diagnosis for lesions that cross the corpus callosum and this can be a feature that separates it from toxoplasmosis, although is not a feature of exclusion. Similarly if haemorrhage has been seen associated with the lesion this is more a feature of toxoplasmosis but absence of haemorrhage does not exclude toxoplasmosis. HIV encephalopathy Separating HIV encephalitis from PML can challenging in real life. HIV encephalitis causes bilateral symmetrical white matter changes, seen as high T2 signal (The T1 sequences can be normal). There is also sparing of the subcortical U-fibres. Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) This is a JC virus mediated phenomenon which causes asymmetrical patchy white matter changes. These can be bilateral. The testable feature is involvement of the cortical U-fibres which separates it from HIV encephalopathy where the U-fibres are spared. NextRaised haematocrit A 27-year-old man presents with a one month history of headache, nausea and vomiting. He is referred to a neurologist who finds a raised haematocrit and requests an MRI. The MRI scan shows a peripheral left cerebellar hemisphere part cystic and part solid lesion with an enhancing mural nodule, in contact with the pial surface.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: All the answers come within the differential diagnosis for the description of enhancing mural nodules however polycythaemia secondary to erythropoietin secretion as part of a paraneoplastic syndrome is a documented association to haemangioblastomas.

stem: A 64-year-old man is brought to A&E by his worried wife. She describes a sudden collapse at home and on examination it is evident that he has loss of power and sensation below T7 on the left, with pain and temperature loss on the contralateral side. An urgent MRI is requested which shows high T2 signal in the T7 vertebral body and high signal of cord at T7. There is no significant adjacent disc disease.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Brown-Sequard syndrome

This is a specific finding where damage to the dorsal columns leads to ipsilateral loss of touch sensation and contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation due to damage to the lateral spinothalamic tracts (contralateral since these ascend after having crossed). There is also ipsilateral motor function loss.

Causes of Brown-Sequard syndrome

Traumatic

Penetrating injury

Mechanical trauma e.g. RTA

Iatrogenic injury

Compression e.g disc herniation

Spinal cord tumour

Vascular/Infarction

Aortic aneurysm repair complication

Vertebral artery dissection

Spinal cord haemorrhage

Spinal cord infarction

The vascular supply to the spinal cord is derived largely from the vertebral arteries or intercostal arteries with one longitudinal running anterior spinal cord artery and two small longitudinally running posterior spinal cord arteries.

The artery of Adamkiewicz is a particularly large segmental artery supplying the anterior spinal artery from around the level of T9. It is responsible for most of the spinal cord blood supply for the lumbar spinal cord. Damage during aortic surgery or trauma can result in spinal cord infarction.

Usually any vascular insult results in a reasonably rapid onset of symptoms. Spinal cord infarctions are no exception. Often more than one vertebral level is affected.

An MRI will showT2 hyperintensity of at least the central grey matter (if not the whole cross-section of the cord) due to oedema. As with intracranial infarctions there will be restriction of diffusion on the DWI sequences.

Particularly in the thoracic spine, the adjacent vertebral body  may also lose its blood supply and undergo infarction.

Demyelination

Demyelination can occur due to multiple sclerosis, ADEM or as an idiopathic process.

Acute idiopathic transverse myelitis is a specific diagnosis of exclusion however. There is inflammation of the spinal cord leading to bilateral motor, sensory and autonomic dysfunction. On imaging there is expansion of the central portion of the cord extending over multiple vertebral levels. The inflamed portion returns high signal on T2 weighted sequences. This occurs most commonly in the thoracic spine and importantly, should involve at least two thirds of the cross sectional area of the cord at the affected level. This is in contrast to a multiple sclerosis plaque which involves under half of the cross sectional area of the cord.

Multiple sclerosis can affect the spinal cord. Lesions tend to be smaller usually confined to 1-2 vertebral levels and affecting less than half of the cross sectional area of the cord. There may be mild focal expansion of the cord, but this is a far less prominent feature than it is with idiopathic transverse myelitis. 90% of patients will have other intracranial lesions. The lesions of MS also return high T2 signal, like their intracranial counterparts. The cervical cord is most commonly affected.

ADEM (acute disseminated encephalomyelitis) is an autoimmune condition which occurs days-weeks following a viral infection. It largely affects the white matter of the brain but the spinal cord can also be affected. It can occur at any age, but it is usually young children who are affected. Patients usually respond very well to steroid therapy and fortunately, most (90%) cases resolve without any residual deficit. On imaging, the affected areas return high T2 signal and there is characteristic sparing of the grey matter.

Spondylitis

Infection of the spine, termed spondylitis, is usually considered as either pyogenic or tuberculous (with a couple of notable exceptions). There is some overlap in the features of the two

Tuberculous spondylitis - Around half of patients have no pulmonary disease and spondylitis accounts for around 5% of all infections with tuberculosis. The L1 vertebral body is the most commonly affected level but usually more than one levels is affected. Within the vertebral body it is the anterior aspect which is affected first. This is thought to be due to the subligamentous spread of the bacterium, under the anterior longitudinal ligament. The disc height is usually preserved until relatively late on in the disease which can make the condition very difficult to detect on x-ray since neither periosteal reactions nor reactive sclerosis are likely to be seen either. Calcification to the disc is common though, and virtually pathognomonic when present.

Pyogenic spondylitis tends to progress rapidly. The associated abscesses, if present, do not have time to calcify or become thickened and the posterior elements are usually spared. Disc height loss occurs earlier.

Tuberculous spondylodiscitis

Staphylococcal spondylodiscitis

Calcification (almost pathognomonic)

No calcification

Involvement of the posterior elements

Posterior elements spared

Insidious onset

More acute onset

Less loss of disc space

More loss of disc space

Gibbus deformity (angular kyphosis)

No gibbus deformity

Multiple levels involved

One level involved

Lateral Medullary Syndrome (aka Wallenburg syndrome)

This is caused by either a vertebral artery occlusion or PICA occlusion and is one of those syndromes that is far more common in exams than in real life. There is a short list of slightly unusual symptoms any combination of which, in the exam context, should make you suspicious for this syndrome:

Cerebellar involvement – DANISH mnemonic as per medical school

Autonomic dysfunction – ipsilateral Horners syndrome, hiccoughs

Sensory symptoms – symptoms of sensory loss are common place in the stroke world but in this syndrome it is specifically loss of pain and temperature sensation in the contralateral face. Patients can also experience ipsilateral stabbing pains; pain symptoms are highly unusual in the stroke world and usually point to a different diagnosis.

Ipsilateral bulbar symptoms – dysphagia, dysarthria etc.

Subacute combined degeneration

This is a curious condition which can be subtle to detect. A deficiency of vitamin B12 (usually caused by malabsorption) leads to degneration within the dorsal columns of the cord. The dorsal columns carry nerves responsible for position and vibration sense and as such patients present with loss of these senses as well as sensory ataxia (balance significantly deteriorates when the patients eyes are shut thereby excluding visual stabilisation as opposed to sensory stabilisation), and hyperreflexia.

On an MRI scan there will be (if the resolution allows), a longitudinal line of high T2 signal within the cord on sagittal sequences, and often a characterisitc 'inverted-V' shape of high T2 signal on axial sequences. In some cases the 'V' is clearly seen and in others it is harder to appreciate and the finding is more of high T2 signal bilaterally and symmetrically in the region of the posterior columns.

stem: A 58-year-old man presents with a two year history of a painless palpable swelling in his left parotid. USS shows it to be mobile and superficial to the facial nerve. On MRI there is a septated well defined mass in the parotid tail with low intensity on T1 and high intensity on T2.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This is a classic description for a Warthin tumour. A squamous cell carcinoma in this location would be a metastatic deposit from a scalp SCC and would be unlikely not to progress in the time frame given. Adenoid cystic carcinoma is a relentlessly growing oral tumour although a small percentage arise from the parotid gland. In the parotid it would usually be painful due to invasion of the facial nerve; this tumour is notorious for perineural spread. Both the lymphomas mentioned would be unlikely to demonstrate stability over two years, in addition to the parotid being unlikely primary sites.

stem: Which sinuses drain via the osteomeatal complex.
prompt: Select one answer only.
options: Anterior ethmoid sinus, posterior ethmoid sinus and nasolacrimal duct
Anterior ethmoidal sinus, agger nasi, frontal sinus
Frontal sinus, sphenoid sinus and ethmoid sinuses
Nasolacrimal duct, agger nasi, frontal sinus
explanation:
The anatomy of the sinuses can vary hugely but is usually left to the ENT surgeons to fully capture.

The nasolacrimal duct drains to an orifice inferior to the inferior turbinate.

The sphenoid sinus drains via the sphenoethmoidal recess.

The Agger nasi cell is the name given to the anterior most ethmoid air cell

The osteomeatal complex is best appreciated on coronal sequences at the superomedial aspect of the maxillary sinus. It drains the frontal, maxillary and anterior and middle ethmoid sinuses.

stem: A 36-year-old man complains of painless facial swelling and is referred for an ultrasound scan. The scan shows bilateral partoid swelling with cysts and cervical lymph node enlargement. There is no necrosis within the lymph nodes.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
HIV parotitis

This occurs in around 5% of patients with HIV. There is diffuse lymphocytosis with enlargement of the cervical lymph nodes and hypoechoic/cystic areas seen in bilaterally enlarged parotid glands. The whole of the gland is affected.

Warthin tumour

A Warthin tumour is a differential diagnosis for a painless parotid lump and has an association with smokers. Different sources describe different imaging characteristics. A Warthin tumour usually presents as bilateral asymptomatic masses or possibly multiple unilateral masses.

Sjogren syndrome

This can cause parotid swelling and is usually unilateral when it does. It would give a cystic appearance. You would however expect the usual xerostomia and xerophthalmia too. In advanced disease there is sialectasis which is better appreciated either on a sialogram or an MRI than ultrasound.

Mumps

Mumps is usually caused by a paramyovirus and leads to diffuse tender enlargement of the parotid glands. This can be bilateral or unilateral. The diagnosis is usually evident clinically and requires no imaging.

stem: A 50-year-old man is seen in a neurology outpatient clinic with complaints of progressive memory loss and some movement problems. He subsequently undergoes an MRI scan of his brain. You suspect he may have a neurodegenerative condition.
prompt: Which of the following findings is INCORRECTLY matched to its condition?
options: Blurring of structures in the midbrain - Parkinson's disease
Disproportionate involvement of the hippocampi - Alzheimer disease
Sparing of the hippocampi - Lewy body dementia
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which finding is INCORRECTLY matched.

Huntington disease

There are relatively few radiological manifestations of Huntington disease. The usual one described is atrophy of the heads of the caudate nuclei with consequential prominence of the adjacent lateral ventricle frontal horns with a ‘box’ like appearance. Various studies have been done to quantify the extent of this atrophy.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease

There are three types of this prion transmitted disease; the one linked to the BSE (bovine spongiform encephalopathy) epidemic of the late 1980s and 1990s, a rare familial variant, and finally a sporadic version which accounts for the vast majority of the cases. Clinically there is a rapidly progressive dementia with ataxia and myoclonus which should be the give-away feature even before imaging features are discussed.  On MRI, the reported finding is of high T2/FLAIR signal in the basal ganglia bilaterally and symmetrically (particularly the putamen). The pulvinar sign is often described in association with cJD which describes high FLAIR signal in the pulvinar thalamic nuclei (called the hockey stick sign). Strangely the signal changes are a rare cause of restriction of diffusion, seen as bright areas on DWI. Important negatives for this condition are the lack of enhancement with contrast and the lack of white matter involvement (since the white matter is protected by its myelin sheath).

Lewy body dementia

A core clinical feature to this dementia is the fluctuant nature of the symptoms. Parkinsonian features can also develop although these are usually subsequent to the memory decline. Visual hallucinations are also a feature.  Radiologically there is a generalised decrease in cerebral volume (sparing the hippocampi). Temporo-parietal hypoperfusion on HMPAO Tc99m SPECT scanning is indicative of Lewy body dementia. Involvement of the occipital cortex, which is typically spared in Alzheimers disease, sets the two apart from one another on PET studies. The cingulate island sign has also been ascribed to Lewy body dementia, where there is preservation of metabolism in the  mid-posterior cingulate gyrus. If present, this is said to be specific for Lewy body dementia.

Alzheimer disease

The radiological findings of this well known disease are diffuse sulcal and ventricular enlargement. There is a disproportionate effect to the anterior temporal lobes, hippocampi and sylvian fissures with sparing of the sensorimotor and visual cortices, thalami and cerebellum.

Parkinson's disease

Generalised cerebral atrophy occurs with Parkinson's disease but is a highly non-specific feature. There are, however, radiological findings in the midbrain which although subtle, are far more specific. Parkinson's disease occurs when there is neuronal loss in the substantia nigra, specifically the pars compacta of the substantia nigra. On a T2 weighted MRI image this appears as blurring of the intermediate signal intensity line which separates the two adjacent low intensity structures (these are the pars reticulata of the substantia nigra and the red nucleus).

A DAT scan (Dopamine Active Transfer) can be performed to confirm the diagnosis. This uses the radiopharmaceutical I-123 Ioflupane to image dopamine transporters in the brain. These are present in the highest concentrations in the putamina and caudate nuclei. In patients with true Parkinson's disease (as opposed to other similar conditions), there will be loss of uptake in the posterior putamen. This can be an asymmetric finding. Colloquially speaking the appearance of a these areas on a normal patient resembles a comma and on a patient with Parkinson's disease they become more like full stops.

stem: A 41-year-old man presents with a left Horner syndrome. His MRI shows, among other things, what is describes as ‘T2 crescentic high signal’.
prompt: To what does this description pertain?
explanation:
The crescenteric high signal in the question is the ‘sickle sign’ or ‘fried egg’ sign refers to the appearance of T1 fat saturated sequences where a slice transverse through the vessel shows hyperintensity in a crescenteric or circumferential shape to the wall of the affected vessel. Fat saturated T1 sequences may be the most sensitive sequence for cerebral artery dissections but similar findings can still be seen on T2. Unlike large vessel dissections the anatomy here is usually too small to see a dissection flap.

An ipsilateral PCOM or PCA aneurysm can cause symptoms similar to a Horner syndrome. The aneurysms can cause mass effect on the ipsilateral oculomotor nerve causing ptosis and pupil dilatation.

A vertebral artery dissection can cause a Horner syndrome due to lateral medullary syndrome. Vertebral artery dissections are most commonly seen in the setting of trauma, and are altogether much rare than internal carotid artery dissections.

stem: A 73-year-old man presents with a left homonymous hemianopia.
prompt: What is the most likely cause for this?
options: Branch retinal artery occlusion in the left eye
Left posterior cerebral artery (PCA) territory infarction
Right posterior cerebral artery (PCA) territory infarction
explanation:
There are two facets to the question; the first is in knowing that a homonymous hemianopia suggests a problem in the contralateral optic tract and the second is in knowing the arterial supply to the optic tracts.

A left branch retinal artery occlusion would give a left sided hemianopia or quadrantanopia.

A left PCA infarction might cause a right homonymous hemianopia.

Meningiomas are usually slow growing and incidentally discovered. This would be a very unusual presentation of a meningioma.

stem: A 45-year-old man is involved in a high-speed road traffic accident. He sustains a significant head injury and a CT head is performed. This shows intracranial blood at the vertex which does not cross the midline, but crosses a suture line and extends part-way into the interhemispheric fissure, although the other smaller fissures are unaffected.
prompt: Which of the following would best explain these findings? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
The learning point here is how a haemorrhage deals with the sutures. Extradural (aka epidural) haematomas do cross the midline but do not cross suture lines as this is where the dura is attached to the skull. Subdural haematomas on the other hand do not cross the midline but do extend along the falx, dipping down and affecting both sides of the falx cerebri on the coronal views for example. Combined haematomas (ie extradural and subdural) are possible but on balance the question seems to imply that it is one haematoma rather than two with separate properties for each.

A subarachnoid haemorrhage can be seen as high density on CT within the small fissures on the surface of the brain, as well as into the larger fissures such as the interhemispheric fissure. Obviously very small subarachnoid haemorrhages can be very hard to spot on CT scans and a high index of suspicion is required.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

stem: A 50-year-old woman has an USS thyroid which shows a solid looking region in the left thyroid lobe with punctuate echogenic foci. There are associated malignant looking lymph nodes in the left cervical chain. You suspect she has a thyroid malignancy and grade the scan as U5.
prompt: Which of the following regarding thyroid cancer is correct? Select ONE answer only.
options: Anaplastic thyroid cancers usually arise in adolescent patients
Calcification in a thyroid mass is most suggestive of medullary thyroid cancer
Calcification within a lymph node is most suggestive of papillary thyroid cancer
Familiar inheritance patterns with thyroid cancer mostly relate to papillary thryoid cancer
Medullary thyroid cancer is the most common type of thyroid cancer
explanation:
Calcification and thyroid cancers:

Calcification within lymph node metastases of thyroid cancer can occur with both medullary and papillary thyroid cancer although is more common with papillary thyroid cancer. When performing an USS of a lymph node in the context of a thryoid malignancy it is challenging to determine if there is metastatic involvement or not. The presence of calciifcaiton should raise the suspicion of involvement however this is not always present. The loss of normal hilar morphology is a more reliable sign as node becomes taken over by tumour cells and the lymph node hilum becomes destroyed.

Medullary thyroid cancer - 10% – can have a familial pattern and/or association with other endocrine malignancies. Medullary thyroid cancer usually demonstrates granular calcification and nodal spread in 50% of cases.

Papillary thyroid cancer - 65% - Punctate calcification and regional lymph nodes in 40% of patients and is of a low reflectivity on ultrasound. Anaplastic thyroid cancer is usually in an older age range. Although it is Medullary thyroid cancer which is most commonly seen in familial thyroid cancer patterns, there are some rarer inherited syndromes which are associated with Papilary thyroid cancer.

Anaplastic thyroid cancer - 1% - can be ruled out as it affects an older age range.

Secondary hyperparathyroidism can be ruled out because it doesn’t explain the malignant looking lymph nodes (or the thyroid mass).

Thyroid lymphoma does not typically demonstrate calcification.

stem: Which of the following features is NOT usually used in the context of a paraganglioma?
prompt: Select one answer only.
explanation:
Paragangliomas can be found in the body under a number of guises. All are histologically identical and encompass carotid body tumours, phaeochromocytomas, and glomus tumours. They demonstrate similar and characteristic imaging features throughout the body.

Pulsatile tinnitus is a feature of a Glomus Tympanicum.

Splaying of the carotid arteries is a feature of carotid body tumours.

Flow voids or the classic ‘salt and pepper’ description applies to all paragangliomas.

Avid contrast enhancement is also seen since these tumours are highly vascular in nature.

Polycythaemia should be associated with haemangioblastomas as a consequence of erythropoietin production.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents acutely unwell. Of note in her medical history she has been taking the oral contraceptive pill. She undergoes a venous phase CT scan. Your colleague points out the filling defect which has caused her problems.
prompt: What is the best description of this diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Static blood within the sagittal sinus gives rise to low signal on T1. Normally the sagittal sinus will appear as a flow void on T1w.

The empty delta sign is a post-contrast CT finding. Bilateral haemorrhages can be a secondary consequence to a sagittal sinus thrombosis which may point towards the diagnosis but the thrombosis itself is recognised by the empty delta sign on post-contrast CT.

Dense triangle sign pertains to the acute thrombus as it appears on an unenhanced CT scan.

On an MRI, static blood within the sagittal sinus gives rise to low signal on T1, although the thrombus itself is likely to be high in signal (if subacute in nature). Normally the sagittal sinus will appear as a flow void on T1w. Blooming artefact can be seen on T2* gradient echo sequences and is a strong indicatory of the diagnosis. Confusion can arise with time-of-flight 3D reformatted images and great care should be taken not to overdiagnose flow artefactas thrombosis. Careful reference should always be made to the source images and where there is doubt a CT venogram may be of more use.

The associated infarctions can often be haemorrhagic and parasagittal haemorrhages are very specific for a sagittal sinus thrombosis, but subarachnoid haemorrhage is not likely to be related.

stem: An 86-year-old man is found to have a ring enhancing lesion on contrast enhanced CT of his head.
prompt: What is the most helpful sequence to diagnose it further with MRI?
explanation:
There is a detailed differential diagnosis for a solitary ring enhancing lesion. Adding in patient demographics and probability the top two possibilities would be a neoplastic cause or an abscess. Of the options provided T2W with contrast would be of no use and T1W with contrast is unlikely to enhance the situation beyond the current state. FLAIR would be most useful were we considering the possibility of a demyelinating lesion and certainly this would be in the wider differential diagnosis however demyelinating conditions rarely present this late in age and we are therefore left with DWI.

CNS neoplasms which can cause a ring-enhancing pattern include primarily GBM, metastases and Lymphoma. Of these, restricted diffusion can be seen with lymphoma and some GBMs. The high cellularity of both GBM and lymphoma gives rise to this feature. The restriction in diffusion of an abscess will be within the central pus whereas the central necrosis of a GBM should not restrict. The pattens can be complex and vary from case to case but ultimately the pattern of the restriction of diffusion can further the diagnosis.

stem: You are reviewing the HMPAO images from a patient who presented to his GP with a gradual decline in memory. You suspect the patient may have Alzheimer's disease.
prompt: Which of the following would support this diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
options: Reduced uptake in the precuneus and cingulate gyrus
Reduced uptake of the frontal lobes
explanation:
Functional imaging in dementia

Tc99m-HMPAO SPECT and 18F-FDG PET produce very similar patterns when used to image patients with cognitive decline however the latter is considered to have a greater sensitivity and specificity and is therefore preferred.

Two structures bear particular importance in the imaging of dementia; the precuneus and the cingulate gyrus. Both are best appreciated on sagittal views.

Precuneus: The precuneus is located on the medial surface of each hemisphere, in the posterior parietal lobe. It has functions in motor planning, working memory and also connections to the visual pathways.

The cingulate gyrus: The cinculate gyrus is also located on the medial side of each hemisphere and runs anteroposteriorly just above the corpus callosum. The cingulate gyrus has complex functions to do with learning, emotional response and memory.

Alzheimer's disease

The radiological findings of this well-known disease are diffuse sulcal and ventricular enlargement. There is a disproportionate effect to the anterior temporal lobes, hippocampi and sylvian fissures with sparing of the sensorimotor and visual cortices, thalami and cerebellum. Functional studies (Tc-HMPAO SPECT or F-18 FDG PET) show reduced uptake in the precuneus, posterior cingulate gyrus, frontal and temporoparietal lobes but with characteristic sparing of the sensorimotor cortex and basal ganglia bilaterally. Importantly there is also sparing of the occipital lobes, which helps differentiate it from Lewy body dementia where the occipital lobes are involved. Other differences between the two conditions are seen with specific dopamine transporter agent imaging techniques

Lewy body dementia

There is a generalised decrease in cerebral volume (sparing the hippocampi). Temporo-parietal hypoperfusion on HMPAO Tc99m SPECT scanning is indicative of Lewy body dementia. Involvement of the occipital cortex, which is typically spared in Alzheimer’s disease, sets the two apart from one another on PET studies. The cingulate island sign has also been ascribed to Lewy body dementia, where there is preservation of metabolism in the mid-posterior cingulate gyrus. If present, this is said to be specific for Lewy body dementia.

Vascular dementia

Technically vascular dementia presents as a step-wise decline due to the finite number of small vascular insults that take place. The imaging features should be fairly familiar to candidates from day to day reporting. There are multifocal bilateral white matter changes which can be seen on CT when severe. Inclusion of susceptibility weighted sequences on an MRI scan allows detection of microhaemorrhages suggestive of a parallel diagnosis of cerebral amyloid angiopathy where present.

stem: You are reviewing the CT scan of a 65-year-old man who has presented to the Emergency Department following a fall. He is otherwise fit and well, and has been scanned under the NICE guidelines for the management of head injuries. There is no intracranial haemorrhage but you notice a destructive lesion involving the left side of the clivus. There is arc like calcification within it.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Chondrosarcoma

In some cases there can be a lot of overlap between clival chondrosarcomas and clival chordomas. If a mass is determindly off-midline however, a chondrosarcoma is far more likely. These arise from tiny remnants of cartilage in the synchondrosis between the petrous temporal bone laterally and the occipital bone medially. Patients may present with cranial neuropathies which would be less usual for a chordoma when the nerves traversing the petrous temporal bone are affected. The abducens (CN VI) nerve is most often affected and CN III, V, VII and VIII may also be involved.

Intralesional calcifications take the form of the classic 'arcs and rings' seen with chondrosarcomas elsewhere in the body. On an MRI scan the signal characteristics can be similar to a chordoma with isointensity on T1 to brain parenchyma and high T2 signal. Chondrosarcomas are also likely to enhance with contrast.

Chordoma

These tumours are chiefly found in either the clivus or the sacrum. In the clivus they arise from the synchondrosis (primary cartilaginous joint) between the occipital bone inferiorly and the sphenoid bone superiorly. This is a midline joint and consequently the resultant chordoma is classically midline in nature. This helps to distinguish it from a chondrosarcoma which can appear very similar.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

Chordomas are aggressive, lobulated tumours which cause destruction of surrounding bone but lobulated mass effect on the pons with so-called 'thumbprinting' of the pons. Adjacent vascular structures, if not frankly invaded, are displaced. Posterior displacement of the basilar artery is a useful finding. Within the mass there are often calcific fragments representing either sequestered bone or dystrophic tumoral calcifications, or both. On an MRI scan the mass will be isointense to brain parenchyma on T1 and usually high in signal on T2. Most enhance with contrast.

Skull base metastasis and multiple myeloma

A myelomatous or metastatic process must always be kept in the differential diagnosis for a skull base mass however this would be less usual (although obviously not impossible) in a patient without a known primary site or known disease. On an MRI scan there will be loss of the high T1 marrow signal, as with other aggressive bony lesions, however the T2 signal is usually low or isointense.

NextMRI neck findings

A 55-year-old man undergoes a radical neck dissection for a squamous cell carcinoma, making a slow but uneventful recovery. He is discharged after 10 days. At his follow up appointment a few weeks later he complains of problems swallowing and speaking. An MRI scan is requested which shows signal change and atrophy of the left side of his tongue.

What are the likely signal changes?

High signal on T2 and low on T1

High signal on both

Low signal on T1 and isointense on T2

Low signal on T2 and high on T1

Low signal on both

At his follow up appointment a few weeks later he complains of problems swallowing and speaking. An MRI scan is requested which shows signal change and atrophy of the left side of his tongue.
prompt: What are the likely signal changes?
options: High signal on T2 and low on T1
Low signal on T1 and isointense on T2
Low signal on T2 and high on T1
explanation:
In the days following a denervation injury there will be oedema giving high T2 signal.

Some atrophic changes may be present coexistant with so-called acute inflammation. As the denervation progresses, the atrophy will become more pronounced with time.

High signal on T2 and low on T1 suggests acute inflammation which is the most likely finding during early recovery.

Low signal on T2 and high signal on T1 suggests chronic fatty replacement which could be expected at approximately 18 months post-op.

The other answers given are non-specific.

stem: A 55-year-old lady with worsening headache has a CT scan which shows a thickened optic nerve with linear plaque-like calcification and optic canal hyperostosis.
prompt: With which condition is this finding most commonly associated?
explanation:
There are a limited number of mainstream phakomatoses (NF1, NF2, Sturge-Weber, von Hippel-Lindau, and Tuberous sclerosis) and they all have fairly well definable features.

NF1 is the ‘peripheral’ version. There are plenty of cerebral features described however NF2 is almost exclusively cerebral and is therefore by comparison the ‘central’ version. There are many and varied skeletal manifestations of NF1.

What has been described in the question is an optic nerve sheath meningioma (with a so-called tram-track sign), therefore pathognomonic of NF2. Hyperostosis is a good pointer towards the lesion being a meningioma as opposed to an optic nerve glioma which would be indicative of NF1.

Optic disc drusen is a bit of a red herring in this question. It is accumulation of calcified hyaline material which can sometimes be seen on CT at the junction between the optic nerve and the retina.

stem: A 46-year-old woman with a history of subarachnoid haemorrhage for which she received conservative management now complains of new onset limb weakness. She undergoes an MRI scan of her spine which shows thickening of the lumbar roots.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Arachnoiditis

The nerve roots here are are described as ‘thickened’ which is one of the main descriptors for this condition. Other terms perhaps more often used are ‘clumping of the nerve roots’ or the ‘empty thecal sac sign’ where the nerve roots are so adherent to the posterior aspect of the space that they become next to invisible. Arachnoiditis can occur secondary to surgery, meningitis, subarachnoid haemorrhage, myelography and can also be idiopathic in origin.

Disc sequestration

This is the term used to describe the finding when a part of the disc material has completely separated itself from its parent disc and is seen free within the canal.

Post-op fibrosis

MRI scans are often performed to look for post-op fibrosis or scar tissue and to differentiate it from recurrent disc pathology. The important imaging feature in such cases is enhancement Scar tissue will show enhancement with contrast whereas disc material will not.

Superficial siderosis

Superficial siderosis occurs when there is deposition of haemosiderin over the pial and ependymal surfaces. This is often thought to be secondary to recurrent subarachnoid haemorrhage. On MRI there is blooming artefact on the susceptibility weighted images and low signal in particular on the T2 weighted sequences.

stem: A 50-year-old man is seen in a neurology outpatient clinic with complaints of progressive memory loss and some movement problems. He subsequently undergoes an MRI scan of his brain. There is high T2 and high FLAIR signal in the basal ganglia bilaterally. You notice that the abnormal areas also show restriction of diffusion.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease

There are three types of this prion transmitted disease; the one linked to the BSE (bovine spongiform encephalopathy) epidemic of the late 1980s and 1990s, a rare familial variant, and finally a sporadic version which accounts for the vast majority of the cases. Clinically there is a rapidly progressive dementia with ataxia and myoclonus which should be the give-away feature even before imaging features are discussed.  On MRI, the reported finding is of high T2/FLAIR signal in the basal ganglia bilaterally and symmetrically (particularly the putamen). The pulvinar sign is often described in association with cJD which describes high FLAIR signal in the pulvinar thalamic nuclei (called the hockey stick sign). Strangely the signal changes are a rare cause of restriction of diffusion, seen as bright areas on DWI. Important negatives for this condition are the lack of enhancement with contrast and the lack of white matter involvement (since the white matter is protected by its myelin sheath).

Image © Medical Exam Prep

Huntington disease

There are relatively few radiological manifestations of Huntington disease. The usual one described is atrophy of the heads of the caudate nuclei with consequential prominence of the adjacent lateral ventricle frontal horns with a ‘box’ like appearance. Various studies have been done to quantify the extent of this atrophy.

Lewy body dementia

A core clinical feature to this dementia is the fluctuant nature of the symptoms. Parkinsonian features can also develop although these are usually subsequent to the memory decline. Visual hallucinations are also a feature.  Radiologically there is a generalised decrease in cerebral volume (sparing the hippocampi). Temporo-parietal hypoperfusion on HMPAO Tc99m SPECT scanning is indicative of Lewy body dementia. Involvement of the occipital cortex, which is typically spared in Alzheimers disease, sets the two apart from one another on PET studies. The cingulate island sign has also been ascribed to Lewy body dementia, where there is preservation of metabolism in the  mid-posterior cingulate gyrus. If present, this is said to be specific for Lewy body dementia.

Alzheimer disease

The radiological findings of this well known disease are diffuse sulcal and ventricular enlargement. There is a disproportionate effect to the anterior temporal lobes, hippocampi and sylvian fissures with sparing of the sensorimotor and visual cortices, thalami and cerebellum.

Parkinson's disease

Generalised cerebral atrophy occurs with Parkinson's disease but is a highly non-specific feature. There are, however, radiological findings in the midbrain which although subtle, are far more specific. Parkinson's disease occurs when there is neuronal loss in the substantia nigra, specifically the pars compacta of the substantia nigra. On a T2 weighted MRI image this appears as blurring of the intermediate signal intensity line which separates the two adjacent low intensity structures (these are the pars reticulata of the substantia nigra and the red nucleus).

A DAT scan (Dopamine Active Transfer) can be performed to confirm the diagnosis. This uses the radiopharmaceutical I-123 Ioflupane to image dopamine transporters in the brain. These are present in the highest concentrations in the putamina and caudate nuclei. In patients with true Parkinson's disease (as opposed to other similar conditions), there will be loss of uptake in the posterior putamen. This can be an asymmetric finding. Colloquially speaking the appearance of a these areas on a normal patient resembles a comma and on a patient with Parkinson's disease they become more like full stops.

stem: A 43-year-old man presents with a unilateral Horner syndrome. You suspect he may have an internal carotid artery dissection.
prompt: What is the best investigation to perform?
explanation:
On T1w fat saturated images the dissection appears as a crescenteric high signal aka ‘the sickle sign’ or ‘the fried egg’. A slice transverse through the vessel shows hyperintensity in a crescenteric or circumferential shape to the wall of the affected vessel. Fat saturated T1 sequences may be the most sensitive sequence for cerebral artery dissections but similar findings can still be seen on T2. Unlike large vessel dissections the anatomy here is usually too small to see a dissection flap.

The other classic cause of a Horner syndrome might be an ipsilateral PCOM or PCA aneurysm.

On duplex ultrasound a dissection manifests as a thickened hypoechoic vessel wall with a low flow due to the stenotic effect of the dissection flap but in the acute setting ultrasound has largely been superseded by cross-sectional imaging and therefore these findings are more likely to be incidentally picked up in cases where dissection is not suspected.

The main feature of a dissection on a plain CT would be a crescenteric high attenuation rim representing the acute/subacute mural haematoma formed within the false lumen. The remaining true lumen may be narrowed compared to the contralateral side. With such a minimal question there is an argument to suggest that a plain CT to rule out a haemorrhagic stroke would be the most appropriate imaging however this would be an unusual presentation in an unusual age range for this eventuality.

CT angiography does have an excellent sensitivity and specificity in the diagnosis of craniocervical dissections although image interpretation can be hindered by streak artefact from the skull base. Usually in the DGH setting however this is the test that the patient would be most likely to undergo first. That does not, however, mean it is the best test, it is simply a matter of pragmatism that most hospitals would be able to arrange a CTA on a more emergent basis than an MRA.

MRA imaging is more useful in the diagnosis of carotid artery dissection than in vertebral artery dissection but is thought of as the modality of choice.

No investigation would only be pertinent if a mis-diagnosis of Bell palsy had been made.

Overall this is a tricky question. In the real world you could make a case for either CTA or MRA (in the absence of the option of DSA which would be the gold standard). On balance the current trend seems to be that MRA is the best answer to give.

stem: A 64-year-old man presents with an acute left third cranial nerve palsy and a headache. A CT scan shows subarachnoid haemorrhage. Most of the blood is concentrated around the quadrigeminal cistern.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The quadrigeminal cistern sits behind the midbrain, just above the cerebellum. The ambient cisterns run around the posterolateral aspect of the midbrain on either side joining to the interpeduncular cistern and is essentially an extension of the quadrigeminal cistern.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

The posterior communicating artery (PCom) runs between the internal carotid artery and the posterior cerebral artery. The PComs sit anterior to the midbrain and blood from an aneurysm of the PCom will extend into the interpeduncular cistern, ambient cisterns and thereby to the quadrigeminal cistern.

The third cranial nerve runs parallel to the posterior communicating artery and dives under the posterior cerebral artery. The association between PCOM or PCA pathology and third nerve palsy signs is classical. If a patient has a painful ptosis, a PCOM aneurysm should be considered. It will be an ipsilateral pathology because the Oculomotor nerve is post-ganglionic at this point.

The diagnostic pathway to investigate for intracranial aneurysms following a subarachnoid haemorrhage is:

CT angiogram

Invasive angiogram

Second invasive angiogram after approx 10 days.

Although in this patient’s case the diagnosis of a subarachnoid haemorrhage has not been fully established, the presence of an aneurysm must be excluded.

Bear in mind that the correct answer (regarding management) may change if the wording of the questions is different. For example a DSA invasive angiogram would be the gold standard investigation for an aneurysm but is not usually done first; a CTA is therefore the next best test in the first instance.  Similarly an MRI scan would be the next best test to confirm the diagnosis of a subarachnoid haemorrhage but does not have a sufficiently low false negative rate to exclude an aneurysm. In the answers provided here, with the exception of the unenhanced CT, only angiographic options are available and hence this is not the correct answer.

stem: You are reviewing a CT of a 73-year-old man who has an acquired cholesteatoma.
prompt: Which of the following is NOT correct? Select ONE answer only.
options: The Prussak space is found behind the superior part of the tympanic membrane
The head of the malleus is situated in the epitympanum
The incus is connected to the tympanic membrane
The stapes is connected to the oval window of the cochlea
The stapes is situated in the mesotympanum
explanation:
Please note that the question asks for the answer which is NOT correct.

The anatomy of the middle ear is complex but important and contains a number of specific anatomical terms.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

The epitympanum, also known as the attic, is the superior portion above the highest point of the tympanic membrane. It contains the head of the malleus and the short crus of the incus (These give the appearance of an ice-cream cone on an axial CT).

Image © Medical Exam Prep

The Prussak space is found within the epitympanum and is a tiny space at the top of the tympanic membrane, just behind the scutum. Its clinical relevance is that it is the usual origin for pars flaccida cholesteatomas.

The aditus ad antrum connects the epitympanum to the mastoid antrum and thence the mastoid air cells.

The tegmen mastoidium (tegmen means roof) is the point at which the mastoid air cells meet the temporal lobe of the brain.

The tegmen tympani is the point at which the upper most extent of the epitympanum reaches the temporal lobe of the brain.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

The mesotympanum is the space posterior to the tympanic membrane and contains the body of the incus, the manubrium (connected to the tympanic membrane) and the anterior process of the malleus and the stapes. The stapes is connected to the incus as well as the oval window of the cochlea. There is also a round window placed more inferiorly which bulges to allow compression waves transmitted from the stapes to the oval window to travel through the cochlea.

The hypotympanum is a far less significant space than either the epitympanum or the mesotympanum. It begins at the inferior most extent of the tympanic membrane. The Eustachian tube opens into the hypotympanum anteriorly.

stem: A 64-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department by his worried wife. She describes a sudden collapse at home and on examination it is evident that he has loss of power and sensation below T7 on the left, with pain and temperature loss on the contralateral side. An urgent MRI is requested which shows high T2 signal in the T7 vertebral body and high signal of cord at T7. There is no significant adjacent disc disease.
prompt: Which ONE of the following is NOT a cause of Brown-Sequard syndrome?
options: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord
explanation:
**Please note this question asks which answer is NOT a cause.**

Brown-Sequard syndrome

This is a specific finding where damage to to one side of the spinal cord causes ipsilateral loss of touch sensation and contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation due to damage to the lateral spinothalamic tracts (contralateral since these ascend after having crossed). There is also ipsilateral motor function loss.

Causes of Brown-Sequard syndrome

Traumatic:

Penetrating injury

Mechanical trauma e.g. RTA

Iatrogenic injury

Compression e.g. disc herniation

Spinal cord tumour

Vascular:

Aortic aneurysm repair complication

Vertebral artery dissection

Spinal cord haemorrhage

Spinal cord infarction

The vascular supply to the spinal cord is derived largely from the vertebral arteries or intercostal arteries with one longitudinal running anterior spinal cord artery and two small longitudinally running posterior spinal cord arteries.

The artery of Adamkiewicz is a particularly large segmental artery supplying the anterior spinal artery from around the level of T9. It is responsible for most of the spinal cord blood supply for the lumbar spinal cord. Damage during aortic surgery or trauma can result in spinal cord infarction.

Usually any vascular insult results in a reasonably rapid onset of symptoms. Spinal cord infarctions are no exception. Often more than one vertebral level is affected.

An MRI will showT2 hyperintensity of at least the central grey matter (if not the whole cross-section of the cord) due to oedema. As with intracranial infarctions there will be restriction of diffusion on the DWI sequences.

Particularly in the thoracic spine, the adjacent vertebral body may also lose its blood supply and undergo infarction.

Subacute combined degeneration

This is a curious condition which can be subtle to detect. A deficiency of vitamin B12 (usually caused by malabsorption) leads to degeneration within the dorsal columns of the cord. The dorsal columns carry nerves responsible for position and vibration sense and as such patients present with loss of these senses as well as sensory ataxia (balance significantly deteriorates when the patient’s eyes are shut thereby excluding visual stabilisation as opposed to sensory stabilisation), and hyperreflexia.

On an MRI scan there will be (if the resolution allows), a longitudinal line of high T2 signal within the cord on sagittal sequences, and often a characteristic 'inverted-V' shape of high T2 signal on axial sequences. In some cases, the 'V' is clearly seen and in others it is harder to appreciate, and the finding is more of high T2 signal bilaterally and symmetrically in the region of the posterior columns.

stem: A 48-year-old patient is admitted to A+E following a first ever seizure. The consultant notices a facial rash. A collateral history raises no further symptoms.
prompt: What is the most likely unifying diagnosis?
explanation:
This question is a little sparse on detail.

In theory SLE could present as seizures subsequent to cerebral abscess formation. On the whole, vascular events are more common, but less likely to present as seizures. The brain parenchyma is not often involved in SLE however the exception is haemorrhage or abscess formation. (Neuropsychiatric symptoms do occur.). There is a rare entity called Libman-Sacks endocarditis where sterile vegetations grow on the cardiac valves. Some sources say that these can be the focus for subsequent septic cerebral emboli.

Wegener granulomatosis

Wegener granulomatosis has recently been re-christened as ‘granulomatosis with polyangiitis’. It can affect the CNS in a variety of ways. Granulomatous lesions, vasculitis causing small infarctions, and haemorrhage are all features. Classically the patient will have a ‘saddle’ nose due to collapse of the nasal septum and cartilaginous nasal bridge.

Behcet syndrome

Behcet syndrome is classically described as a triad of oral and genital ulcers associated with one of several ocular manifestations. Its effect on the CNS tends to be as meningoencephalitis or venous sinus thrombosis. In theory either could present with seizures but it would be a stretch to describe oral ulcers as a facial rash.

Multiple sclerosis

Facial rashes and seizures are not features of multiple sclerosis.

stem: A 45-year-old man with known HIV presents with deteriorating memory problems and word finding difficulties. He undergoes an MRI scan which shows bilateral white matter high signal on T2 and FLAIR in an asymmetric pattern. There is no mass effect. The radiologist notes involvement of the subcortical U-fibres.
prompt: What is the most likely explanation?
explanation:
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML)

This is a JC virus mediated phenomenon which causes asymmetrical patchy white matter changes. These can be bilateral. The testable feature is involvement of the cortical U-fibres which separates it from HIV encephalopathy where the U-fibres are spared. The lack of a mass effect helps differentiate both PML and HIV encephalopathy from toxoplasmosis, cryptococcus and tuberculomas.

HIV encephalopathy

Separating HIV encephalitis from PML can challenging in real life. HIV encephalitis causes bilateral symmetrical white matter changes, seen as high T2 signal (The T1 sequences can be normal). There is also sparing of the subcortical U-fibres.

Cryptococcus

This is an opportunistic yeast-like fungus which therefore requires a degree of immunocompromise, typically AIDS. The cryptococcomas are non-enhancing low density lesions in the basal ganglia. These show as high signal on T2 sequences. A granulomatous meningitis can also occur. They can be differentiated from VR spaces on FLAIR where VR spaces will suppress (being CSF in content) whereas the mucoid cryptococcomas will not.

Toxoplasmosis

Toxoplasmosis is a more common finding in AIDS patients than lymphoma is, by a large margin. On MRI it is seen as multiple ring enhancing lesions, which can show haemorrhage particularly following treatment. One of the stronger differentiators between toxoplasmosis and lymphoma is the SPECT findings. This is sometimes termed ‘hypometabolic’ meaning the lesions do not demonstrate SPECT uptake. The table below gives some general features of the two conditions. There is however considerable overlap in the imaging features despite these broad trends.

Toxoplasmosis

Lymphoma

Number of lesions

Multiple lesions

Single lesion (can be multiple)

Predilection/involvement of

Basal ganglia

Corpus callosum

DWI

Range of appearances

Restricts

Thallium SPECT

Negative

Avid

MRS choline

Decreased

Increased

MR perfusion

Decreased rCBV

Increased rCBV

Cerebral tuberculosis

A cerebral tuberculoma would be difficult to differentiate from toxoplasmosis or lymphoma. Classically though they are described as target lesions situated in the corticomedullary regions. They can calcify with treatment which would differentiate them well from other CNS infections.

stem: An elderly diabetic patient complains of severe right ear pain. She has visible erythema and granulation tissue in the right external auditory canal but it seems her symptoms are far in excess of the findings on examination. She has a 6th nerve palsy, retrobulbar pain and on CT scanning there is fluid in the mastoid air cells, middle ear and ill-defined change in the petrous apex.
prompt: Which of the following best explains these findings?
explanation:
Gradenigo syndrome

Gradenigo syndrome refers to the triad of otitis media, retro-orbital pain and abducens nerve palsy which results from an abscess in the aerated petrous apex – petrous apicitis. It is usually caused by either pseudomonas or enterococcus. This particular question does confusingly point towards a concurrent presence of malignant otitis externa however this is not given as an option.

stem: A 75-year-old woman taking warfarin for AF falls and sustains a head injury. She undergoes a CT scan which shows an intraparenchymal haemorrhage. She is managed conservatively and 36 hours later undergoes an MRI scan for follow up.
prompt: What will the likely appearance of the haemorrhage be now? Select ONE answer only.
options: Bright on T1 and bright on T2
Bright on T1 and dark on T2
Dark on T1 and bright on T2
Iso on T1 and dark on T2
Isointense on T1 and bright on T2
explanation:
At 2 days old, the bleed is acute; iso/dark on T1 and dark on T2. Chronic bleeds are dark on T1 and dark-rimmed on T2 (bright centre).

This question is to do with the imaging characteristics of blood within the brain. We can think of the intracranial space as a closed box as far as oxygen tensions go which means that blood degrades in a predictable fashion and therefore has predictable appearances on T1 and T2 according to the changes in the haemoglobin molecule. There are a few different methods to help remember the changes in appearance, one of which is the table below:

Time-frame

Haemoglobin

T1

T2

Mnemonic

Hyperacute (hours)

Iso

Bright

- IBBY

Acute (0-2 days)

Intracellular deoxyHb

Dark / Iso

Dark

- IDDY

Early subacute (3-7 days)

Intracellular metHb

Bright

Dark

- BIDDY

Late subacute (8-30 days)

Extracellular metHb

Bright

Bright

- BABY

Chronic (> 30 days)

Intracellular haemosiderin

Dark

Dark rim

- DODO

In real life and for the 2b exam the important distinction is around the subacute stages.

In that case, by and large, if it is bright on T1 it is subacute and T2 then decides if it is early or late subacute. The timeframes given are also important and can form the basis of 2a exam questions.

Signal from chronic haematoma often causes confusion since the T2 signal in particular can be quite variable. In general the haematoma will show a dark haemosiderin ring on T2 weighted images but since the centre becomes effectively CSF, or CSF-like fluid, it can follow CSF signal and would therefore return high signal on T2 weighted sequences.

Of the other answers provided therefore:

Bright on T1 and dark on T2 = Early subacute

Dark on T1 and bright on T2 = Chronic

Dark on T1 and dark on T2 = Acute

Isointense on T1 and bright on T2 = Hyperacute

Bright on T1 and bright on T2 = Late subacute

stem: You are reviewing an MRI scan of a 45-year-old woman's brain. There is a left intraconal lesion.
prompt: Which of the following is NOT a likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which is NOT a likely diagnosis.

The differential diagnosis for orbital pathology is heavily anatomically based.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

Globe lesions are situated within the eyeball itself.

Retinoblastoma

Melanoma

Retinal detachment

Outside the globe there are three conditions which are included in all of the other orbital compartments namely sarcoidosis, pseudotumours and lymphoproliferative lesions.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

Lymphoproliferative disorders include leukaemias, lymphomas, and less aggressive collections of lymphoid tissue. The term is used particularly in head and neck radiology where histological diagnosis of such entities is key. Some masses on a CT scan can have a 'typical' appearance for a lymphoma but are actually only benign lymphoid hyperplastic tissue and thus the term lymphoproliferative disorder covers both entities accurately.

IgG4 related diseases are one of Radiology’s newest entities. They comprise a constellation of fibrotic conditions affecting virtually every part of the body, mediated by a subclass of Immunoglobulin called IgG4. Where one condition exists others may also be present. The more common of these include:

Orbital pseudotumour

Fibrosing mediastinitis

Reidel thyroiditis

Autoimmune pancreatitis

Sclerosing mesenteritis

Retroperitoneal fibrosis

stem: A 43-year-old lady suspected to have multiple sclerosis following an episode 2 years ago of optic neuritis now presents with paraesthesia. She undergoes an MRI scan.
prompt: Where it the new lesion likely to be?
explanation:
Basal ganglia lesions will likely lead to movement or coordination issues, or spasms.

Lesions of the thalami may be purely sensory or lead to ataxia. This is arguably an alternative answer however the callosoeptal interface is far more classical for multiple sclerosis.

Virchow-Robin spaces are dilated fluid filled spaces surrounding perforating vessels and are a differential diagnosis for multiple sclerosis however will suppress on FLAIR sequences.

Multiple sclerosis

The imaging characteristics of multiple sclerosis should definitely be learnt, as much for real life radiology as for the exams. This is an idiopathic demyelinating disease with oedematous perivascular inflammation in the acute stage progressing to demyelination with proliferation of the astroglia in the chronic phase. There are oblong elliptical plaques of high T2 signal at the callososeptal interface.

Other highly testable features:

Involvement of the middle cerebellar peduncle is specific to multiple sclerosis when attempting to differentiate it from small vessel ischaemic changes

Lesions can cross the midline

Axial T2 sequences are better than FLAIR for posterior fossa lesions

Acute lesions can enhance with contrast, classically in an ‘incomplete ring’

Thalamic involvement is rare and suggests the possibility of ADEM instead

stem: A 28-year-old lady presents with a headache having been unwell for the past 3 days. Of note in her medical history she has been taking the oral contraceptive pill. She undergoes a (non-contrast) MRI scan of her head which shows bilateral infarctions.
prompt: What is the best description of the associated findings?
options: High venous sinus signal on T1
Venous sinus flow void on T1
explanation:
Static blood within the sagittal sinus gives rise to high signal on T1. Normally the sagittal sinus will appear as a flow void on T1w.

The empty delta sign is traditionally a post-contrast CT finding although the same appearance can also be seen on post-contrast T1 sequences. Bilateral haemorrhages can be a secondary consequence to a sagittal sinus thrombosis which may point towards the diagnosis but the thrombosis itself is recognised by the empty delta sign on post-contrast CT.

Dense triangle sign pertains to the acute thrombus as it appears on an unenhanced CT scan.

The associated infarctions can often be haemorrhagic and parasagittal haemorrhages are very specific for a sagittal sinus thrombosis but subarachnoid haemorrhage is not likely to be related.

stem: A 32-year-old man with longstanding poor hearing finds his hearing to be much worse following a minor head trauma.
prompt: What is the most likely explanation?
explanation:
Sudden conductive hearing loss following trauma must raise suspicion of disruption to the bony ossicles. If there is associated sensorineural hearing loss a transverse fracture to the temporal bone should also be suspected.

Transverse petrous temporal bone fractures are associated with sensorineural hearing loss and facial paralysis in 50% of cases

Longitudinal petrous temporal bone fractures are associated with ossicular dislocation, of which incudostapedial dislocation is the most common. Facial paralysis can occur in approximately 10-20% of cases due to oedema.

Tullio phenomenon refers to vertigo and nystagmus induced by loud noises. It is caused by superior semicircular canal dehiscence.

Gradenigo syndrome refers to the triad of otitis media, retro-orbital pain and Abducens nerve palsy which results from an abscess in the aerated petrous apex – petrous apicitis.

Menieres disease is an idiopathic condition of the inner ear structures giving rise to symptoms principally of vertigo and tinnitus. Radiologically the vestibular aqueduct is seen to be either small or not visible.

A carotico-Cavernous fistula is classically associated with trauma. The patient often makes an uneventful initial recovery but complains of painful left eye swelling and a third nerve palsy days to weeks later. CT may show a prominent superior ophthalmic vein.

stem: A 70-year-old man who had a nasopharyngeal cancer resected 5 years previously now presents with an enhancing irregular temporal fossa mass. His neurological exam is normal.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: A new primary head and neck cancer
explanation:
Most patients with recurrent disease (ie metastatic spread) recur within 3 years of treatment but a 5 year interval is well within the bounds of expectation. Direct spread from remaining tumour on the other hand is far less likely at this time interval.

Radiation necrosis can occur many years following treatment however applies to the temporal lobes of the brain rather than the soft tissues of the temporal fossa and is highly unlikely to be accompanied by a normal neurological exam.

BCC stands for Basal Cell Carcinoma.

stem: A 34-year-old lady wakes up with unilateral facial nerve paralysis affecting her face. She takes herself to A and E where she is investigated with an MRI head.
prompt: Which part of the facial nerve is most likely to be affected?
explanation:
The question refers to Bells palsy.

The seventh cranial nerve undergoes a number of turns as it crosses through the temporal bone.

The pontine (or Cisternal) segment runs from the pons to the internal auditory meatus. This can enhance Bell palsy.

The Labyrinthine (or meatal) segment runs from the internal auditory meatus to the geniculate ganglion and enhancement is most typically associated with Bells palsy.

The Tympanic portion runs horizontally from the geniculate ganglion. It is also seen to enhance with Bells palsy but since it is known to enhance normally too this is not a distinguishing feature.

The mastoid portion runs vertically (and gives off the nerve to stapedius). It can also enhance normally.

The parotid portion runs distally from the stylomastoid foramen and lies lateral to the retromandibular vein.

stem: A 42-year-old man presents with a seizure. A CT head shows significant asymmetrical white matter oedema in the left frontal region which crosses the corpus callosum and has a central area of low attenuation.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This question strays into the territory of ‘lesions which cross the corpus callosum’ for which there is a defined differential. (Things which cross the midline: GBM, lymphoma, infarction, trauma, radiation, metastases, MS). The central low attenuation is likely due to tumour necrosis which is strongly suggestive of a glioblastoma multiforme.

PML (progressive multifocal leucoencephalopathy) is an HIV related condition caused by the JC virus which is classically described as having asymmetrical high T2 signal but there isn’t anything else in the question which points to this.

Gliomatosis cerebri is a horrible tumour seen as generalised high T2 signal involving at least three lobes but is usually found in younger patients than this.

An anaplastic astrocytoma is a main player in the differential diagnosis for ‘lesions which cross the corpus callosum’ but does not usually demonstrate central necrosis at diagnosis.

Thus the answer for this question comes down to lymphoma or GBM. Extensive oedema is more consistent with glioblastoma than lymphoma. On MRI, both can be low on T1 and high on T2.

stem: A 65-year-old man presents with headache, dizziness and problems with speech and swallowing. He undergoes an MRI scan which shows a well circumscribed mass of heterogeneous T2 signal near the foramen magnum and causing expansion of the hypoglossal canal. There is strong contrast enhancement.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This is an uncommon presentation of a common condition. Schwannomas are mainstream for the neuroradiologist but schwannomas of the hypoglossal nerve are a little more unusual. Nonetheless they exhibit the same radiological features of a typical vestibular schwannoma ie. Well circumscribed, high T2 signal with foraminal expansion and avid contrast enhancement. By contrast a metastatic process would be more aggressive, causing bony destruction not remodelling. A meningioma would not cause expansion of the canal. Ependymomas are tumours of the 4th ventricle and tend to occur in a younger cohort. Epidermoid cysts do not demonstrate contrast enhancement.

stem: You are reviewing the HMPAO images from a patient who presented to his GP with a gradual decline in memory.
prompt: Which of the following findings is correctly matched to its diagnosis?
options: Involvement of the occipital lobes - Lewy body dementia
Reduced uptake in the precuneus and cingulate gyrus - Pick disease
Reduced uptake of the frontal lobes - Alzheimer disease
Susceptibility artefact bilaterally but asymmetrically - Parkinson's disease
Temporoparietal hypoperfusion bilaterally and symmetrically - Vascular dementia
explanation:
Functional imaging in dementia

Tc99m-HMPAO SPECT and 18F-FDG PET produce very similar patterns when used to image patients with cognitive decline however the latter is considered to have a greater sensitivity and specificity and is therefore preferred.

Two structures bear particular importance in the imaging of dementia; the precuneus and the cingulate gyrus. Both are best appreciate on sagittal views.

Precuneus: The precuneus is located on the medial surface of each hemisphere, in the posterior parietal lobe. It has functions in motor planning, working memory and also connections to the visual pathways.

The cingulate gyrus: The cinculate gyrus is also located on the medial side of each hemisphere and runs anteroposteriorly just above the corpus callosum. The cingulate gyrus has complex functions to do with learning, emotional response and memory.

Alzheimer disease

The radiological findings of this well known disease are diffuse sulcal and ventricular enlargement. There is a disproportionate effect to the anterior temporal lobes, hippocampi and sylvian fissures with sparing of the sensorimotor and visual cortices, thalami and cerebellum. Functional studies (Tc-HMPAO SPECT or F-18 FDG PET) show reduced uptake in the precuneus, posterior cingulate gyrus, frontal and temporoparietal lobes but with characteristic sparing of the sensorimotor cortex and basal ganglia bilaterally. Importantly there is also sparing of the occipital lobes, which helps differentiate it from Lewy body dementia where the occipital lobes are involved. Other differences between the two conditions are seen with specific dopamine transporter agent imaging techniques

Lewy body dementia

A core clinical feature to this dementia is the fluctuant nature of the symptoms. Parkinsonian features can also develop although these are usually subsequent to the memory decline. Visual hallucinations are also a feature.  Radiologically there is a generalised decrease in cerebral volume (sparing the hippocampi). Temporo-parietal hypoperfusion on HMPAO Tc99m SPECT scanning is indicative of Lewy body dementia. Involvement of the occipital cortex, which is typically spared in Alzheimers disease, sets the two apart from one another on PET studies. The cingulate island sign has also been ascribed to Lewy body dementia, where there is preservation of metabolism in the  mid-posterior cingulate gyrus. If present, this is said to be specific for Lewy body dementia.

Vascular dementia

Technically vascular dementia presents as a step-wise decline due to the finite number of small vascular insults that take place. The imaging features should be fairly familiar to candidates from day to day reporting. There are multifocal bilateral white matter changes which can be seen on CT when severe.  Inclusion of susceptibility weighted sequences on an MRI scan allows detection of microhaemorrhages suggestive of a parallel diagnosis of cerebral amyloid angiopathy where present.

Parkinson's disease

Generalised cerebral atrophy occurs with Parkinson's disease but is a highly non-specific feature. There are, however, radiological findings in the midbrain which although subtle, are far more specific. Parkinson's disease occurs when there is neuronal loss in the substantia nigra, specifically the pars compacta of the substantia nigra. On a T2 weighted MRI image this appears as blurring of the intermediate signal intensity line which separates the two adjacent low intensity structures (these are the pars reticulata of the substantia nigra and the red nucleus).

A DAT scan (Dopamine Active Transfer) can be performed to confirm the diagnosis. This uses the radiopharmaceutical I-123 Ioflupane to image dopamine transporters in the brain. These are present in the highest concentrations in the putamina and caudate nuclei. In patients with true Parkinson's disease (as opposed to other similar conditions), there will be loss of uptake in the posterior putamen. This can be an asymmetric finding. Colloquially speaking the appearance of a these areas on a normal patient resembles a comma and on a patient with Parkinson's disease they become more like full stops.

stem: You are performing an ultrasound scan on the neck of a patient with a known head and neck cancer. There is an abnormal lymph node by the internal jugular vein. It is inferior to the hyoid bone but superior to the vocal cords.
prompt: At what level is the node?
explanation:
Lymph node levels of the neck are best learnt by studying a colourful diagram of the lateral view of the neck.

Essentially the boundaries are the hyoid bone, the cricoid cartilage, the anterior and posterior borders of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. If you can remember those, and the rough pattern you should be able to work out which level is being described in the exam.

prompt: Which of the following is NOT a differential diagnosis for this appearance? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which answer is NOT a differential diagnosis.

There is a differential diagnosis for opaque maxillary antrum. Wegener’s disease is included in it, but Goodpasture's is not.

A 67-year-old man presents with sinus fullness and nasal discharge. Examination demonstrates a large nasal mass and he undergoes further imaging to investigate. A homogenous mass in the maxillary antrum is seen which is intermediate in signal on T2 weighted sequences. There is adjacent bony destruction.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Antrochoanal polyp

Esthesioneuroblastoma

Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma

Sinonasal lymphoma

Squamous cell carcinoma

Image © Medical Exam Prep NextSinus mass A 67-year-old man presents with sinus fullness and nasal discharge. Examination demonstrates a large nasal mass and he undergoes further imaging to investigate. A homogenous mass in the maxillary antrum is seen which is intermediate in signal on T2 weighted sequences. There is adjacent bony destruction.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The main differential for a nasal mass is as follows:

Squamous cell carcinoma

This is the most common malignancy of sinonasal track. The maxillary antrum is involved in 80% of cases. It is often seen as an aggressive antral soft tissue mass, which is low in signal on T2.

Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma

This affects 'exclusively' adolescent male patients. There will be dark flow voids on T1 weighted sequences and the mass will be brightly enhancing. Radiation therapy treats this in 80% of cases, and interventional radiological embolisation can be used to treat haemorrhagic complications at presentation if required.

Esthesioneuroblastoma

This tumour has a bimodal distribution, affecting people in their 20s and 60s. There is a dumbbell shaped tumour with waist at the cribriform plate. The mass will brightly enhance.

Sinonasal lymphoma

This most commonly affects older people (60s and older). It is commonly seen in the nasal cavity rather than the sinuses. There will be a homogenous mass with bony destruction which returns low signal on T2 weighted sequences.

Antrochoanal polyp

This occurs in young adults with obstructive nasal symptoms. They arise from the maxillary sinuses and causes widening of the maxillary ostium.

stem: Among other problems, a middle aged lady begins to notice symptoms of polyuria and polydipsia. She is found to have diabetes insipidus.
prompt: Which of the following would be the LEAST likely diagnosis?
explanation:
There are a number of different ways to divide up the causes of diabetes insipidus. Traumatic, inflammatory or neoplastic for example. Microscopic polyangiitis is not usually associated with diabetes insipidus although no-doubt there are case reports in the literature linking the two. Another important cause not listed is a craniopharyngioma.

Arguably LCH affecting the brain is rare in adults however when it does occur it does have a particular affinity for the pituitary.

stem: A 40-year-old woman complaining of blurred vision is referred for an MRI scan by her neurologist. This shows T2 and FLAIR hyperintensities in the corpus callosum orientated perpendicularly to the lateral ventricles. One of the lesions shows restriction of diffusion and enhancement with contrast. The rest do not.
prompt: What is the most likely explanation?
explanation:
Multiple sclerosis

This is an idiopathic demyelinating disease with oedematous perivascular inflammation in the acute stage progressing to demyelination with proliferation of the astroglia in the chronic phase. There are oblong elliptical plaques of high T2 signal at the callososeptal interface.

Other highly testable features:

Involvement of the middle cerebellar peduncle is specific to multiple sclerosis when attempting to differentiate it from small vessel ischaemic changes

Lesions can cross the midline

Axial T2 sequences are better than FLAIR for posterior fossa lesions

Acute lesions can enhance with contrast, classically in an ‘incomplete ring’

Thalamic involvement is rare and suggests the possibility of ADEM instead

Cryptococcus

This is an opportunistic yeast-like fungus which therefore requires a degree of immunocompromise, typically AIDS. The cryptococcomas are non-enhancing low density lesions in the basal ganglia. These show as high signal on T2 sequences. A granulomatous meningitis can also occur. They can be differentiated from VR spaces on FLAIR where VR spaces will suppress (being CSF in content) whereas the mucoid cryptococcomas will not.

Astrocytoma

Multifocal astrocytomas would not be impossible but are statistically unlikely.

Antiphospholipid syndrome

Antiphospholipid syndrome is technically a differential diagnosis to the findings of multiple sclerosis on MRI however is largely only included for the sake of completeness.

Hurler syndrome

This unpleasant disease is a mucopolysaccharidosis and like most others is autosomal recessive in inheritance. It affects very young children and is usually fatal within the first 12 months of life. Prominent perivascular spaces are seen on MRI brain, hence its inclusion here as a theoretical differential diagnosis.

stem: A 70-year-old man undergoes an MRI scan of the base of his skull. He has previously undergone surgery for a left sided cholesteatoma and the surgeon is concerned there may be a recurrence. Within the surgical cavity on the left there is a mass which does not enhance on the post-contrast sequences but does restrict diffusion.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Cholesteatomas are difficult to manage as they have a high recurrence rate. Imaging has a significant role to play in the management of recurrent cholesteatomas; distinguishing recurrence from post-operative granulation tissue or fluid is important.

Diagnosis

Restricts Diffusion

Recurrent cholesteatoma
