Post-contrast sequences for recurrent cholesteatomas require a delay of around 45 minutes from giving the contrast to acquiring images as the granulation tissue is slow to take up contrast. This has obvious down-sides to any modern day busy MRI schedule. However since the management of post-operative granulation tissue and post-operative fluid is largely identical, namely expectant, it is not important to differentiate the one from the other. Thus findings on diffusion weighted sequences are the most important thing in post-operative cholesteatoma imaging.

Cholesteatoma

Cholesteatomas (Acquired or congenital) are histolologically epidermoid cysts. On imaging the finding of non-dependant soft tissue and bony erosion within the middle ear is typical for a cholesteatoma.

There are two types of acquired cholesteatoma:

Pars flaccida (80%) – classically erodes the scutum and extends superiorly

Pars tensa (20%) – classically erodes the ossicles, extending medially

These refer to the two parts of the tympanic membrane from which they arise.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

In due course, if left unattended, a cholesteatoma will expand to fill the entire middle ear. Prior to this point they can be seen as non-dependant soft tissue within the middle ear. Dependant soft tissue within the middle ear suggests the presence of fluid or pus and the diagnosis of a middle ear infection. Once a cholesteatoma has filled the middle ear completely however no gas remains from which to discern dependency.

There are a number of theories as to how cholesteatomas arise. One theory is that following a perforation of the tympanic membrane entry of desquamated stratified keratinised squamous epithelium from the external auditory canal into the middle ear is permitted. There it adheres to the tympanic membrane and proliferates unrelentingly causing a soft tissue mass to form and eventually leading to bony erosion of the ossicles, scutum and/or other parts of the middle ear.

A congenital cholesteatoma behaves in a similar manner but is present from birth due to an aberrant location of a tiny island of keratinised squamous epithelium.

Cholesterol granuloma

A cholesterol granuloma occurs as a sequela of recurrent bouts of otitis media. Haemorrhage within the middle ear leads to the formation of granulation tissue. On imaging this is seen as non-specification of the middle ear on CT. Bony changes can occur chronically with bony expansion, or displacement and even destruction of the ossicles. The signals characteristics on MRI are therefore important to distinguish it from a cholesteatoma. Whereas a cholesteatoma on MRI is isointense to brain parenchyma on T1, a cholesterol granuloma will show high signal in the middle ear on T1 due to the paramagnetic effects of methaemoglobin. On clinical examination the ENT surgeon may report a bulging blue tympanic membrane. This is classical. Dehiscence of the jugular bulb is an important differential diagnosis to exclude as this will also give a blue tympanic membrane on examination but the management is radically different!

stem: A 65-year-old diabetic presents with severe ear pain and palsy of the facial and glossopharyngeal nerves. He undergoes a CT scan which shows osteomyelitis of the skull base and is diagnosed with malignant otitis externa.
prompt: What is the most common cause of this?
explanation:
Malignant otitis externa

This is an extremely unpleasant condition seen in elderly diabetic patients who present with pain levels disproportionately high compared to the external signs of their disease. Imaging shows osteomyelitis of the skull base, seen better on MRI than on CT. Multiple cranial neuropathies can be present, as can venous sinus thrombosis. It is almost always caused by pseudomonas aeruginosa.

stem: A 54-year-old complains to his GP of morning headaches and visual changes. He is found to have a bitemporal hemianopia and referred for further investigations. An MRI shows a suprasellar mass.
prompt: Which of the following would help differentiate a craniopharyngioma from a pituitary adenoma or a Rathke cleft cyst?
explanation:
Craniopharyngiomas was previously thought to have a bimodal age distribution with a peaks at around age 12 and age 50. The two different age distributions actually represent different tumour types with overlapping features. In children these are adamantinomatous craniopharyngiomas and in adults they are papillary craniopharyngiomas. Both present with symptoms attributable to their sella/suprasella location. In children this includes growth retardation due to compression of the hypothalamus. Calcification is more common in the paediatric group. Avid enhancement post-gadolinium is a good differentiating feature from Rathke cleft cysts which will only show mural enhancement. Adenomas enhance variably. Adenomas can also show cystic degeneration.

Compared to a Rathke's Cleft Cyst or Pituitary adenoma the epicentre of a craniophryngioma is usually suprasellar though in many cases distinguishing these lesions from one another is not straightforward at all.

stem: A 43-year-old man is brought to see his GP by his wife who is concerned that his behaviour has become increasingly erratic. He has also started making sudden movements which he says he cannot control. He is examined and referred onto a neurologist when the GP finds myoclonus. He undergoes an MRI scan. You suspect he may have Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.
prompt: Which of the following features is consistent with this diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
options: High FLAIR signal in the thalami
Low T2 signal in the putamina
explanation:
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease

There are three types of this prion transmitted disease; the one linked to the BSE (bovine spongiform encephalopathy) epidemic of the late 1980s and 1990s, a rare familial variant, and finally a sporadic version which accounts for the vast majority of the cases. Clinically there is a rapidly progressive dementia with ataxia and myoclonus which should be the give-away feature even before imaging features are discussed. On MRI, the reported finding is of high T2/FLAIR signal in the basal ganglia bilaterally and symmetrically (particularly the putamen). The pulvinar sign is often described in association with cJD which describes high FLAIR signal in the pulvinar thalamic nuclei (called the hockey stick sign). Strangely the signal changes are a rare cause of restriction of diffusion, seen as bright areas on DWI. Important negatives for this condition are the lack of enhancement with contrast and the lack of white matter involvement (since the white matter is protected by its myelin sheath).

Image © Medical Exam Prep

stem: A 54-year-old man collapses while playing golf. On arrival at the Emergency Department the blood pressure in his arms is found to be different. He is thought to have suffered a stroke and undergoes carotid Doppler study. The sonographer believes he may have subclavian steal syndrome.
prompt: Which of the following is NOT a possible cause of subclavian steal syndrome? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which answer is NOT a possible cause.

Subclavian steal syndrome occurs when blood supplying the arm (usually the left arm) travels via the ipsilateral vertebral artery in order to bypass a proximal obstruction of the subclavian artery. The distal subclavian artery ‘steals’ blood from the vertebral artery circulation. This gives rise to two different categories of symptoms:

Arm - weaker pulses, numbness, paraesthesia, fingertip necrosis

Brain - syncope, ischaemic symptoms

The most likely cause of subclavian steal would be atherosclerosis. Takayasu aortitis and aortic dissections can also cause subclavian steal but would not be at the top of a differential list without further prompts from the history. A cervical rib can also cause subclavian steal syndrome via stenosis, intimal damage and consequent thrombosis.

Poland syndrome

This is a congenital condition where there is hypoplasia or aplasia of the pectoralis major muscle on one side in association with abnormalities in the ipsilateral hand such as syndactyly, and hypoplasia of the middle phalanx. The absence of the large pectoralis major muscle is seen on a chest radiograph as abnormal hyperlucency on the affected side.

prompt: Given the most likely diagnosis, what is the most likely finding on MRI to explain this?
options: Bilateral asymmetrical confluent areas of high T2 signal
Bilateral symmetrical T2 hyperintensities of the basal ganglia
Bilateral symmetrical white matter changes with sparing of the subcortical U-fibres
Unilateral T2 high signal in the white matter of the medial temporal lobe and insular region

Multiple sclerosis

This is an idiopathic demyelinating disease with oedematous perivascular inflammation in the acute stage progressing to demyelination with proliferation of the astroglia in the chronic phase. There are oblong elliptical plaques of high T2 signal at the callososeptal interface.

Acute lesions can enhance with contrast, classically in an ‘incomplete ring’

Thalamic involvement is rare and suggests the possibility of ADEM instead

Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis – ‘bilateral asymmetrical confluent areas of high T2 signal’

This is an autoimmune, post-viral demyelinating entity usually affecting young adults or children. MRI findings of bilateral asymmetrical areas of T2/FLAIR hyperintensities are classical. These can be confluent or punctuate. There is an excellent and dramatic response to steroids.

HIV encephalopathy – ‘Bilateral symmetrical white matter changes with sparing of the subcortical U-fibres’

Separating HIV encephalitis from PML can challenging in real life. In short HIV encephalitis causes bilateral symmetrical white matter changes, seen as high T2 signal (The T1 sequences can be normal). There is also sparing of the subcortical U-fibres.

Cryptococcus - ‘bilateral symmetrical T2 hyperintensities of the basal ganglia’

This is an opportunistic yeast-like fungus which therefore requires a degree of immunocompromise, typically AIDS. The cryptococcomas are non-enhancing low density lesions in the basal ganglia. These show as high signal on T2 sequences. A granulomatous meningitis can also occur. They can be differentiated from VR spaces on FLAIR where VR spaces will suppress (being CSF in content) whereas the mucoid cryptococcomas will not.

Herpes simplex encephalitis - Unilateral T2 high signal in the white matter of the medial temporal lobe and insular region

HSV encephalitis in immunocompetent individuals usually gives a classical appearance of high T2 signal particularly affecting the temporal and frontal lobes but also with a predilection for the rest of the limbic system too.  Cytotoxic oedema can cause a degree of mass effect and also restriction of diffusion on DWI. There is a classical feature to separate it from Japanese encephalitis which is sparing of the basal ganglia.

One of the main differential diagnoses for HSV encephalitis would be a low grade glioma.

stem: A 30-year-old West African lady presents with a right Bell palsy and symptoms consistent with diabetes insipidus. Her admission chest x-ray is documented to be abnormal. On MRI there is diffuse meningeal enhancement with nodular enhancement of the spinal cord. The brain parenchyma appears normal.
prompt: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Sarcoidosis

Although only a small percentage of sarcoid patients develop CNS signs these are classical, with multiple cranial neuropathies, meningeal and pituitary involvement.

What separates sarcoid meningitis from tuberculous meningitis which would probably be the best other option is the lack of parenchymal involvement.

Both tuberculous and fungal meningitis also affect the basal cisterns and both have the propensity to cause an obstructing hydrocephalus secondary to debris.

Carcinomatous meningitis commonly derives from breast cancer, although lung cancer and melanoma are other possibilities. There is a classic description of ‘zuckerguss’ (sugar coating) where thin areas of subarachnoid enhancement follow the gyral convolutions. Leptomeningeal nodularity is also seen, hence the inclusion here as a possible answer, however the patient demographic fits better with sarcoidosis.

HIV encephalitis causes cognitive problems leading to a dementia. As well as cortical atrophy there can be subtle increases in the T2 signal intensity but meningeal enhancement is not described.

stem: A 45-year-old man suffers a low speed road traffic collision and complains subsequently of a headache. He is found to have nausea, dysarthria and hemiataxia. A vertebral artery dissection is suspected.
prompt: What would be the best sequence on MRI to detect this?
explanation: A post-traumatic vertebral artery dissection classically presents as a third nerve palsy and cerebellar signs. The ‘sickle sign’ or ‘fried egg’ sign refers to the appearance of T1 fat saturated sequences where a slice transverse through the vessel shows hyperintensity in a crescenteric or circumferential shape to the wall of the affected vessel. Unlike large vessel dissections the anatomy here is usually too small to see a dissection flap.

stem: A patient undergoes a CT angiogram for a suspected cerebral artery aneurysm following presentation with a subarachnoid haemorrhage.
prompt: From which vessel does the anterior choroidal artery arise?
explanation: The anterior choroidal artery arises from the internal carotid artery. Another important arterial anatomy fact to remember is the PICA usually arises from the vertebral arteries (70%).

prompt: Which of the following is NOT a feature of Neurofibromatosis type 2? Select ONE answer only.

Please note the question asks which option is NOT a feature.

Although cafe-au-lait spots are more prominent in neurofibromatosis type 1, they can also be found in type 2 too, but are far less common. Lisch nodules however are specific to Neurofibromatosis type 1, as are the bony dysplasias seen.

prompt: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
The differential diagnosis for orbital pathology is heavily anatomically based.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

Globe lesions are situated within the eyeball itself.

Retinoblastoma

Melanoma

Retinal detachment

Outside the globe there are three conditions which are included in all of the other orbital compartments namely sarcoidosis, pseudotumours and lymphoproliferative lesions.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

Lymphoproliferative disorders include leukaemias, lymphomas, and less aggressive collections of lymphoid tissue. The term is used particularly in head and neck radiology where histological diagnosis of such entities is key. Some masses on a CT scan can have a 'typical' appearance for a lymphoma but are actually only benign lymphoid hyperplastic tissue and thus the term lymphoproliferative disorder covers both entities accurately.

IgG4 related diseases are one of Radiology’s newest entities. They comprise a constellation of fibrotic conditions affecting virtually every part of the body, mediated by a subclass of Immunoglobulin called IgG4. Where one condition exists others may also be present. The more common of these include:

Orbital pseudotumour

Fibrosing mediastinitis

Reidel thyroiditis

Autoimmune pancreatitis

Sclerosing mesenteritis

Retroperitoneal fibrosis

stem: A 67-year-old man is admitted following a stroke. He undergoes an MRI scan which shows high DWI signal and low ADC in the fronto-parietal lobe as well as high DWI and high ADC signal in the medial posterior temporal lobe.
prompt: Which of the following combinations best explains these findings?
options: Acute ACA infarct and old MCA infarct
Acute MCA and old PCA infarct
Acute MCA infarct and old ACA infarct
Acute PCA infarct and old ACA infarct
Acute PCA infarct and old MCA infarct
explanation: Acute infarctions are seen as bright areas on DWI with a corresponding low signal area on the ADC map, however in the 7-15 days following a stroke there is first pseudonormalisation and then reversal of the ADC signal. This occurs as cerebral necrosis and the increased water content of the affected tissue gives rise to t2 shine through effect. The medial posterior temporal lobe is a slightly clumsily worded anatomical location. Largely speaking if the brain tissue is adjacent to the falx it is NOT supplied by the MCA.

stem: An 80-year-old man who had a total hip replacement following a fall three years previously visits his dentist complaining of pain and swelling to the left side of the jaw. His dentist is concerned and organises an OPG which shows a large mixed lytic and sclerotic lesion with subperiosteal bone resorption evident. A subsequent MRI shows an associated soft tissue mass too.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
BONJ = Bisphosphonate related Osteonecrosis of the Jaw. This condition can also be caused by monoclonal antibody therapy. Note the question asks for the diagnosis not the aetiology, hence the answer is osteonecrosis. BONJ is associated with soft tissue oedema which in the vignette is given as a soft tissue ‘mass’. While this is obviously not strictly accurate, it does reflect the level of obscurity sometimes seen in the exam questions and serves as a reminder to think a little laterally; a habit which is just as important for day to day reporting as it is to an exam.

An ameloblastoma (aka adamantinoma) is classically described as having a soap-bubble appearance with cortical destruction. Ameloblastomas also erode the overlying teeth, a feature which is almost unique to lucent jaw lesions.

A dentigerous cyst (aka follicular cyst) develops around the crown of an unerupted tooth. They are, however, typically painless.

An odontogenic keratocyst is a unilocular lucent lesion which demonstrates a smooth border. They can be indistinguishable from dentigerous cysts given that they are often associated with an unerupted tooth. They also have an association with Gorlin syndrome (BCCs).

Image © Medical Exam Prep

explanation: The main features of neurofibromatosis 1 and 2 are summarised in the diagrams below:

stem: A 40-year-old patient undergoes a CT venogram for suspected venous sinus thrombosis. The reporting registrar sees a structure draining the superficial middle vein into the transverse sinus.
prompt: What normal venous structure is she describing?
explanation:
Vein of Labbe

Large draining vein connecting the transverse sinus and the superficial middle vein.

Vein of Trolard

Usually smaller than the vein of Labbe. Connects the superficial middle vein and sagittal sinus. A larger vein of Labbe is associated with a smaller vein of Trolard and vice versa.

Basal vein of Rosenthal

This deep vein passes lateral to the midbrain and eventually drains into the vein of Galen.

Vein of Galen

The confluence of the internal cerebral veins results in the vein of Galen.

Straight sinus

Drains the inferior sagittal sinus into (usually) the confluence of sinuses.

stem: A 60-year-old woman is brought to her GP by her husband with subacute onset short term memory loss. More recently he thinks she has been experiencing hallucinations too. An MRI is performed which shows high T2 signal in the medial temporal lobes bilaterally. She is investigated for a paraneoplastic syndrome.
prompt: Which of the following is the most likely primary tumour?
explanation: This question is about limbic encephalitis. The limbic system comprises the olfactory tract, temporal lobes, cingulate gyrus and insular cortex. Limbic encephalitis has either a paraneoplastic aetiology or an autoimmune one. The described involvement of the mesial temporal lobes is classical. In the case of a paraneoplastic syndrome the classical cause is a lung tumor, specifically bronchial small cell lung cancer. Of the other options provided breast cancer has also been found to be associated with limbic encephalitis but is far less classical. Other possible options would have been thymic and testicular cancers. The presence of psychotic symptoms is meant to distinguish limbic encephalitis from HSV encephalitis although there is often overlap in the literature. Limbic encephalitis will show no haemorrhage which can also differentiate it from HSV encephalitis. Furthermore limbic encephalitis does not cause restriction in diffusion.

stem: You are reviewing the MRI scan of a 37-year-old lady who has a constellation of symptoms for which she is under review by neurology.  Recently she has noticed a deterioration in her vision.
prompt: Which of the following would be the best sequence to examine for optic atrophy?
explanation: Optic atrophy is difficult to pick up on an MRI scan unless you are specifically looking for it. On a T2 weighted coronal sequence (particularly a CISS, heavily T2 weighted sequence) scrolling through the optic nerves you may be able to appreciate that there is too much CSF surrounding the optic nerve, particularly if it is a unilateral finding.

stem: An elderly patient with memory problems undergoes a CT head and an HMPAO SPECT. The hippocampi are normal but there is low activity in the occipital lobes as well as reduced in the frontal lobes bilaterally.
prompt: These findings are most in-keeping with which of the following diagnoses?
explanation:
Lewy body dementia

A core clinical feature to this dementia is the fluctuant nature of the symptoms. Parkinsonian features can also develop although these are usually subsequent to the memory decline. Visual hallucinations are also a feature. Radiologically there is a generalised decrease in cerebral volume (sparing the hippocampi). Occipital lobe hypoperfusion on HMPAO Tc99m SPECT scanning is indicative of lewy body dementia.

Alzheimer disease

The radiological findings of this well known disease are diffuse sulcal and ventricular enlargement. There is a disproportionate effect to the anterior temporal lobes, hippocampi and sylvian fissures with sparing of the sensorimotor and visual cortices, thalami and cerebellum.

Vascular dementia

Technically vascular dementia presents as a step-wise decline due to the finite number of small vascular insults that take place. The imaging features should be fairly familiar to candidates from day to day reporting. There are multifocal bilateral white matter changes which can be seen on CT when severe. Inclusion of susceptibility weighted sequences on an MRI scan allows detection of microhaemorrhages suggestive of a parallel diagnosis of cerebral amyloid angiopathy where present.

Korsakoff syndrome

This presents as a triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia and is attributable to thiamine deficiency. There is high T2 signal in the thalami, periaqueductal region and mammillothalamic tract. This is usually in relation to chronic alcohol excess but can is caused by thiamine deficiency from any cause.

Pick disease

When there is disproportionate atrophy of the frontal and temporal lobes in an unusually young patient Pick disease should be suspected. This can sometimes be described as enlargement of the frontal horns but the concept is the same; volume loss of the frontal and temporal lobes.

stem: A 45-year-old man is involved in a high speed road traffic accident. He sustains a significant head injury and a CT head is performed. This shows intracranial blood at the vertex which crosses the midline, straddling the falx and displacing the superior sagittal sinus inwards.
prompt: Which of the following would best explain these findings?
explanation:
This is a trickily worded question on two accounts. The first is that ‘straddle’ is a clumsy word to be using in this circumstance and the second is that this is a UK exam and in the UK we say extradural not epidural. Be that as it may, the learning point here is how the haemorrhage deals with the sutures. Extradural haematomas do cross the midline but do not cross suture lines as this is where the dura is attached to the skull. The exception is vertex haematomas which can extend between the bone and the superior sagittal sinus, displacing the superior sagittal sinus inwards. Subdural haematomas on the other hand do not cross the midline but do extend along the falx, dipping down and affecting both sides of the falx cerebri on the coronal views for example. Combined haematomas (ie extradural and subdural) are possible but on balance the question seems to imply that it is one haematoma rather than two with separate properties for each.

© Medical Exam Prep

stem: A 60-year-old man is undergoing re-staging following chemotherapy and radiotherapy for lymphoma which had been thought to be successful. On his PET-CT scan there is high signal around his neck bilaterally in the supraclavicular spaces.
prompt: Which of the following would best explain these findings?
options: Bilateral pancoast tumours secondary to radiotherapy
explanation: Brown fat is meant to be the ‘good’ type of fat. It is useful for generating heat and is supposed to be more prevalent in Inuits for obvious reasons. Non-inuit persons do also have some brown fat and it is found in classical locations. It is found in the supraclavicular fossa and is a reasonably often encountered confounding factor to PET-CT interpretation.

stem: A 17-year-old boy suffers trauma to the head after falling over on ice. He is drowsy and mildly confused, but without focal neurology and undergoes a CT head scan. This demonstrates an intracranial 3mm superficial crescentic area of high density at the vertex which crosses the midline.
prompt: In which compartment does the haematoma lie?
explanation:
Although extradural haematomas are unlikely to cross the sutures, this can happen and given the falx prevents subdural haematoma from crossing the midline, this must be an extradural haematoma. Subarachnoid blood would be described within the sulci and a creseteric high density at the vertex would not be a usual description for this.

stem: Image © Medical Exam Prep NextSubarachnoid haemorrhage A 49-year-old woman experiences a thunderclap headache and is brought to hospital with reduced GCS by her worried husband. She is found to have a subarachnoid haemorrhage.
prompt: What is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Technically trauma is the most common cause of subarachnoid haemorrhage but intracranial aneurysms are the most common cause, by a large margin, in non-traumatic cases.

The diagnostic pathway to investigate for intracranial aneurysms following a subarachnoid haemorrhage is:

CT angiogram

Invasive angiogram

Second invasive angiogram after approx 10 days.

Moyamoya disease is progressive occlusion/arteritis of the distal ICA causing the formation of a large network of tiny collateral vessels seen on angiogram as a ‘puff of smoke’. It is predominantly found in children or young adults and can present with subarachnoid haemorrhage.

Eclampsia is a hypertensive condition associated with pregnancy which can lead to subarachnoid haemorrhage.

stem: A 73-year-old lady is seen in a neurology clinic and undergoes an MRI scan of her brain as well as a nuclear medicine study. There is global cerebral atrophy and on the T2 weighted sequences there is blurring of the pars compacta in the midbrain. The nuclear medicine study shows reduced uptake in the posterior putamina bilaterally.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Parkinson's disease

Generalised cerebral atrophy occurs with Parkinson's disease but is a highly non-specific feature. There are, however, radiological findings in the midbrain which although subtle, are far more specific. Parkinson's disease occurs when there is neuronal loss in the substantia nigra, specifically the pars compacta of the substantia nigra. On a T2 weighted MRI image this appears as blurring of the intermediate signal intensity line which separates the two adjacent low intensity structures (these are the pars reticulata of the substantia nigra and the red nucleus).

A DAT scan (Dopamine Active Transfer) can be performed to confirm the diagnosis. This uses the radiopharmaceutical I-123 Ioflupane to image dopamine transporters in the brain. These are present in the highest concentrations in the putamina and caudate nuclei. In patients with true Parkinson's disease (as opposed to other similar conditions), there will be loss of uptake in the posterior putamen. This can be an asymmetric finding. Colloquially speaking the appearance of these areas on a normal patient resembles a comma and on a patient with Parkinson's disease they become more like full stops.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

There are two anatomical areas of the brain which are particular important in the field of neurodegenerative nuclear medicine.

The cingulate gyrus - next to the corpus callosum

The precuneus - between the cingulate sulcus and the parieto-occipital sulcus

Image © Medical Exam Prep

Pick's disease is also called frontotemporal dementia

As the name would suggest, the main abnormalities are seen in the frontal and temporal lobes, including the anterior part of the cingulate gyrus. These areas show low metabolism on PET studies. The posterior part of the cingulate gyrus and the precuneus are spared.

Lewy body dementia

A core clinical feature to this dementia is the fluctuant nature of the symptoms. Parkinsonian features can also develop although these are usually subsequent to the memory decline. Visual hallucinations are also a feature.  Radiologically there is a generalised decrease in cerebral volume (sparing the hippocampi). Temporo-parietal hypoperfusion on HMPAO Tc99m SPECT scanning is indicative of Lewy body dementia. Involvement of the occipital cortex, which is typically spared in Alzheimers disease, sets the two apart from one another on PET studies. The cingulate island sign has also been ascribed to Lewy body dementia, where there is preservation of metabolism in the  mid-posterior cingulate gyrus. If present, this is said to be specific for Lewy body dementia.

Alzheimer's disease

Neuronal loss with Alzheimer's disease occurs first in the mesial temporal lobe which can be seen as cerebral volume loss there on an MRI scan. To assess this region the scan should be viewed on a coronal sequence through the level of the pons, where the hippocampi can be seen clearly. Although medial temporal lobe atrophy is not remotely specific for Alzheimer's disease, it is almost always present. Early changes in metabolism can be seen in the posterior part of the cingulate gyrus and the precuneus on PET studies, as well as in the posterior temporal and parietal lobes. Classically there is sparing of specific areas such as the anterior cingulate gyrus the basal ganglia, and the occipital lobes.

Huntington’s disease

There are relatively few radiological manifestations of Huntington disease. The usual one described is atrophy of the heads of the caudate nuclei with consequential prominence of the adjacent lateral ventricle frontal horns with a ‘box’ like appearance. Various studies have been done to quantify the extent of this atrophy. On functional studies there can be low activity in the caudate nucleus head and putamen.

stem: A 50-year-old lady presents with a worst ever headache and has equivocal findings for a subarachnoid haemorrhage on CT scan two days later. She is unable to tolerate a lumbar puncture.
prompt: What would be the next best test to confirm the diagnosis?
explanation:
The diagnostic pathway to investigate for intracranial aneurysms following a subarachnoid haemorrhage is:

CT angiogram

Invasive angiogram

Second invasive angiogram after approx 10 days.

Although in this patient’s case the diagnosis of a subarachnoid haemorrhage has not been fully established, the presence of an aneurysm must be excluded.

Bear in mind that the correct answer may change if the wording of the questions is different. For example a DSA invasive angiogram would be the gold standard investigation for an aneurysm but is not usually done first; a CTA is therefore the next best test in the first instance.  Similarly an MRI scan would be the next best test to confirm the diagnosis of a subarachnoid haemorrhage but does not have a sufficiently low false negative rate to exclude an aneurysm. In the answers provided here, with the exception of the unenhanced CT, only angiographic options are available and hence this is not the correct answer.

stem: A 70-year-old man develops worsening conductive hearing loss which does not improve following ear syringing. He undergoes a CT scan and this shows non-dependant soft tissue density within the left middle ear. In addition the malleus and incus cannot be identified.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Cholesteatoma

Cholesteatomas (Acquired or congenital) are histolologically epidermoid cysts. On imaging the finding of non-dependant soft tissue and bony erosion within the middle ear is typical for a cholesteatoma.

There are two types of acquired cholesteatoma:

Pars flaccida (80%) – classically erodes the scutum and extends superiorly

Pars tensa (20%) – classically erodes the ossicles, extending medially

These refer to the two parts of the tympanic membrane from which they arise. There is a lot of overlap between the appearances of these two types; both can and do erode the ossicles. Absence of ossicular erosion is by no means specific for a pars flaccida cholesteatoma.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

In due course, if left unattended, a cholesteatoma will expand to fill the entire middle ear. Prior to this point they can be seen as non-dependant soft tissue within the middle ear. Dependant soft tissue within the middle ear suggests the presence of fluid or pus and the diagnosis of a middle ear infection. Once a cholesteatoma has filled the middle ear completely however no gas remains from which to discern dependency.

There are a number of theories as to how cholesteatomas arise. One theory is that following a perforation of the tympanic membrane entry of desquamated stratified keratinised squamous epithelium from the external auditory canal into the middle ear is permitted. There it adheres to the tympanic membrane and proliferates unrelentingly causing a soft tissue mass to form and eventually leading to bony erosion of the ossicles, scutum and/or other parts of the middle ear.

A congenital cholesteatoma behaves in a similar manner but is present from birth due to an aberrant location of a tiny island of keratinised squamous epithelium.

Cholesteatomas are difficult to manage as they have a high recurrence rate. Imaging has a significant role to play in the management of recurrent cholesteatomas; distinguishing recurrence from post-operative granulation tissue or fluid is important.

Diagnosis

Post-contrast sequences for recurrent cholesteatomas require a delay of around 45 minutes from giving the contrast to acquiring images as the granulation tissue is slow to take up contrast. This has obvious down-sides to any modern day busy MRI schedule. However since the management of post-operative granulation tissue and post-operative fluid is largely identical, namely expectant, it is not important to differentiate the one from the other. Thus findings on diffusion weighted sequences are the most important thing in post-operative cholesteatoma imaging.

Cholesterol granuloma

A cholesterol granuloma occurs as a sequela of recurrent bouts of otitis media. Haemorrhage within the middle ear leads to the formation of granulation tissue. On imaging this is seen as non-specification of the middle ear on CT. Bony changes can occur chronically with bony expansion, or displacement and even destruction of the ossicles. The signals characteristics on MRI are therefore important to distinguish it from a cholesteatoma. Whereas a cholesteatoma on MRI is isointense to brain parenchyma on T1, a cholesterol granuloma will show high signal in the middle ear on T1 due to the paramagnetic effects of methaemoglobin. On clinical examination the ENT surgeon may report a bulging blue tympanic membrane. This is classical. Dehiscence of the jugular bulb is an important differential diagnosis to exclude as this will also give a blue tympanic membrane on examination but the management is radically different!

Aberrant internal carotid artery

An aberrant internal carotid artery can cause a pulsatile mass in the middle ear. The question usually asked on this topic is slightly different and to do with the persistent stapedial artery and consequential aplastic foramen spinosum (anatomically – ‘the heel of the high-heeled shoe’). The stapedial artery in such cases arises from the internal carotid artery and runs through the stapes, becoming the middle meningeal artery (which usually arises from the external carotid artery and courses through the foramen spinosum).

stem: A 40-year-old man presents with a first seizure. His MRI scan shows a lesion in the left temporal lobe which is largely heterogenous in signal but has a distinct dark rim on the T2 weighted sequences.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The classical feature of a cavernoma (aka cavernous haemangioma) on MRI is the ‘popcorn’ appearance caused by a bright lobulated centre surrounded by a rim of hypointensity. Haemosiderin deposition causes the blooming artefact on susceptibility weighted sequences. It is perhaps slightly counterintuitive that there can be no enhancement on post-contrast CT scans, given the vascular nature of these lesions, however when we consider that flow within the lesion may be very slow then this makes a little more sense. Another important distinguishing feature from other lesions is the fact that, unlike metastases, there is no mass effect or oedema from these lesions, despite the fact that they can often present with seizures.

Cerebral amyloid angiopathy gives rise to micro-haemorrhages at the grey-white matter junction which are well seen as blooming artefact on susceptibility weighted sequences.

Parry-Romberg syndrome is a rare phakomatosis syndrome causing hemifacial atrophy. It can be associated with seizures.

stem: A 43-year-old man is brought to see his GP by his wife who is concerned that his behaviour has become increasingly erratic. He has also started making sudden movements which he says he cannot control. He is examined and referred onto a neurologist when the GP finds myoclonus. He undergoes an MRI scan. You suspect he may have Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.
prompt: Which of the following features is LEAST likely to be found? Select ONE answer only.
options: High FLAIR signal in the thalami
High T2 signal in the putamina
Restricted diffusion in the caudate nuclei
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which feature is LEAST likely to be found.

Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease

There are three types of this prion transmitted disease; the one linked to the BSE (bovine spongiform encephalopathy) epidemic of the late 1980s and 1990s, a rare familial variant, and finally a sporadic version which accounts for the vast majority of the cases. Clinically there is a rapidly progressive dementia with ataxia and myoclonus which should be the give-away feature even before imaging features are discussed. On MRI, the reported finding is of high T2/FLAIR signal in the basal ganglia bilaterally and symmetrically (particularly the putamen). The pulvinar sign is often described in association with cJD which describes high FLAIR signal in the pulvinar thalamic nuclei (called the hockey stick sign). Strangely the signal changes are a rare cause of restriction of diffusion, seen as bright areas on DWI. Important negatives for this condition are the lack of enhancement with contrast and the lack of white matter involvement (since the white matter is protected by its myelin sheath).

Image © Medical Exam Prep

stem: A 76-year-old man is admitted with cerebellar ataxia and spinothalamic tract involvement.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Lateral Medullary Syndrome (aka Wallenburg syndrome)

This is caused by either a vertebral artery occlusion or PICA occlusion.

This is a classic scenario for an exam question and is one of those syndromes that is far more common in the exam world than in the real world. There is a short list of slightly unusual symptoms any combination of which, in the exam context, should make you suspicious for this syndrome:

Cerebellar involvement – DANISH mnemonic as per medical school

Autonomic dysfunction – ipsilateral Horners syndrome, hiccoughs

Sensory symptoms – symptoms of sensory loss are common place in the stroke world but in this syndrome it is specifically loss of pain and temperature sensation in the ipsilateral face. Patients can also experience ipsilateral stabbing pains; pain symptoms are highly unusual in the stroke world and usually point to a different diagnosis.

Ipsilateral bulbar symptoms – dysphagia, dysarthria etc.

stem: A 33-year-old man has worsening unilateral nasal obstruction and epistaxis. His GP finds a polypoid mass in the left nasal cavity. A CT scan shows a soft tissue mass arising from the lateral wall of the nasal cavity with bony destruction of the medial wall of the maxillary sinus and heterogenous enhancement post-contrast.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: There are many different names for what is most commonly called an inverted papilloma. The classical history is given here. It is a vascular tumour most usually arising from the lateral wall of the nasal cavity but which characteristically causes destruction of the medial wall of the maxillary sinus.

stem: A 64-year-old man presents with acute onset limb weakness and sensory disturbance. MRI of the spine demonstrates an intramedullary lesion. Multiple sclerosis is considered in the differential diagnosis.
prompt: Which of the following MRI features is LEAST consistent with multiple sclerosis?
options: High T2 signal extending over one to two vertebral segments
explanation:
Multiple sclerosis commonly affects the spinal cord, most frequently the cervical region. Typical MS plaques are small, focal lesions that extend over one to two vertebral segments, involve less than half of the cross-sectional area of the cord, and demonstrate high T2 signal. The grey matter is usually spared, and the majority of patients have additional intracranial white matter lesions, which support the diagnosis.

Marked spinal cord expansion is not characteristic of multiple sclerosis. While very mild focal expansion may occasionally be seen, significant or diffuse cord expansion is more suggestive of alternative inflammatory conditions such as acute transverse myelitis or acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, where there is extensive inflammation and oedema.

Why not the other options?

Cervical spinal cord involvement: This is typical of multiple sclerosis and is the most commonly affected spinal region.

High T2 signal extending over one to two vertebral segments: This is a classic imaging feature of MS spinal cord plaques.

Associated intracranial white matter lesions: Approximately 90% of patients with MS have intracranial lesions, making this a supportive imaging feature.

Grey matter sparing: MS predominantly affects white matter tracts, with relative preservation of grey matter in spinal cord lesions.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents acutely unwell. Of note in her medical history she has been taking the oral contraceptive pill. She undergoes an unenhanced CT scan. Your colleague points out the sagittal sinus thrombosis which has caused her problems.
prompt: What is the best description of this diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
The empty delta sign is a post-contrast CT finding. Bilateral haemorrhages can be a secondary consequence to a sagittal sinus thrombosis which may point towards the diagnosis but the thrombosis itself is recognised by the empty delta sign on post-contrast CT.

Dense triangle sign pertains to the acute thrombus as it appears on an unenhanced CT scan.

On an MRI, static blood within the sagittal sinus gives rise to low signal on T1, although the thrombus itself is likely to be high in signal (if subacute in nature). Normally the sagittal sinus will appear as a flow void on T1w. Blooming artefact can be seen on T2* gradient echo sequences and is a strong indicatory of the diagnosis. Confusion can arise with time-of-flight 3D reformatted images and great care should be taken not to overdiagnose flow artefactas thrombosis. Careful reference should always be made to the source images and where there is doubt a CT venogram may be of more use.

The associated infarctions can often be haemorrhagic and parasagittal haemorrhages are very specific for a sagittal sinus thrombosis but subarachnoid haemorrhage is not likely to be related.

stem: A 22-year-old passenger involved in a road traffic collision. She makes an uneventful recovery but a week later complains of painful left eye swelling and a third nerve palsy. A CT head shows a prominent superior ophthalmic vein.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This is the classic presentation for a carotico cavernous fistula.

Moyamoya disease is progressive occlusion/arteritis of the distal ICA causing the formation of a large network of tiny collateral vessels seen on angiogram as a ‘puff of smoke’. It is predominantly found in children or young adults.

CADASIL (Cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy). The typical patient is a youngish adult (30-50s) with recurrent TIAs/strokes, and/or psychiatric symptoms such as depression, psychosis. The classical area affected is the anterior temporal lobes and external capsules.

stem: A 28-year-old who has had a diarrhoea and vomiting bug for the last week becomes increasingly lethargic and presents acutely with a seizure. An initial CT scan is reported as normal but an MRI scan shows high signal on FLAIR in the parasagittal cortex bilaterally.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Dehydration secondary to a diarrhoea and vomiting bug is a known cause of sagittal sinus thrombosis. The FLAIR high signal pertains to acute infarctions caused by the thrombosis. The other diagnoses listed are reasonable enough (to a greater or lesser extent) but do not account for the diarrhoea and vomiting bug being included in the history. A sagittal sinus thrombosis can present with seizures.

stem: You are reviewing the MRI scan of a 37-year-old lady who has a constellation of symptoms for which she is under review by neurology. Recently she has noticed a deterioration in her vision.
prompt: Which of the following would be the best sequence to examine for optic atrophy? Select ONE answer only.
explanation: Optic atrophy is difficult to pick up on an MRI scan unless you are specifically looking for it. On a T2 weighted coronal sequence (particularly a CISS, heavily T2 weighted sequence) scrolling through the optic nerves you may be able to appreciate that there is too much CSF surrounding the optic nerve, particularly if it is a unilateral finding.

stem: A 70-year-old man presents with acute confusion and deterioration in balance. A CT head shows a hyperdense lesion in the cerebellum. He is admitted to an acute medical ward and given steroids. After 4 days he undergoes another CT head scan following a fall on the ward. The lesion appears to have completely resolved.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Primary CNS lymphoma is known colloquially as the ‘vanishing tumour’ because the lesion seen initially can dramatically reduce following steroids. Slight hyperdensity on unenhanced CT scans is another classic feature for lymphoma.

stem: You are reviewing an MRI scan of a 9-year-old boy. The images are heavily degraded by motion artefact but, as well as a spinal tumour and posterior vertebral scalloping, in the brain you can also see some high T2 signal in the region of the optic chiasm. The pituitary gland appears normal. On the post-contrast sequences there seems to be some enhancement of the same area.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The optic nerves, are actually extensions of the central nervous system and are surrounded by glial cells and therefore develop gliomas (usually astrocytomas) as opposed to schwannomas which can develop around the other cranial nerves. Optic nerve gliomas cause kinking and fusiform enlargement of the optic nerve, which can be sufficient enough as to cause bony expansion of the optic canal. Historically, this feature could be picked up on a frontal radiograph of the face and is a favourite film for many 'experienced' radiologists.

Most patients are young, usually below the age of 10, and there is a strong association with Neurofibromatosis type 1.

Approximately 30% of patients with NF1 have an optic nerve glioma

Approximately 30% of patients with an optic nerve glioma have NF1.

The gliomas have variable signal intensities being broadly low in intensity on T1 and high in intensity on T2 with similarly variable enhancement with contrast. Signal abnormalities may also extend posteriorly to involve the optic chiasm and posterior optic tracts.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

stem: A 16-year-old man falls at home and sustains a right supraorbital facial laceration. He is reviewed in A&E and facial x-rays are requested at triage. The x-rays show complete opacification of the left maxillary sinus.
prompt: Which of the following is most likely as a differential diagnosis for this appearance? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
There is a differential diagnosis for opaque maxillary antrum. Wegener’s disease is included in it, but Churg-Strauss is not.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

stem: A 30-year-old woman had a routine blood test for insurance purposes which showed her to be thyrotoxic. She underwent an ultrasound scan of her thyroid which showed a normal sized thyroid with a focal lesion in the left lobe of the thyroid. She had recently had a respiratory infection in past few weeks.
prompt: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Dequervain thyroiditis is a lymphocytic infiltration of the thyroid with a likely viral aetiology. Thyroid nodules are very common and neither Follicular or Papillary carcinomas are associated with thyrotoxicity. Graves disease does also cause hyperthyroidism but there is usually diffuse enlargement of the thyroid. Hashimoto thyroiditis is usually associated with a hypothyroid state.

stem: A 10-year-old girl undergoes a trauma CT scan following an RTC. Among other things, the CT shows a lucent lesion in the mandible.
prompt: Which of the following is NOT a likely differential diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which option is NOT a likely differential diagnosis.

Brown tumours are a feature of hyperparathyroidism which is highly unlikely in a patient of this age.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

An ameloblastoma (aka adamantinoma) is classically described as having a soap-bubble appearance with cortical destruction. Ameloblastomas also erode the overlying teeth, a feature which is almost unique to lucent jaw lesions. They are more usually multilocular and show fluid-fluid levels on MRI. Although painless, they are locally aggressive.

An odontogenic keratocyst is a unilocular lucent lesion which demonstrates a smooth border. They can be indistinguishable from dentigerous cysts given that they are often associated with an unerupted tooth. They also have an association with Gorlin syndrome (BCCs).

A dentigerous cyst (aka follicular cyst) develops around the crown of an unerupted tooth. They are typically painless however.

Osteonecrosis of the jaw. This condition can be caused by bisphosphonate use or monoclonal antibody therapy. Clinically the bone of the jaw is exposed and radiologically there are aggressive bony features such as permeative destruction with periosteal reactions.

An odontoma is usually a small lucent lesion between the roots of the teeth. It can cause resorption of adjacent teeth however the description given is much more classical for an ameloblastoma.

stem: A 31-year-old lady with pre-eclampsia who delivered by normal vaginal delivery 2 days ago develops sudden onset cortical blindness. She has been receiving treatment for pre-eclampsia both before and after delivery. She is taken for a scan. There are bilateral parieto-occipital changes.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Classically PRES (posterior reversible leukoencephalopathy syndrome)presents as a visual disturbance in a pregnant or post-partum patient with pre-eclampsia and CT shows haemorrhages in the posterior fossa. The main underlying pathological process is vasogenic oedema. Technically PRES is not exclusive to pregnancy or the post-partum period, and often with a history (implied or provided) of pre-eclampsia. Other causes such as SLE or immunosuppression are also technically feasible. Cortical blindness is the classical symptom.

Sheehan syndrome is pituitary apoplexy due to hypovolaemic shock and can be consequential to delivery.

HELLP syndrome stands for Haemolysis, Elevated liver enzymes, and low platelet. It can cause DIC.

Sagittal sinus thrombosis would be a possible differential diagnosis and without any additional information as to the imaging findings it would only be the classical nature of the vignette described which would make PRES a better answer over sagittal sinus thrombosis.

Pick disease is fronto-temporal neurodegeneration presenting as dementia.

stem: A 22-year-old passenger involved in a road traffic collision. She makes an uneventful recovery but a week later complains of painful left eye swelling and a third nerve palsy.
prompt: Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following would increase the diagnostic certainty? Select ONE answer only.
options: Ill-defined enlargement and enhancement of the recti muscles
Multifocal diffuse high FLAIR signal foci bilaterally
Multiple flow voids in the basal ganglia
explanation:
This is the classic presentation for a carotico cavernous fistula. The fistula causes increased pressure within the superior ophthalmic vein which becomes prominent on CT or MRI scans.

Moyamoya disease is progressive occlusion/arteritis of the distal ICA causing the formation of a large network of tiny collateral vessels seen on angiogram as a ‘puff of smoke’. It is predominantly found in children or young adults.

CADASIL (Cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy). The typical patient is a youngish adult (30-50s) with recurrent TIAs/strokes, and/or psychiatric symptoms such as depression, psychosis. The classical area affected is the anterior temporal lobes and external capsules.

Thyroid eye disease - Bilateral proptosis

CADASIL - Multifocal diffuse high FLAIR signal foci bilaterally

Orbital pseudotumour - Ill-defined enlargement and enhancement of the recti muscles

Moyamoya disease - multiple flow voids in the basal ganglia

stem: A 53-year-old woman presents to her GP with painless lump in her right cheek region. Although it has been there for 10 months she reports it to be gradually increasing in size, and now measures 1.5cm. She would like it removed before her son’s wedding. On MRI it shows low intensity on T1, and high on T2 with multicystic appearance.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pleomorphic adenoma is the 80% condition. 80% are in found in the parotid gland, 80% of those are in the superficial lobe. Overall 80% are benign. They are slow growing and usually present as a painless lump. They show low T1 signal and high T2 signal on MRI – think of them as cystic in this regard although their mucoid matrix can give rise to hyperintense areas centrally.

A Warthin tumour is a differential diagnosis for a painless parotid lump but has an association with smokers. Different sources describe different imaging characteristics. A Warthin tumour usually presents as bilateral asymptomatic masses or possibly multiple unilateral masses.

Adenoid cystic carcinoma although also a slow growing process is far more common in the minor salivary glands than in the parotid. A particularly salient feature of this tumour is its propensity for peri-neural spread with paralysis of the recurrent laryngeal nerve seen as a classical feature.

stem: A 45-year-old man with HIV has an MRI which shows ring enhancing lesions and leptomeningeal enhancement.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Cerebral tuberculosis

A cerebral tuberculoma would be difficult to differentiate from toxoplasmosis or lymphoma. Classically though they are described as target lesions situated in the corticomedullary regions. They can calcify with treatment which would differentiate them well from other CNS infections. In this particular case the co-existent meningeal enhancement suggests the answer to beTB.

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML)

This is a JC virus mediated phenomenon which causes asymmetrical patchy white matter changes. These can be bilateral. The testable feature is involvement of the cortical U-fibres which separates it from HIV encephalopathy where the U-fibres are spared. The lack of a mass effect helps differentiate both PML and HIV encephalopathy from toxoplasmosis, cryptococcus and tuberculomas.

HIV encephalopathy

Separating HIV encephalitis from PML can challenging in real life. HIV encephalitis causes bilateral symmetrical white matter changes, seen as high T2 signal (The T1 sequences can be normal). There is also sparing of the subcortical U-fibres.

Cryptococcus

This is an opportunistic yeast-like fungus which therefore requires a degree of immunocompromise, typically AIDS. The cryptococcomas are non-enhancing low density lesions in the basal ganglia. These show as high signal on T2 sequences. A granulomatous meningitis can also occur. They can be differentiated from VR spaces on FLAIR where VR spaces will suppress (being CSF in content) whereas the mucoid cryptococcomas will not.

Toxoplasmosis

Toxoplasmosis is a more common finding in AIDS patients than lymphoma is, by a large margin. On MRI it is seen as multiple ring enhancing lesions, which can show haemorrhage particularly following treatment. One of the stronger differentiators between toxoplasmosis and lymphoma is the SPECT findings. This is sometimes termed ‘hypometabolic’ meaning the lesions do not demonstrate SPECT uptake. The table below gives some general features of the two conditions. There is however considerable overlap in the imaging features despite these broad trends.

stem: A 64-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department by his worried wife after becoming unwell at home. He has neurological signs and an MRI spine is requested which shows abnormalities within the spinal cord. You suspect he may have multiple sclerosis.
prompt: Which of the following is most consistent with multiple sclerosis? Select ONE answer only.
options: High T2 signal affecting 1-2 vertebral levels, grey matter involved, mild cord expansion
High T2 signal affecting 1-2 vertebral levels, grey matter spared, gross cord expansion
Low T2 signal affecting 1-2 vertebral levels, grey matter involved, no cord expansion
Low T2 signal affecting 3-4 vertebral levels, grey matter involved, no cord expansion
Low T2 signal affecting 3-4 vertebral levels, grey matter spared, cord expansion
explanation:
In general cord expansion is far more of a prominent feature in acute idiopathic transverse myelitis than MS however it can occur with MS, and it’s presence should certainly not exclude MS as a differential diagnosis.

Demyelination

Demyelination can occur due to multiple sclerosis, ADEM or as an idiopathic process.

Acute idiopathic transverse myelitis is a specific diagnosis of exclusion. There is inflammation of the spinal cord leading to bilateral motor, sensory and autonomic dysfunction. On imaging there is expansion of the central portion of the cord extending over multiple vertebral levels. The inflamed portion returns high signal on T2 weighted sequences. This occurs most commonly in the thoracic spine and importantly, should involve at least two thirds of the cross-sectional area of the cord at the affected level. This is in contrast to a multiple sclerosis plaque which involves under half of the cross-sectional area of the cord.

Multiple sclerosis can affect the spinal cord. Lesions tend to be smaller usually confined to 1-2 vertebral levels and affecting less than half of the cross-sectional area of the cord. There may be mild focal expansion of the cord, but this is a far less prominent feature than it is with idiopathic transverse myelitis. 90% of patients will have other intracranial lesions. The lesions of MS also return high T2 signal, like their intracranial counterparts. The cervical cord is most commonly affected. Gray matter can be affected (particularly in the spine) but it is white matter plaques which are by far the dominant feature.

ADEM (acute disseminated encephalomyelitis) is an autoimmune condition which occurs days-weeks following a viral infection. It largely affects the white matter of the brain, but the spinal cord can also be affected. Gray matter, particularly the basal ganglia are also often involved. It can occur at any age, but it is usually young children who are affected. Patients usually respond very well to steroid therapy and fortunately, most (90%) cases resolve without any residual deficit. On imaging, the affected areas return high T2 signal.

stem: A 12-year-old boy undergoes a CT head following a road traffic accident. This is otherwise normal except for a relatively small midline mass. This is mainly cystic but with some calcifications peripherally and is closely associated with pineal gland.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pineoblastomas classically occur in childhood but pineocytomas can occur at any age, adult or child.

Of pineal gland masses the more cystic a mass the less likely it is to be aggressive. On one end of the spectrum a pineoblastoma, as an aggressive mass, is most likely to be solid in nature. At the other end, pineal cysts are cystic and pineocytomas can be found somewhere in the middle. Of note though this is a spectrum of radiological appearance only, the histological differences are distinct. Similarly germinomas, as aggressive lesions, are also solid masses which engulf calcification. An arachnoid cyst on the other hand, will be entirely cystic. A dermoid would therefore be the most likely differential diagnosis here although no mention is made of any fat content and the question specifies an association with the pineal gland making a pineocytoma a more relevant answer.

stem: A 64-year-old gentleman is reviewed in clinic with a presentation of slowly progressive memory loss. The neurologist suspects he may have Alzheimer's disease and requests imaging to support the diagnosis.
prompt: Which is the most sensitive test if Alzheimer's disease is suspected?
explanation: Thallium is used in the differentiation of lymphoma and Toxoplasmosis (lymphoma demonstrating increased uptake). Although SPECT can be used in the diagnosis of Alzheimers disease, PET has been demonstrated as the most sensitive investigation for its detection, with bilateral temporoparietal hypoperfusion a classical finding. PET does have a poor specificity (false positive of 35%), but is a sensitive investigation for Alzheimers.

stem: A patient with known neurofibromatosis type two is found to have expansion and enhancement of the optic nerve sheath.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
There are a limited number of mainstream phakomatoses (NF1, NF2, Sturge-Weber, von Hippel-Lindau, and Tuberous sclerosis) and they all have fairly well definable features.

NF1 is the ‘peripheral’ version. There are plenty of cerebral features described however NF2 is almost exclusively cerebral and is therefore by comparison the ‘central’ version. There are many and varied skeletal manifestations of NF1.

Optic sheath neuromas are a feature of NF1 whereas meningiomas pertain to NF2.

Orbital pseudotumours purportedly can affect any part of the orbit, including the optic nerve sheath.

Graves disease does not affect the optic nerve, only the extra-ocular muscles (NB. Not the tendons).

Coats disease is a paediatric condition causing vascular malformations in the retina.

stem: A 54-year-old woman with a known history of breast cancer complains of a 5 month history of tongue weakness and difficulty manipulating food to the back of her throat. On examination she had right sided hemiatrophy of the tongue with deviation to the right on protrusion.
prompt: Which of the following is the most likely MRI imaging finding?
explanation:
Understanding cranial nerve anatomy is crucial. Damage to the hypoglossal nerve will cause the symptoms described. Cranial nerves IX, X and XI all pass through the jugular foramen and a metastasis here would give rise to Vernet syndrome (Vernet syndrome is the name for a collection of symptoms caused by pathology at the jugular foramen and consequentially affecting cranial nerves IX, X and XI ie. Loss of taste to the posterior third of the tongue, vocal cord paralysis, dysphasia, weakness of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius.). A metastasis to the tongue itself would present as an increase in tissue rather than hemiatrophy.

Carcinomatous meningitis most commonly derives from breast cancer, although lung cancer and melanoma are other possibilities. There is a classic description of ‘zuckerguss’ (sugar coating) where thin areas of subarachnoid enhancement follow the gyral convolutions. Leptomeningeal nodularity can also be seen.

stem: An 84-year-old man with a presentation of progressive memory loss undergoes an 18F-FDG PET study.
prompt: Reduced metabolism in which of the following areas would suggest a diagnosis of Alzheimers rather than Pick’s disease?
explanation: Pick’s disease is also known as Frontotemporal dementia, with these areas most severely affected. The temporoparietal region is classically affected in Alzheimer's, with involvement of the parietal region key for differentiation between the two.

stem: You are reviewing the CT scan of a 65-year-old heavy smoker who has presented to the Emergency Department following a fall. He is currently fit and well although his wife reports that he underwent a left lung lobectomy the previous year. He has been scanned under the NICE guidelines for the management of head injuries. There is no intracranial haemorrhage but you notice a destructive lesion involving the clivus. He goes on to have an MRI scan and the lesion returns low signal on both T1 and T2. There is enhancement on the post-contrast sequences.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Skull base metastasis and multiple myeloma

A myelomatous or metastatic process must always be kept in the differential diagnosis for a skull base mass however this would be less usual (although obviously not impossible) in a patient without a known primary site or known disease. On an MRI scan there will be loss of the high T1 marrow signal, as with other aggressive bony lesions, however the T2 signal is usually low or isointense.

Chondrosarcoma

In some cases there can be a lot of overlap between clival chondrosarcomas and clival chordomas. If a mass is determindly off-midline however, a chondrosarcoma is far more likely. These arise from tiny remnants of cartilage in the synchondrosis between the petrous temporal bone laterally and the occipital bone medially. Patients may present with cranial neuropathies which would be less usual for a chordoma when the nerves traversing the petrous temporal bone are affected. The abducens (CN VI) nerve is most often affected and CN III, V, VII and VIII may also be involved.

Intralesional calcifications take the form of the classic 'arcs and rings' seen with chondrosarcomas elsewhere in the body. On an MRI scan the signal characteristics can be similar to a chordoma with isointensity on T1 to brain parenchyma and high T2 signal. Chondrosarcomas are also likely to enhance with contrast.

Chordoma

These tumours are chiefly found in either the clivus or the sacrum. In the clivus they arise from the synchondrosis (primary cartilaginous joint) between the occipital bone inferiorly and the sphenoid bone superiorly. This is a midline joint and consequently the resultant chordoma is classically midline in nature. This helps to distinguish it from a chondrosarcoma which can appear very similar.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

Chordomas are aggressive, lobulated tumours which cause destruction of surrounding bone but lobulated mass effect on the pons with so-called 'thumbprinting' of the pons. Adjacent vascular structures, if not frankly invaded, are displaced. Posterior displacement of the basilar artery is a useful finding. Within the mass there are often calcific fragments representing either sequestered bone or dystrophic tumoral calcifications, or both. On an MRI scan the mass will be isointense to brain parenchyma on T1 and usually high in signal on T2. Most enhance with contrast.

stem: You are reviewing an MRI scan of a 45-year-old woman's brain. There is a left conal lesion.
prompt: Which of the following is NOT a likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which is NOT a likely diagnosis.

The differential diagnosis for orbital pathology is heavily anatomically based.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

Globe lesions are situated within the eyeball itself.

Retinoblastoma

Melanoma

Retinal detachment

Outside the globe there are three conditions which are included in all of the other orbital compartments namely sarcoidosis, pseudotumours and lymphoproliferative lesions.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

Lymphoproliferative disorders include leukaemias, lymphomas, and less aggressive collections of lymphoid tissue. The term is used particularly in head and neck radiology where histological diagnosis of such entities is key. Some masses on a CT scan can have a 'typical' appearance for a lymphoma but are actually only benign lymphoid hyperplastic tissue and thus the term lymphoproliferative disorder covers both entities accurately.

IgG4 related diseases are one of Radiology’s newest entities. They comprise a constellation of fibrotic conditions affecting virtually every part of the body, mediated by a subclass of Immunoglobulin called IgG4. Where one condition exists others may also be present. The more common of these include:

Orbital pseudotumour

Fibrosing mediastinitis

Reidel thyroiditis

Autoimmune pancreatitis

Sclerosing mesenteritis

Retroperitoneal fibrosis

stem: A 41-year-old man presents with a left Horner syndrome. Unfortunately owing to his pacemaker he is unable to undergo an MRI scan and the CT scan shows no obvious abnormality.
prompt: Which of the following is NOT a cause of a unilateral Horner syndrome? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:

stem: You are reviewing a CT scan showing a mass invading the foramen ovale.
prompt: What would be the most likely symptoms related to this?
options: Atrophy of the muscles of mastication
Loss of sensation over the maxilla
explanation:
This is an anatomy question pertaining to the contents of the foramen ovale which can be remembered with the following mnemonic.

O = otic ganglion

V = V3

A = Accessory meningeal artery

L = Lesser petrosal nerve

E = emissary veins

The sphenoid bone, with the foramen ovale labelled third from the bottom on the left (from Gray’s Anatomy)

Of these V3 supplies the muscles of mastication and hence invasion of the foramen ovale can be associated with atrophy of these muscles. V2 passes through the foramen rotundum and supplies the skin overlying the maxilla. Anosmia is the word used to describe the inability to smell and in this scenario would imply involvement of the cribriform plate and cranial nerve I. The seventh cranial nerve supplies the stapedius muscle which dampens loud noises.

stem: A 32-year-old lady is undergoing investigation for infertility. An MRI brain shows a 9mm well defined lesion, which is bright on the T1 weighted sequences, at the junction of the anterior and posterior pituitary.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The giveaway on this question is the location of the lesion; between the anterior and posterior pituitary, even in the absence of any other features which would be noted on the scan but which have not been provided and which would usually be used to eliminated any further doubt as to the diagnosis. Rathke's cleft cyst is mostly hyperbright on T2 although both T1 and T2 signal can vary depending on the exact content of the cyst. The lack of symptoms is also a key feature which points away from several of the other diagnoses given. Microadenomas are below 10mm in size, but 80% return low signal on T1 weighted sequences. Craniopharyngiomas are usually lobulated, often contain cystic and calcified areas. Pathologically the appearance of the cholesterol-rich components gives rise to a classical 'machinary oil' type appearance of craniopharyngiomas.

stem: A 43-year-old man is brought into A+E unconscious. There is no history available. During the course of his treatment he goes on to have an MRI scan which shows high T2/FLAIR signal in the basal ganglia, with corresponding low T1 signal to the same areas. The finding is bilateral and symmetrical.
prompt: What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
This question draws on the classic differential diagnosis of ‘basal ganglia signal changes’.

Poisoning

Impairment of mitochondrial function in the highly metabolically active basal ganglia classically causes high T2/FLAIR signal in a bilateral symmetrical fashion but the T1 is usually low in signal. Methanol, cyanide, and carbon monoxide can all cause this. Hopefully the history would be more helpful in establishing the diagnosis than that which has been provided here.

Neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation aka hallervorden-Spatz syndrome

The classic radiological feature which comes up here is the ‘eye of the tiger’ sign where there is low T2 signal in the globus pallidus due to iron accumulation. Confusingly the patient can go on to develop high T2 signal in these areas as gliosis develops. The typical patient will be a young woman with a family history of movement disorders presenting with rigidity or bradykinesia.

Behcet syndrome

Behcet syndrome is classically described as a triad of oral and genital ulcers associated with one of several ocular manifestations. Its effect on the CNS tends to be as meningoencephalitis or venous sinus thrombosis. In the basal ganglia, in some patients, it can cause lesions with low T1 signal and high T2 signal.

Toxoplasmosis

Infections derived from intrauterine transmission cause periventricular calcifications affecting the basal ganglia. Otherwise, in AIDS related toxoplasmosis the findings are more of multiple ring enhancing lesions.

Toxoplasmosis is a more common finding in AIDS patients than lymphoma is, by a large margin. On MRI it is seen as multiple ring enhancing lesions, which can show haemorrhage particularly following treatment. One of the stronger differentiators between toxoplasmosis and lymphoma is the SPECT findings. This is sometimes termed ‘hypometabolic’ meaning the lesions do not demonstrate SPECT uptake. The table below gives some general features of the two conditions. There is however considerable overlap in the imaging features despite these broad trends.
