A ring solitary ring enhancing lesion in the context of an AIDS patient should raise lymphoma as a strong possibility. Multiple lesions can and do occur however, making the distinction from toxoplasmosis challenging. Lymphoma is also part of the differential diagnosis for lesions that cross the corpus callosum and this can be a feature that separates it from toxoplasmosis, although is not a feature of exclusion. Similarly if haemorrhage has been seen associated with the lesion this is more a feature of toxoplasmosis but absence of haemorrhage does not exclude toxoplasmosis.

stem: A 73-year-old man presents with a quadrantanopia of the left eye.
prompt: What is the most likely cause for this? Select ONE answer only.
options: Branch retinal artery occlusion in the left eye
Left posterior cerebral artery (PCA) territory infarction
Right posterior cerebral artery (PCA) territory infarction
explanation:
A left branch retinal artery occlusion would give a left-sided hemianopia or quadrantanopia.

A right PCA infarction would give a homonymous defect (on the left).

A left PCA infarction might cause a homonymous defect (on the right).

Meningiomas are usually slow growing and incidentally discovered. This would be a very unusual presentation of a meningioma.

stem: A 43-year-old man presents with diplopia and is found to have a ‘down and out’ left eye. The right eye is normal. Left sided ptosis is also documented. He is discharged for outpatient review in ophthalmology by a junior doctor but re-presents a week later having collapsed at home. A CT head shows high attenuation in the subarachnoid space.
prompt: From where is the problem likely to have arisen?
explanation: The third cranial nerve runs parallel to the posterior communicating artery and dives under the posterior cerebral artery. The association between PCOM or PCA pathology and third nerve palsy signs is a classical one from an exam perspective. It will be an ipsilateral pathology because the Oculomotor nerve is post-ganglionic at this point. The other possible answers here involve the basilar artery but the ICA/PCOM answer is the more classical for the scenario described.

stem: A 78-year-old man with a known head and neck SCC is found to have a palpable lymph node at level IIb.
prompt: From where is this most likely to have arisen?
explanation:
Other sites that could also be correct would be the oral cavity, tongue or nasopharynx.

Parotid tumours do also drain to level II but an SCC of the parotid is far less likely than a laryngeal SCC. An SCC of the vocal cords would drain to level III.

Scalp SCCs drain to the parotid gland; metastatic disease in or around the parotid is a known presentation of metastasis of a prior scalp SCC.

stem: A 64-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department by his worried wife after becoming unwell at home. He has neurological signs and an MRI spine is requested which shows abnormalities within the spinal cord. You suspect he may have multiple sclerosis.
prompt: Which of the following is LEAST accurate in the diagnosis of multiple sclerosis? Select ONE answer only.
options: A CT scan is likely to be normal to begin with
Acute lesions are likely to restrict diffusion
Infratentorial foci are more common in children than adults
Involvement of the corpus callosum is common
Ring enhancing lesions suggest acute pathology
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which answer is LEAST accurate in the diagnosis of multiple sclerosis.

Some acute lesions can restrict diffusion however this feature is better associated with subacute or chronic lesions.

Demyelination

Demyelination can occur due to multiple sclerosis, ADEM or as an idiopathic process.

Acute idiopathic transverse myelitis is a specific diagnosis of exclusion. There is inflammation of the spinal cord leading to bilateral motor, sensory and autonomic dysfunction. On imaging there is expansion of the central portion of the cord extending over multiple vertebral levels. The inflamed portion returns high signal on T2 weighted sequences. This occurs most commonly in the thoracic spine and importantly, should involve at least two thirds of the cross-sectional area of the cord at the affected level. This is in contrast to a multiple sclerosis plaque which involves under half of the cross-sectional area of the cord.

Multiple sclerosis can affect the spinal cord. Lesions tend to be smaller usually confined to 1-2 vertebral levels and affecting less than half of the cross-sectional area of the cord. There may be mild focal expansion of the cord, but this is a far less prominent feature than it is with idiopathic transverse myelitis. 90% of patients will have other intracranial lesions. The lesions of MS also return high T2 signal, like their intracranial counterparts. The cervical cord is most commonly affected. Gray matter can be affected but it is white matter plaques which are by far the dominant feature, thus 'sparing' of the gray matter is often used to distinguish MS from ADEM.

ADEM (acute disseminated encephalomyelitis) is an autoimmune condition which occurs days-weeks following a viral infection. It largely affects the white matter of the brain, but the spinal cord can also be affected. Gray matter, particularly the basal ganglia are also often involved. It can occur at any age, but it is usually young children who are affected. Patients usually respond very well to steroid therapy and fortunately, most (90%) cases resolve without any residual deficit. On imaging, the affected areas return high T2 signal.

stem: A gentleman is seen in a neurology outpatient clinic with complaints of progressive memory loss and some movement problems. He subsequently undergoes an MRI scan of his brain. You suspect he may have a neurodegenerative condition.
prompt: Which SINGLE one of the following findings is correctly matched to its condition?
options: Blurring of structures in the midbrain - Alzheimer's disease
Disproportionate involvement of the hippocampi - Parkinson's disease
Sparing of the hippocampi - Lewy body dementia
explanation:
Lewy body dementia

A core clinical feature to this dementia is the fluctuant nature of the symptoms. Parkinsonian features can also develop although these are usually subsequent to the memory decline. Visual hallucinations are also a feature. Radiologically there is a generalised decrease in cerebral volume (sparing the hippocampi). Temporo-parietal hypoperfusion on HMPAO Tc99m SPECT scanning is indicative of Lewy body dementia. Involvement of the occipital cortex, which is typically spared in Alzheimer's disease, sets the two apart from one another on PET studies. The cingulate island sign has also been ascribed to Lewy body dementia, where there is preservation of metabolism in the mid-posterior cingulate gyrus. If present, this is said to be specific for Lewy body dementia.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease

There are three types of this prion transmitted disease; the one linked to the BSE (bovine spongiform encephalopathy) epidemic of the late 1980s and 1990s, a rare familial variant, and finally a sporadic version which accounts for the vast majority of the cases. Clinically there is a rapidly progressive dementia with ataxia and myoclonus which should be the give-away feature even before imaging features are discussed. On MRI, the reported finding is of high T2/FLAIR signal in the basal ganglia bilaterally and symmetrically (particularly the putamen). The pulvinar sign is often described in association with cJD which describes high FLAIR signal in the pulvinar thalamic nuclei (called the hockey stick sign). Strangely the signal changes are a rare cause of restriction of diffusion, seen as bright areas on DWI. Important negatives for this condition are the lack of enhancement with contrast and the lack of white matter involvement (since the white matter is protected by its myelin sheath).

Huntington disease

There are relatively few radiological manifestations of Huntington disease. The usual one described is atrophy of the heads of the caudate nuclei with consequential prominence of the adjacent lateral ventricle frontal horns with a ‘box’ like appearance. Various studies have been done to quantify the extent of this atrophy.

Alzheimer's disease

The radiological findings of this well known disease are diffuse sulcal and ventricular enlargement. There is a disproportionate effect to the anterior temporal lobes, hippocampi and sylvian fissures with sparing of the sensorimotor and visual cortices, thalami and cerebellum.

Parkinson's disease

Generalised cerebral atrophy occurs with Parkinson's disease but is a highly non-specific feature. There are, however, radiological findings in the midbrain which although subtle, are far more specific. Parkinson's disease occurs when there is neuronal loss in the substantia nigra, specifically the pars compacta of the substantia nigra. On a T2 weighted MRI image this appears as blurring of the intermediate signal intensity line which separates the two adjacent low intensity structures (these are the pars reticulata of the substantia nigra and the red nucleus).

Separating HIV encephalopathy from PML can challenging in real life. HIV encephalopathy causes bilateral symmetrical white matter changes, seen as high T2 signal (The T1 sequences can be normal). This is a JC virus mediated phenomenon which causes asymmetrical patchy white matter changes. These can be bilateral. The testable feature is involvement of the cortical U-fibres which separates it from HIV encephalopathy where the U-fibres are spared. stem: You are reviewing a CT scan of the temporal bone from an ENT outpatient clinic. The vestibular aqueduct is very small.
prompt: What is the most likely consequence?
explanation:
Meniere disease is an idiopathic condition of the inner ear structures giving rise to symptoms principally of vertigo and tinnitus. Radiologically the vestibular aqueduct is seen to be either small or not visible.

Pendred syndrome – this is an inherited cause of sensorineural hearing loss. It is associated with a large vestibular aqueduct.

Mondini syndrome – this is a specific malformation of the cochlea where there are only 1.5 turns instead of 2.5. It is associated with a large vestibular aqueduct.

Cochlear hypoplasia – some cochlear hypoplasias can be associated with large vestibular aqueducts.

Tullio phenomenon – this refers to vertigo and nystagmus induced by loud noises. It is caused by superior semicircular canal dehiscence.

stem: A 64-year-old man presents with an acute left third cranial nerve palsy and a headache. A CT scan shows subarachnoid haemorrhage. Most of the blood is concentrated around the quadrigeminal cistern.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
The quadrigeminal cistern sits behind the midbrain, just above the cerebellum. The ambient cisterns run around the posterolateral aspect of the midbrain on either side joining to the interpeduncular cistern and is essentially an extension of the quadrigeminal cistern.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

The posterior communicating artery (PCom) runs between the internal carotid artery and the posterior cerebral artery. The PComs sit anterior to the midbrain and blood from an aneurysm of the PCom will extend into the interpeduncular cistern, ambient cisterns and thereby to the quadrigeminal cistern.

The third cranial nerve runs parallel to the posterior communicating artery and dives under the posterior cerebral artery. The association between PCOM or PCA pathology and third nerve palsy signs is classical. If a patient has a painful ptosis, a PCOM aneurysm should be considered. It will be an ipsilateral pathology because the Oculomotor nerve is post-ganglionic at this point.

The diagnostic pathway to investigate for intracranial aneurysms following a subarachnoid haemorrhage is:

CT angiogram

Invasive angiogram

Second invasive angiogram after approx 10 days.

An MRI is performed and you suspect there may be a spinal cord infarction.
prompt: Which of the following is LEAST consistent with a spinal cord infarction?
options: High T2 signal extending over three vertebral levels
High T2 signal in the adjacent vertebral body
Inverted-V shape of high T2 signal in the posterior columns
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which is LEAST consistent with a spinal cord infarction.

Spinal cord infarction

The vascular supply to the spinal cord is derived largely from the vertebral arteries or intercostal arteries with one longitudinal running anterior spinal cord artery and two small longitudinally running posterior spinal cord arteries.

The artery of Adamkiewicz is a particularly large segmental artery supplying the anterior spinal artery from around the level of T9. It is responsible for most of the spinal cord blood supply for the lumbar spinal cord. Damage during aortic surgery or trauma can result in spinal cord infarction.

Usually any vascular insult results in a reasonably rapid onset of symptoms. Spinal cord infarctions are no exception. Often more than one vertebral level is affected.

An MRI will showT2 hyperintensity of at least the central grey matter (if not the whole cross-section of the cord) due to oedema. As with intracranial infarctions there will be restriction of diffusion on the DWI sequences.

Particularly in the thoracic spine, the adjacent vertebral body  may also lose its blood supply and undergo infarction.

Subacute combined degeneration

This is a curious condition which can be subtle to detect. A deficiency of vitamin B12 (usually caused by malabsorption) leads to degeneration within the dorsal columns of the cord. The dorsal columns carry nerves responsible for position and vibration sense and as such patients present with loss of these senses as well as sensory ataxia (balance significantly deteriorates when the patients eyes are shut thereby excluding visual stabilisation as opposed to sensory stabilisation), and hyperreflexia.

On an MRI scan there will be (if the resolution allows), a longitudinal line of high T2 signal within the cord on sagittal sequences, and often a characteristic 'inverted-V' shape of high T2 signal on axial sequences. In some cases the 'V' is clearly seen and in others it is harder to appreciate and the finding is more of high T2 signal bilaterally and symmetrically in the region of the posterior columns.

stem: You are reviewing the HMPAO images from a patient who presented to his GP with a gradual decline in memory.
prompt: Involvement of which of the following regions of the brain is INCORRECTLY matched to its diagnosis?
options: Precuneus and cingulate gyrus - Alzheimer’s disease
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which region is INCORRECTLY matched.

Functional imaging in dementia

Tc99m-HMPAO SPECT and 18F-FDG PET produce very similar patterns when used to image patients with cognitive decline however the latter is considered to have a greater sensitivity and specificity and is therefore preferred.

Two structures bear particular importance in the imaging of dementia; the precuneus and the cingulate gyrus. Both are best appreciate on sagittal views.

Precuneus: The precuneus is located on the medial surface of each hemisphere, in the posterior parietal lobe. It has functions in motor planning, working memory and also connections to the visual pathways.

The cingulate gyrus: The cinculate gyrus is also located on the medial side of each hemisphere and runs anteroposteriorly just above the corpus callosum. The cingulate gyrus has complex functions to do with learning, emotional response and memory.

Alzheimer's disease

The radiological findings of this well known disease are diffuse sulcal and ventricular enlargement. There is a disproportionate effect to the anterior temporal lobes, hippocampi and sylvian fissures with sparing of the sensorimotor and visual cortices, thalami and cerebellum. Functional studies (Tc-HMPAO SPECT or F-18 FDG PET) show reduced uptake in the precuneus, posterior cingulate gyrus, frontal and temporoparietal lobes but with characteristic sparing of the sensorimotor cortex and basal ganglia bilaterally. Importantly there is also sparing of the occipital lobes, which helps differentiate it from Lewy body dementia where the occipital lobes are involved. Other differences between the two conditions are seen with specific dopamine transporter agent imaging techniques.

Lewy body dementia

A core clinical feature to this dementia is the fluctuant nature of the symptoms. Parkinsonian features can also develop although these are usually subsequent to the memory decline. Visual hallucinations are also a feature.  Radiologically there is a generalised decrease in cerebral volume (sparing the hippocampi). Temporo-parietal hypoperfusion on HMPAO Tc99m SPECT scanning is indicative of Lewy body dementia. Involvement of the occipital cortex, which is typically spared in Alzheimers disease, sets the two apart from one another on PET studies. The cingulate island sign has also been ascribed to Lewy body dementia, where there is preservation of metabolism in the  mid-posterior cingulate gyrus. If present, this is said to be specific for Lewy body dementia.

stem: A 40-year-old man presents with a neck lump. On ultrasound there is a 2cm thyroid lump with punctuate calcification.
prompt: What would you advise next?
explanation:
The U-classification of thyroid nodules was developed to guide the further investigation of thyroid nodules seen on ultrasound. The classification allows the operator to grade nodules numerically rather than requiring a diagnosis which remains the remit of the histopathologist for thyroid cancers. The information in the question points in the direction of Papillary carcinoma of the thyroid however it is the ‘U5’ features within the U-classification which mean that the next stage should be tissue acquisition. This can be either via FNA or core biopsy and (broadly speaking) if the nodule can be seen on ultrasound, it can be sampled under ultrasound guidance. The next stage would usually be discussion at the MDT and further imaging can be decided there.

prompt: What is the next best investigation? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Even in a patient without a history of APCKD, the emphasis of this scenario is on locating or disproving the presence of an aneurysm (or other cause) as the cause of the subarachnoid haemorrhage. This takes precedence over exerting effort disproving the SAH itself, since a symptomatic aneurysm requires urgent treatment to avoid potentially catastrophic consequences.

The diagnostic pathway to investigate for intracranial aneurysms following a subarachnoid haemorrhage is:

CT angiogram

Invasive angiogram

Second invasive angiogram after approx 10 days

Although in this patient’s case the diagnosis of a subarachnoid haemorrhage has not been fully established, the presence of an aneurysm must be excluded.

A lumbar puncture to exclude meningitis would not be an unreasonable choice, but the thunderclap history is far more classical for a subarachnoid haemorrhage. The reality is the patient would get both the lumbar puncture (also for xanthochromia) and the CTA at some point, but from an exam perspective we are looking to find an aneurysm to explain her symptoms whereas meningitis is merely one of the top differential diagnoses. Finding xanthochromia on a lumbar puncture might diagnose the subarachnoid haemorrhage but doesn’t rule out an aneurysm. A catheter angiogram would be the gold standard investigation for an aneurysm but is not usually done first; a CTA is therefore the best investigation in the first instance. Similarly an MRI scan would be the next best test to confirm the diagnosis of a subarachnoid haemorrhage but does not have a sufficiently low false negative rate to exclude an aneurysm.

A secondary consideration is the poor renal function that a patient with APCKD is likely to have. In an emergency situation such as a SAH this takes second place however. Dialysis may be necessary if iodinated contrast is used and the risks/benefits would obviously have to be discussed with the patient themselves, if sufficiently alert, in a real case.

stem: You are reviewing the MRI scan of a 37-year-old lady who has a constellation of symptoms for which she is under review by neurology. Recently she has noticed a deterioration in her vision.
prompt: Which of the following is NOT a cause of optic atrophy? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Optic atrophy is difficult to pick up on an MRI scan unless you are specifically looking for it. On a T2 weighted coronal sequence (particularly a CISS, heavily T2 weighted sequence) scrolling through the optic nerves you may be able to appreciate that there is too much CSF surrounding the optic nerve, particularly if it is a unilateral finding.

Myasthenia Gravis is a muscular condition where there is increased fatiguability of all muscles. The effect can be seen with the ocular muscles particularly well. The optic nerves are unaffected.

Glaucoma occurs when the pressures within the eye are greater than normal. This increased pressure damages the optic nerve and, without treatment, can lead to irreversible optic neuropathy and thereafter optic atrophy.

Optic neuritis is inflammation of the optic nerve and can occur in the context of multiple sclerosis, or in isolation. Like glaucoma, it can progress to neuropathy and atrophy.

Neuromyelitis optica is a specific condition, with similarities to multiple sclerosis, where there is optic neuritis. Usually patients have enlarged optic nerves, but chronic damage leads to optic atrophy.

Parinaud syndrome is the name given to the symptoms caused by compression of the tectal plate. These are highly testable and the main feature is paralysis of vertical gaze.

Tullio phenomenon refers to vertigo and nystagmus induced by loud noises. It is caused by superior semicircular canal dehiscence.

Gradenigo syndrome refers to the triad of otitis media, retro-orbital pain and Abducens nerve palsy which results from an abscess in the aerated petrous apex – petrous apicitis.

Eye of the tiger sign refers to low T2 signal in the globus pallidus due to iron accumulation. This is associated with Hallervoden-Spatz syndrome, with symptoms of spasticity and progressive dementia.

Lateral medullary syndrome aka Wallenburg syndrome is caused by infarction of the lateral medulla oblongata, supplied by the PICA. This causes a characteristic collection of symptoms including ipsilateral stabbing facial pain with contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation and ipsilateral bulbar weakness.

stem: A 53-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of occipital headache. A CT of her head demonstrates hydrocephalus, subarachnoid haemorrhage and a frontal lobe (gyrus rectus) haematoma.
prompt: What is the most likely site for the responsible aneurysm?
explanation:
An anterior choroidal artery is a tiny branch of the internal carotid artery which runs posteriorly and accounts for 4% of aneurysms.

The pericallosal artery is the distal continuation of the anterior cerebral artery, coursing superiorly over the corpus callosum.

Aneurysms at branch points such as at the anterior communicating artery have a much higher risk of rupture.

stem: You are reviewing the MRI scan of a 45-year-old woman's brain who has recently been diagnosed with an orbital haemangioma.
prompt: Which of the following is NOT a feature of an orbital haemangioma?
explanation:
Please note the question asks which option is NOT a feature.

Vascular malformations

There have, historically, been a few different classification systems used to organise vascular anomalies. The most straightforward of these is detailed below.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

Orbital cavernous haemangiomas

These are slow growing, solid vascular masses, similar in nature to other cavernous haemangiomata around the rest of the body. They enhance with contrast and dynamic contrast sequences, if performed, can show the usual gradual 'filling in' phenomenon. Orbital haemangiomas will displace surrounding structures, rather than invading them and pressure effects on adjacent bone can lead to remodelling. On T1 weighted images a dark pseudocapsule may be seen but otherwise the lesion will be isointense to muscle. On T2 weighted images haemangiomas are high in signal.

You suspect he may have a cholesterol granuloma.
prompt: Which of the following is LEAST consistent with this diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which is the LEAST likely diagnosis.

Since the lesion is high in T2 signal, high ADC values may be caused by the T2 shine through effect. Certainly, correlation with the DWI appearances would be needed to draw further conclusions and these have not been provided.

A cholesterol granuloma contains both cholesterol crystals and blood products (hence is bright on T1) whereas a cholesteatoma is isointense to brain parenchyma on T1 and can apparently be seen clinically as a whitish mass behind the tympanic membrane. Clinically a cholesterol granuloma may be described as causing a blue tympanic membrane. The absence of pulsatile tinnitus can help distinguish it from a glomus tympanicum.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

An aberrant internal carotid artery can cause a pulsatile mass in the middle ear. The question usually asked on this topic is slightly different and to do with the persistent stapedial artery and consequential aplastic foramen spinosum (anatomically – ‘the heel of the high-heeled shoe’). The stapedial artery in such cases arises from the internal carotid artery and runs through the stapes, becoming the middle meningeal artery (which usually arises from the external carotid artery and courses through the foramen spinosum).
